answer: Four objects work together. `add`/`set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>]` sets the limit on that one port instance; direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all), location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all), and the threshold values are uint64/int64/decimal64 or na/not-supported (default na). `set pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter>` does the same per resource type and its show also returns default-low-threshold, default-high-threshold, min-value and max-value, e.g. `set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200`. Reporting only happens if `set pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> tca-supervision true` (with data-supervision true); pm-profile-entry default-tca-supervision decides that for newly created resources. `show pm-parameter-errored-seconds` confirms the parameter's units and type (counter or gauge). The raised TCA is read with `show alarm`.

Enable the protocol and authentication: `set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true` (defaults ntp-enabled true, ntp-auth-enabled false, assignment-method both, from manual, dhcp, both). Create the key: `add ntp-key-<key-id> key-type <value> key-value <value> [is-trusted <value>]`, key-id 1..65534, key-type sha-1, aes-cmac, sha-256 or md5, key-value a string of 8..40 characters, is-trusted default false, e.g. `add ntp-key-2 is-trusted true key-type sha-1 key-value Infinera`. Bind it to the server: `add ntp-server-<ip-address> auth-key-id <id>`; ip-address may be IPv4, IPv6 or a DNS name, origin is manual (default) or dhcp, admin-state defaults to unlock. Check it with `show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>`: auth-status (ok, yes, bad, none), reach (377 means all recent probes answered), stratum, when, poll, delay, offset, jitter and condition (sys.peer, reject, candidate). `show ntp ntp-active-server` names the server in use and `show clock time-source` should read ntp.

Traffic is moved with `protection-switch [-f] [operation-type=]<value> [switch-target=]<value> [protection-group=]<value>`, Operational mode only. operation-type is force, lockout, manual or release; switch-target is not needed for release and lockout. Example: `protection-switch protection-group-test operation-type=force switch-target=protection`. The controller is moved with `manual-switchover [-f] [resource=]<value>`, where resource is the AID of the object to switch, e.g. `manual-switchover card-1-3` (G42), `card-1-5` (G32), `card-1-12` (G34c); it prompts 'Controller will switchover and connection to the management interface will be lost. Do you want to continue? [y/n]'. A persistent switch request can also be configured on the group with `set protection-group-<name> pg-request`, values clear (default), manual-to-working, manual-to-protection, forced-to-working, forced-to-protection, protection-lockout and exercise (bidirectional SNCP only).

`set-time` is only applicable when time-source is manual, that is when NTP is not enabled, so an active NTP synchronisation is what rejects your manual setting. Run `show clock` and read time-source (ntp or manual, default manual), current-time, universal-time, timezone (default Universal-Time-Coordinated), DST-active and last-time-jump, which reports jumps in the form '<time1> to <time2>' and ignores jumps of less than 10 seconds. Then `show ntp` for ntp-enabled (default true), ntp-auth-enabled, ntp-active-server and assignment-method, and `show ntp-server-status-<ip-address>` for reach, stratum, offset, jitter, auth-status and condition. If you genuinely want manual time, disable NTP first and use the ISO 8601 form: `set-time 2021-02-06T11:16:58Z`, or a non-UTC offset such as `set-time 2021-04-01T18:46:44+03:00`. The `time` command reports the current time using the system configured timezone.

`show ne` identifies the node: ne-id, ne-name (default '1830 GX'), ne-type (G30 or G40), node-type (ILA, OADM, XPDR), l0-mode-op, ne-vendor, ne-site, ne-location, clli, node-controller-chassis-name (default 1), contact, plus equipment-discovery-ready, alarm-report-ready and recover-mode. `status` (or `status system`) is a dashboard of NE properties, SW labels, uptime, management IP, alarm counts per severity and equipment counts; `status equipment [<chassis-id>]` lists chassis, cards and toms with temperature, power and oper-state. Contents also come from `show equipment`, `show slot` (supported-type, installed-type, current-equipment) and `show inventory`. The cost of the reboot: `restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>]` - with no resource-id it restarts the active controller card, and type defaults to warm. cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting; warm reboots the processor and is non service affecting; shutdown gracefully shuts the card down. Connectivity returns within five minutes. Sub-components are listed with `show card resources`.

Slot 2 of chassis 1 is `slot-1-2`, addressed as `slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>` and showing AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment. The card fitted there is `card-1-2` (`card-<name>`). Hanging off the card are `port-1-2-<port-name>` (`port-<card-name>-<port-name>`), and under each port the function object: `comm-eth-1-2-<port>` for communication ports, `usb-1-2-<port>` for USB, or the pluggable `tom-1-2-<port>` (`tom-<card-name>-<port-name>`; adding a TOM auto-creates the tributary port termination point and deleting the TOM deletes it). Also under the card: `capabilities-1-2`, `sub-component-1-2/<sub-component-name>`, `serdes-1-2-<port>/<serdes-name>`, `current-fw-1-2/<fw-name>` and `led-<location>/<name>`. FRU inventory for the pluggable itself is `show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>`, e.g. `show inventory-1-3-1`, returning hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class (1..8), actual-max-power-draw and fw-status.

What a model can do: `show supported-card-<card-type>` gives node-type-compatibility (all, ILA, OADM), sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width (na, single-slot, double-slot, half-slot, triple-slot), card-height in RUs, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support (default general-c-band), max-power-draw in W, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support (no, yes-with-auto-sensing-baud-rate, yes-with-fixed-baud-rate), default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config (default false), supported-bands (default standardC-band) and supported-features. Related capability views are `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>`, `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name>` and `show tom-type-<tom-type>`. What the card in your chassis is actually doing: `show card-<name>` with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, category, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name, max-power-draw, power-profile, last-reboot-reason, last-reboot-time, parent-card, subcard-list, admin-state (default unlock), oper-state and avail-state. `show capabilities-<name>` reports the installed card's own capabilities.

The chain of stated pre-conditions is: `add ospf-instance-<instance-id> router-id <dotted-quad> [version <ospfv2|ospfv3>] [router-id-mode <manual|use-loopback>]`, instance-id 0..255, version default ospfv2, router-id-mode default use-loopback - and if router-id-mode is use-loopback the ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. Then `add ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>` (ospf-area-type normal); the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Then `add ospf-interface-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>`; the instance and area must be present, and ospf-if-name is a leafref to an existing interface if-name. Defaults there: enable true, hello-interval 10 (1..32767 s), router-dead-interval 40 (4..65535 s), retransmission-interval 5, transmit-delay 1, ospf-cost 10, priority 1, ospf-if-routing auto. Progress is read with `show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id>`: state runs down, init, 2-way, exstart, exchange, loading, full, with role drother, dr, bdr or ptp. Its pre-condition is that the neighbor NEs also have instance, area and interface configured and are properly connected with DCN interface bridges; the neighbor entry is deleted when the OSPF interface goes down. `clear ospf <instance>` removes and restarts an instance.

Per controller card use `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>` where location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> (for example 1-1 and 1-3) and swload-state is active, inactive or installable, e.g. `show software-load-1-5/active`. It returns swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status (validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed or timeout), swload-information, swload-activation-type (direct, warmstart, coldstart), swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. The individual pieces are `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` with state installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), version and description, and one level deeper `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`. Firmware bundled with that load is `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`; versions of the same firmware can differ per equipment-type.

Per port and direction use `show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/ingress`: total-frames-out counts LLDP frames transmitted through the port, total-frames-in counts frames received, and error-frames, total-discarded-frames, total-discarded-tlvs, total-unrecognized-tlvs and total-ageouts (all default 0) plus last-change-time and last-clear-time tell you why nothing was learned. The egress direction is not supported, and all counters for a port freeze whenever lldp-admin-status is disabled on it. `show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/ingress` shows what was actually discovered - chassis-id and chassis-id-subtype, port-id, port-description, system-name, system-description, capabilities, age, last-update and ttl - and this data is kept until the port is decommissioned or manually cleared. `show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port>` shows what this node advertises: chassis-id is the chassis serial number, port-id the port AID, port-description the port name and system-name the NE name. Globally, `show lldp hold-on-timer` (default 900 seconds) is applied when a neighbor sends no TTL TLV; `clear topology` removes learned neighbor information.

`show slot`, or `show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>` / `show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>`, lists every holder with AID, supported-type, installed-type, oper-state, avail-state and current-equipment; an unpopulated position shows the supported-type, an empty installed-type and current-equipment '---'. FRU detail for what is installed is `show inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>` (or `show inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>` for a pluggable): hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes and fw-status (not-applicable, current, not-current, unavailable). Firmware level is `show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name>`, giving fw-version, expected-fw-version and fw-status (current, not-current, unavailable) - for example current-fw-1-1/CORE_BOOT 0x20 against expected 0x28 shows not-current. Equipment detected but not yet accepted by the Node Controller appears under `show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>`.

`show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information]` lists the downloaded manifests; manifest-signature is a hex string up to 1024 and downloaded-on is a YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ timestamp. The contents are `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, where state is installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown) - that is the per-piece install result. Firmware carried in the package is `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`, and packaged FRU data per equipment type is `show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>`. To compare against what is really on the node, use `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>` and `show sw-subcomponent-...` (same installed/not-installed/installation-failed/unknown states) and `show packaged-fw`; overall installation progress across versions is `show upgrade-status`.

Alarm severity defaults come from the alarm-severity-profile, a system-managed object that cannot be deleted: `set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <critical|event|major|minor|not-reported|warning>` and `show alarm-severity-profile`. The per-alarm entry inside it is `alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location>`, with direction na, ingress or egress and location na, near-end or far-end; show also returns service-affecting (indeterminate, sa, nsa, sa-nsa). Examples: `set alarm-severity-entry-OTU2/TIM/ingress/near-end severity minor`, `set alarm-severity-entry-tom/EQPTCOMFAIL severity major`. PM defaults come from the equally system-managed pm-profile: `set pm-profile global-data-supervision <auto-enabled|manual>` (default manual, where manual means the flag is controlled per pm-profile-entry or pm-control-entry), and `set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> [default-data-supervision <true|false>] [default-tca-supervision <true|false>]`, which state whether newly created resources of that type get PM data supervision and threshold crossing supervision automatically enabled.

The deciding object is `ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>`. Its `action` attribute gives the IPsec treatment of the datagrams: protect, bypass or discard, default protect. The same entry carries mandatory `priority` (uint8, giving precedence between SPD entries), ipsec-protocol ESP, mode tunnel (default) or transport, esn default true, anti-replay-window 32..1024 default 64 (used when action is protect), dynamic-ts default disabled and alarm-report-control default allowed. Underneath it hangs `ipsec-traffic-selector-<local-instance>/<peer>/<spd-entry>/<ts-name>` with next-layer-protocol (any = 0, opaque = 255, or a number 0-255; default any), and under each traffic selector hang `local-subnet` and `remote-subnet` .../<prefix>, and `local-ports` and `remote-ports` .../<start>/<stop>, where start may be all, opaque or a port number and stop defaults to 0 (0 only accepted when start is all or opaque). All SPD entries for one peer are grouped by `security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name>`.

`trusted-certificate-<id>` is the X509v3 CA certificate, root and intermediate, trusted by the system - the trust anchor, and the target of the trust-chain leafrefs. `local-certificate-<id>` is this node's own identity: the X.509v3 end-entity certificate representing one of the various secure application identities, and it uniquely adds self-signed, used-by (secure-applications, ikev2-peers using it) and subject-alternative-names. `peer-certificate-<id>` is the far end: the X509v3 end-entity certificate representing a trusted remote peer for the L1 encryption secure application, and it uniquely adds white-listed, true when it has no trust chain and was explicitly white-listed at import. All three are set/show only and share version v3, serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain, valid-from, valid-to, status, public-key-length (rsa2048/3072/4096, ecdsa256/384/521), certificate-bytes in PEM, revocation-mode (auto default, force-revoked, force-unrevoked), alarm-report-control (default allowed) and label. The fourth object is the plain `certificate` command: `show certificates`, `show certificate-revocation` and `clear certificate`.

Material arrives with `import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]`, Operational mode, importing one or more certificates in PEM format. The certificate type is local-certificate, peer-certificate or trusted-certificate, e.g. `import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=trusted-cert-1 <string in PEM format>`. The -i flag additionally imports any intermediate certificates in a PEM bundle, or those referenced through the AIA extension for a single-certificate file; root certificates must be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix (for /CN=Nokia: trusted-certificate-Nokia-1, trusted-certificate-Nokia-2). The passphrase decodes encrypted trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundle input. Removal is `clear [-f] certificate [type=]<trusted|local|peer> [id=]<id>`; the id must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type, and <tab> lists the clearable ids. Bulk types are purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. `show certificates` lists what is installed.

`access-rule-<access-rule-list-name>/<access-rule-name>` holds the decision: its mandatory `action` is permit or deny, applied when the filters match - path (default *), module-name (default *), attribute and attribute-value (leaf-lists, max 10 entries of 64 characters) and operation (create, read, update, delete, execute; default *). `access-rule-list-<name>` groups those rules by user-group and holds the ordering: the list is processed in order as given by sequence-id, lower ids first. Note that both act on management access to YANG data nodes, RPCs, notifications and external commands, not on forwarded traffic. Actual packet filtering is `acl-<name>` (type IPv4 or IPv6, bound to an interface such as 1-AUX-1, DCN, DCN-B) with its `ace-<name>/<sequence-id>` entries, whose action is drop (default), accept or reject. The one with nothing to do with traffic at all is `sw-control-rule-<service-name>`: it overrides the action on software service failure, fail-action being default-action, ignore or system-restart.

Rules are processed in sequence-id order and lower number ids are processed first, so of two matching rules the one with the lower sequence-id takes effect; this applies both to access-rule entries within a list and to the access-rule-list objects themselves, since the access-rule-list is processed in the order given by sequence-id. If sequence-id (uint16) is not supplied on add, it is set to the currently used latest id plus 1, so the entry goes to the end of the list; the id can be changed over the lifetime of the list to re-sort entries. On `access-rule-list-<name>`, the `user-group` attribute is a leaf-list of user-group names with a maximum of 20 user-groups referenced; its default value '*' is the match-all representation, meaning the list applies to all existing user-groups. The system supports a maximum of 500 access-rules across all access-rule-lists, and every access-rule must be given an action of permit or deny at creation.

The trap community string is not part of snmp-community; the guide states that the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object. Set it with `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]`, or on an existing target with `set snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string <value>`. trap-community-string is a string of 0..32 characters and defaults to 'infinera'; snmp-version defaults to v2c (v2c or v3, snmpv3-user only applies when v3), target-port defaults to 162 (range 0..65535), target-transport is udp and enabled defaults to true. `snmp-community-<name>` with community-string (1..32 characters) and community-string-access read-only governs polling access only, and the global agent is `set snmp [enabled <true|false>] [port <1..65535>]` (defaults true and 161). Confirm with `show snmp-target-<target-name> trap-community-string`.

`external-fiber-connection` is the object filled in by something other than you: the guide states it is set autonomously by TNMS and that, although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. It represents the physical link between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations: `add external-fiber-connection-<name> src-port-name <value> dst-port-name <value> [label] [scope] [src-node-id] [src-card-name] [dst-node-id] [dst-card-name] [fiber-connection-type]`, with scope general-purpose (default) or cable-id and fiber-connection-type one-way or two-way (default two-way). Only entries with scope cable-id are included in the CableID path and verified. The object you do write yourself is `fiber-connection-<name>`, the physical link between two distinct ports or sub-ports in the same NE in an OADM/ILA topology, configured with src-port, dst-port and fiber-connection-type (default two-way). `show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> fiber-connection-list` shows the supporting fiber connection path of an entity.

To give the node an address use `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`, for example `add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0` or `add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0'`; show returns netmask and origin (static default, dhcp, auto-config). The interface itself is `interface-<if-name>`, with ipv4-enabled default true and ipv4-address-assignment-method static (default) or dhcp. The two look-alikes are read-only LLDP objects about advertised management addresses, not configuration: `show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]` reports the management address received from the remote system on that port and direction, and `show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>` reports the same information for the local LLDP ports. if-subtype takes unknown, if-index or system-port-number. Neither of them assigns an address to an interface.

The stated pre-condition on ipv4-address is that a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. So check the interface first: `show interface-<if-name>` and set `ipv4-address-assignment-method` to static (values static, dhcp; default static) with ipv4-enabled true before adding. The other refusals are value validation on the address itself: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), 127 (loopback) and 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental) are disallowed, and only valid netmasks are accepted. To see which interfaces are available, type '?' after `ipv4-address-` and the system displays the object completion options; `show interface` lists them with if-type (ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp, hdlc), supporting-port, backup-port, vrf, protection-mode, admin-state and oper-state. The syntax is `add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>`, and `delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>` removes it.

Everything the node is using is under `show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]`, which shows the list of system routes from various sources such as dynamic protocols and static routes; source-protocol names the origin (OSPF, BGP, static, and so on) and special-next-hop is none (default), blackhole or unreachable. The tables holding them are `show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]`, address-family being ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast, with one system-controlled default RIB per routing instance per supported address family. Resolved next hops are `show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]`, e.g. `show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN`. Hand-typed routes are added with `add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label] [special-next-hop <value>]`; distance is 1..255 default 1, advertised default false, origin manual (default) or dhcp. `ipv6-static-route` is the IPv6 equivalent.

`local-ports` and `remote-ports` belong to the management IPsec/IKEv2 tunnel. Both are keyed `<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>` and sit under an ipsec-traffic-selector inside an ipsec-spd-entry. start takes all, opaque or a port number; stop is a port number defaulting to 0, and 0 is only accepted by the system when start is all or opaque. Examples: `add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53`, `add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all`, `add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49`. `connection-ports` is the connectivity one and has nothing to do with security: `show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]` maps a degree (1..20) to the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card, for example connection-ports-1/1 to port-1-3-dwdm-line1. index is always 1 in 1830 GX because dwdm-line ports are bi-directional, and the OMS of the corresponding dwdm port is created as a consequence.

The copy is made with `take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]`, Operational mode, which stores the current state of the Configuration database into one of the available backup slots. db-instance is temp (the default, used for manual backup and restore), manual (permanent storage), or the automatic instances onehour, oneday, oneweek, plus rollback; description is up to 128 characters. It is refused unless db-passphrase is configured, either globally as part of security-policies (`set security-policies db-passphrase`) or given on the command; the passphrase needs a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain dictionary words, and may use special characters from the 85-character Z85 set. Automatic snapshots are also disabled until it is set, and taking an instance that already exists, such as oneweek, overwrites the existing file. Putting it back: `activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]`, default false, with the pre-condition that a snapshot must have been taken. List what exists with `show database` or `show database-<database-type>`.

activate is one Operational-mode command with distinct parameters. swimage activates the currently installable image and implies a system restart; optional db-action is auto (default), empty-db, upgrade-db or rollback, and label names the image/manifest. database activates the currently inactive database, also implying a restart, with db-instance (manual, oneday, onehour, oneweek, rollback, temp), db-passphrase (40..200 chars), restart-type cold (default) or warm, and sanity-check-override (default false); NE name, shelf serial number and software version are checked first. Other forms: activate-file, location-led on a chassis or card (led-mode flash default or solid, timeout 0..120 s, default 0), eqpt-fw (resource plus fw-image-name), krp, otdr and otdr-fiber-check, and loopback (WSS loopback on an NMC). For the database case there is also a separate command: activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override], which requires a snapshot taken beforehand with take-snapshot.

show capabilities-<name> is the per-card one: name is the card name and it retrieves that card's capabilities. show l0-capabilities is the photonic one: it shows the capability details related to the node's Layer 0 functions and takes no parameters. show oadm-capabilities is the add/drop one: it reports max-degrees (maximum number of working degrees, 20; 0 if not supported, and 0 by convention for ILA node type, which has only 2 fixed directions) and max-adgs (maximum number of Add/Drop Groups, 110; 0 if not supported). Degrees and ADGs are only supported on OADM node types. All three are show-only and are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

show controller-card-<name> shows only the controller: redundancy-status (active, standby, not-in-service; default not-in-service), redundancy-standby-status (ready-synchronized, not-ready-synchronizing, not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out, card-not-present; default not-ready-synchronizing), number-of-switchover-events and time-of-last-switchover (both visible only on the active controller), and additional-details (0..128 chars). card is the card-base object with parameters common to every card type: add/set/show/delete with required-type, required-subtype, card-mode, chassis-name, slot-name, subslot-name, power-profile, category, last-reboot-reason/time, admin-state (lock, maintenance, unlock; default unlock), oper-state and avail-state. show supported-card-<card-type> is the per-model capability view: category, node-type-compatibility, supported-subtype, default-card-mode and supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, max-power-draw, is-field-replaceable, location-led-support, console-port-support, support-serdes-config (default false), supported-bands and supported-features.

macsec-entity is the Ethernet MACsec object: add/set/show/delete macsec-entity-<name> with supporting-facility (for example ethernet-6-3-3), enabled (true/false, default true), link-security-control must-secure (default) or should-secure, replay-protection enable/disable, and replay-protection-window 0..4294967295 (default 0). Its cipher in force is read back as negotiated-cipher-suite; the configurable cipher term lives in mka-policy, attribute macsec-cipher-suite. secure-entity is the optical/L1 one: supporting-facility plus remote-secure-entity (remote optical-carrier on 1830 GX G40, remote ODU on G30, remote OTUFlex for CHM7/CHM7x), enabled (default false), re-key-frequency 3600..86400 s (default 28800), re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic or continue-traffic (default continue-traffic) and traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s (default 0). Its cipher terms are read-only in secure-entity-sa-proposal: encryption-algorithm aes-gcm-16, encryption-key-length key-length-256, integrity-algorithm none, dh-group ecp-521.

ase-idler-service is the per-card ASE idler filling function on the band spectrum: add/delete/set/show, function idler, with ase-idler-enable (enabled/disabled, default disabled) and read-only ase-idler-state (ase-enabled, ase-partially-enabled, ase-faulted, ase-disabled; default ase-disabled). Example: set ase-idler-service-1-8 ase-idler-enable enabled. ase-idler-source is the pump that produces the ASE signal: set/show only, function ase-idler-source, with pump-enable (enabled/disabled, default disabled), read-only pump-state, target-output-power -3.00..20.50 dBm (default 13), plus admin-state, label and alarm-report-control. Example: set ase-idler-source-1-3.1-ase pump-enable enabled target-output-power 15.00. sw-service does not belong with them: show sw-service-<sv-name> / show sw-services lists the software services and containers running on the node, with equipment, location, state (off, ok, fail), state-details, cpu-usage, memory-usage, uptime, last-start-time and reboot-count.

They are not harmless. change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]enabled|disabled toggles Zero Touch Provisioning: change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot; change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops it if already in progress, and can be run while ZTP is running. Current state is read with show ztp. clear [-f] recover-mode clears the recover-mode flag, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring traffic settings, so it may be traffic impacting; it has no parameters. Both are Operational mode and both prompt for confirmation unless -f is given. The carrier-mode objects are by contrast read-only: show golden-carrier-mode-<card-type>/<carrier-mode>, show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> and show gcmt just list carrier mode tuples such as 600E.84P or 100X.73U with capacity, client-mode, baud-rate, application, compatibility-id and status.

State is on third-party-app: set/show third-party-app-<app-name> with state (running, stopped, failed; default stopped) and enable (true/false, default false; if enabled the app is started and is also enabled again on system restart), plus version, vendor, product, information (0..1024 chars) and label. show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> gives version, state and information per location. The firmware side is third-party-fw: show third-party-fw-<fw-name> with file-status (valid, invalid, missing), path, version, crc, vendor, part-number, nsa-upgrade-version, present-in-eqpt and applicable-eqpt; this is also the list you use to pick an image for activate eqpt-fw. To clear it, use clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>, which clears third party apps. To act on it without clearing, appctl [app-name=] [command=] supports restart, netls and exec, with target defaulting to system and up to 50 optional parameters.

The per-session object is cli-session-config: set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value> sets the rows before pausing, range 10..1000, default 40 (cli-columns is 80..4000, default 80). Also per session are interactive-mode (true/false, default true, not persistent) and display-timestamp (default false). So use set cli-session-config-<your-session-id> cli-lines 60. The protocol as a whole is cli: enabled (default true; CLI cannot be disabled from within a CLI session), port for CLI access via ssh (1..65535, default 22), script-dir, default-interactive-mode (default true, affects only newly created sessions), and show-alarm-columns (default default-columns, global effect on all CLI sessions). The two system configuration objects are config (show config displays the non-default system configuration, fully recursive from the current CLI scope, optionally limited to an entity-id or entity-type) and extended-config (add/delete/show extended-config-<name>, a non-standard config that introduces exceptional behavior globally; the name must match one known by the system).

The generic attribute assignment is set: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]. It requires at least one attribute-value pair on the same managed entity, supports wildcards (card-*, port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), ranges card-1-[1..4] and lists interface-[DCN,CRAFT], and asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or implicitly affects multiple instances. The separate operations: set-alarm-state [state=] [[acknowledge-text=]] (all-alarms | [alarm-id-list=]) changes the operator state of an alarm; state is mandatory and may be none, ack or close, alarm-id-list takes 1 to 10 alarm ids, and acknowledge-text is 0..256 chars. set-time [new-time=] changes the system time and is only applicable when time-source is manual (NTP not enabled), in ISO 8601 form such as 2017-01-12T10:22:25Z or with +/-hh:mm. The one ending in -set is named-value-set, an add/set/show/delete entry keyed <db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> holding a value string of 1..1024 characters.

mc is the Media Channel, a slice of spectrum on an OMS: add mc-<name> parent-oms <value> lower-frequency <value> upper-frequency <value>; frequencies are in MHz, center-frequency and slot-width (upper minus lower) are calculated by the system, and auto-delete (disabled by default) lets the system remove the MC once it has no NMC. nmc is the Network Media Channel, the actual carrier inside an MC or OMS: add nmc-<name> parent-facility <value> center-frequency <value> [width]; center-frequency range 190650000..196700000 MHz, width 15000..200000 MHz with default 35000, set to the 3 dB signal bandwidth matching the transponder baud rate. For both, parent-facility/parent-oms is only set on creation and the supporting card must be part of a Degree, not an ADG. The fillers are read-only views of the spectrum the system fills in: mc-f (Media Channel Filler) shows lower-frequency, upper-frequency and slot-width; nmc-f (Network Media Channel Filler) is set/show and adds alloc- and actual- lower/upper-frequency and bandwidth (alloc-bandwidth default 75000 MHz), power-actual-tx/rx and monitoring-state (enabled by default).

The scan is launched with activate: activate otdr [entity=]<port> [[otdr-file-prefix=]] for a manual measurement, or activate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<ots-r-id> for a manual OTDR-based fiber check, which runs up to 3 OTDR tests and is rejected if a manual scan or an automatic Raman fiber check is already running. Tuning lives on otdr-ptp: otdr-range (auto, or 0..300.0 km, recommended fiber length plus 10 percent), otdr-pulse-width (auto, or 10..20000 ns), otdr-measurement-speed (fast, medium, slow, precision, auto, high-precision), otdr-ior (auto or 1.0..2.0), otdr-fiber-type, otdr-resolution (auto or 0.4..100.0), otdr-direction-mode (default counter-prop-in-service), peak-power (auto or 5..14.5) and launching-fiber-length 0..50 m (default 0). The answer comes out on otdr-ptp: otdr-fiber-break-distance gives the break distance in km, or not-available, plus otdr-last-measurement and the .sor file in otdr-last-measurement-file. Live status is on the otdr object (otdr-state not-available/idle/measuring/finished/fail, otdr-measurement-time, otdr-measurement-direction, otdr-error); automatic runs report on ots-r-auto-otdr (auto-otdr-state, external-attenuation-rx-measured, total-reflectance-rx-measured).

For the name server, dns-server-<address> carries an origin attribute: dhcp means the address was assigned to the system by a DHCP server, manual means it was configured by hand; the default is manual. An entry with origin dhcp keeps being re-supplied, and the documented way to keep it is to convert it by setting origin to manual. Whether DHCP-sourced values are accepted at all is the dns container attribute assignment-method: manual, dhcp or both, default both (dns also has enabled, default true, and search). For the relay, the global object dhcp-relay has mode disabled (default), ipv4 or ipv6, plus server-address, and at least one server IP must be configured when it is enabled. Per interface, if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> has dhcp-relay-enabled (true/false, default false) and it obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so a relay does nothing until both the global mode is set with a server address and the interface flag is set to true.

clear [-f] system [type=]<value> [[target=]] [[restart-behavior=]] [[action=]] has three types. factory-reset resets the system, or a specific chassis/card given as target, to factory configuration: it stops target traffic services and removes the respective files and user configurations, and may imply loss of connectivity; it does not take effect on 1830 GX G30 optical carrier cards OCC2T/OCC2E, and the shutdown option is not supported on L0 cards. full-wipe cleans the entire system and reinstalls the software on the controller and line cards, removing all files, configurations and software, after which a base software reinstall from ONIE is required to recover. inactive only clears the inactive software partition. With no target the entire system is cleared; restart-behavior is restart (default) or shutdown. The option that leaves logs and performance data behind is clear database, which sets the NE database to default and reboots: the guide states it does not wipe logs, PM data and other non-configuration data. Its clear-type is full (default), keep-networking or initialize-from-script.

Read show unprovisioned-inventory: it lists detected inventory that has not yet been accepted by the Node Controller in a multi-chassis configuration. It is keyed by <chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name> (slot-name is empty when the item is the chassis itself) and reports hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number, clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, and detection-timestamp, the last time the Node Controller detected that unprovisioned equipment. On the chassis side, show chassis-<name> gives is-node-controller (true/false), chassis-role (unknown, main-chassis or sub-chassis; default unknown), expected-serial-number (which is how you tell the node controller the serial number of a sub-chassis) and equipment-discovery-ready, which stays false until all equipment has been discovered at startup. The chassis is taken in by provisioning it, for example add chassis-4 required-type G42 expected-serial-number MA3322090659.

control-mode on the amplifier object decides it: auto-max-pw (default), the auto mode targeting maximum output power, or manual. In manual you set gain-target, 0..40 dB, default 0.0, and read back gain-operating; in auto you only bias the system value with gain-adjustment, -20.00..20.00 dB, default 0, supported only where function is pa or inline. Whether auto is available at all is reported by amp-control-support: auto, or manual-only. gain-range-control follows control-mode automatically (manual with manual, auto with auto-max-pw) and gain-range-target is standard, low or high. Things that stop output entirely: amplifier-enable disabled (default disabled), noting that output power also depends on the OSC signal for node-type ILA and on the OMS facilities and an existing OXcon for node-type OADM; forced-shutdown true (default false), which forces one amplifier of a dual-band card down; admin-state lock; and an input OLOS shutdown after olos-shutdown-soak-timer, 0..2000 ms, default 0, which olos-shutdown-disable set to true suppresses at the cost of the OLOS-SHUTDOWN-DISABLED alarm.

show protection-unit-<protection-group-name>/<protection-unit-name> tells you which member is carrying traffic: state is active, standby, available or unknown, and role is working or protection. The group view show protection-group-<name> adds pg-state (no-request, sf-on-working, sf-on-protection, sd-on-working, wait-to-restore, forced-to-protection, frozen and so on; default unavailable), last-switch-trigger, remaining-wtr and switch-failure-reason. Behaviour on a switch is set on protection-group: protection-type y-cable (default) or snc-n, switching-mode unidirectional (default) or bidirectional, reversion-mode revertive or non-revertive (default non-revertive), hold-off-timer 0..10000 ms in 1 ms steps (default 0), wtr-timer 60..720 s in 1 s steps (default 300, revertive only), and the four triggers client-side-olos-trigger, client-side-sd-trigger, network-side-csf-trigger and network-side-sd-trigger, each enabled or disabled, all default disabled. Manual action is via pg-request, or the protection-switch command with operation-type force, lockout, manual or release.

Trigger the check with verify [-f] fiber-connection [target-select=]<port-id> [allow-switching]; omit the port and all paths are verified. allow-switching defaults to false, meaning only active paths are checked; true allows the system to initiate OPSM switching so inactive (protection) paths are covered too. The precondition is that the equipment-policies attribute cable-id-control is set to enabled. It prompts for confirmation unless -f is used, is non-blocking, and while it runs the system raises CID-verification-in-progress against the NE. Watch progress with show cable-id-status: cable-id-state is idle, running-incl-switching or running-no-switching, and test-progress reads N out of M completed. Per port-pair results are in show cable-id-path-<name>: card-type-a/port-a and card-type-z/port-z, port-a-to-port-z-last-test-status and the reverse (not-verified, pass, fail), path-status per direction, last-test-qualifier (up-to-date or out-dated), last-test-timestamp, and additional-info naming the failure (Cable-ID TxLOS, Cable-ID RxLOS, Cable-ID-MISMATCH, Cable-ID-RxLOF, Power out-of-range, timeout). show -r adds the supporting fiber connections; terminate cable-id stops running tests.

Where authentication is sent is decided by security-policies aaa-authentication-method: local-only (the default), local-first-then-remote, remote-first-then-local, or remote-unavailable-then-local. With the default local-only the node authenticates locally only and never contacts the server, which matches your RADIUS box seeing no request. Authorization has its own policy, aaa-authorization-method, also default local-only, and a change to it requires the user to log out and back in. The server itself is aaa-server-<server-name>: protocol-supported RADIUS (default) or TACACSPLUS, server-address, server-priority 1..10, enabled (default true), shared-secret (max 64 characters, longer values are rejected), server-port default 49, server-port-authentication default 1812, server-port-accounting default 1813, role-supported (authentication, authorization, accounting), source-ip and common-password. What happens when it does not answer is governed by timeout, 1..90 s, default 5, and retry, 0..5, default 3, with the stated rule that timeout x (retry + 1) should be less than 5 minutes.

For the automation account use ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>: each entry holds a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication, added as add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key <base64>. Attributes are public-key (0..2048 chars, OpenSSH/PEM form key-type SPACE base64 SPACE comment), public-key-algorithm (ecdsa-sha2-nistp256/384/521, ssh-rsa2048/3072/4096) and label; the user may be local or remote. You also need security-policies ssh-authentication-method set to public-key or public-key-or-password, since the default is password. For the remote host the node copies files to, use ssh-known-host-<id>: add with address (hostname, IPv4 or IPv6), public-key-algorithm (as above plus ssh-ed25519 from R9.0) and public-key. Whether an unlisted host is accepted is security-policies ssh-strict-host-key-checking: strict allows only known hosts, relaxed (the default) allows any. ssh-host-key holds the node's own SSHv2 host keys, one per supported algorithm, auto-generated in the default DB and replaced or added by ssh-keygen ([-t rsa|ecdsa|ed25519, default rsa] [-b key length] [-l label]).

The key agreement policy is mka-policy-<name>, referenced by the macsec entity of an Ethernet facility: add/set/show/delete with key-server-priority (used by MKA to elect the key server), macsec-cipher-suite (cipher suites for Secure Association Key derivation), confidentiality-offset (the number of octets in an Ethernet frame sent as unencrypted plain text), and sak-rekey-interval, which is what sets how often the session key rolls over: the SAK rekey interval in seconds, range 0 or 30..65535, default 30 s. The per-facility instance is macsec-mka-<name>: it points at the policy with mka-policy, and carries connectivity-association-key and connectivity-association-key-name (each 0..64 chars), is-key-server (default false), psk-configured-timestamp, psk-lifetime in days (range 1..173, default 14), psk-expiration-warning and psk-lifetime-enable. The channels themselves are read-only: show sc-tx-<name>/<index> and show sc-rx-<name>/<index> give sci-tx or sci-rx (16-character hex Secure Channel Identifier), state (in-use or not-in-use as reported by the MKA stack), association-number, key-identifier and next-packet-number.

NETCONF listens on port 830 for access via ssh and is enabled by default (enabled true); it cannot be disabled from within a NETCONF session. hello-timeout is 1..3600 seconds, default 2, and annotate-cli-name defaults to false. gNMI over gRPC uses port 50051 and is also enabled by default; gnmi-get-encoding-granularity is per-path or per-object, default per-object, and the grpc object is system managed and cannot be manually deleted. RESTCONF is enabled by default as well, but its HTTP side is the one off out of the box: http-enabled defaults to false and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode, while https-enabled defaults to true. http-port defaults to 8080 and https-port to 8181, both 1..65535, and cookie-timeout is 1..300 minutes, default 5. For comparison, the CLI protocol object listens on port 22 and is enabled by default.

restart [-h] [-f] [<resource-id>] [<type>] [<sub-component>] defaults to a warm start when type is omitted, and with no resource-id it restarts the active node controller card rather than a line card. warm reboots the card processor and is non service affecting, with connectivity regained within five minutes (on XMM4 a warm reboot is non service affecting but visibility is lost for 3 minutes). cold reboots all components and sub-components and is service affecting, again with connectivity back within five minutes. shutdown gracefully shuts the card down and it becomes unreachable. So restart card-1-4 gives a warm, non service affecting reboot. You cannot assume every card behaves the same: the guide states that not all cards support all restart types, and that a cold reboot of XMM4 is not service affecting while a cold reboot of CHM6, UCM4 and similar is. Restartable entities are card (cold, warm, shutdown), card sub-component (cold, warm) and tom (cold only). Confirmation is required unless -f is given; sub-components are listed with show card resources.

Three pieces have to be in place. First a template keyed by the TOM part number: add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>], where ports-applicable is a list of up to 20 port names (1..16 chars each) or all, and by default all ports are considered. Second, the parameter values inside it, one per entry: add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<name> value <value>, for example add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3 (names such as RxEQ, TxEQ, TxEQAdaptive, RxAmplitude, RxPreCursor, RxPostCursor). Third, and required, the global switch: set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates true; its default is disabled and application of serdes-templates depends on this flag being true. Enabling it is not retroactive, templates apply from that moment onward; disabling it has no impact on existing serdes configuration. Templates apply to all line cards that support serdes (supported-card attribute support-serdes-config true). When a TOM with the matching part-number is plugged in the template is applied automatically. Manual serdes settings are kept even if they deviate; swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template, and apply-template forces re-application.

ots is the Optical Transport Section, the fiber span itself: fiber-type-tx/rx (default SSMF), fiber-length-tx/rx (auto or 0..500.0 km), span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive (0..80 dB, 99 meaning not configured), span-loss-reference configured or measured (default measured), external-attenuation-tx/rx 0..30 dB, span-loss-aging-margin-rx 0..10 dB (default 1.0), target-power-setting manual, auto (default) or auto-plan, and laser-safety-mode OPLM or APSD. oms is the Optical Multiplex Section, the multiplexed band on a degree: monitoring-mode, grid-mode flexible (default) or fixed-50G-96ch, fixed-75G-64ch, fixed-100G-48ch, fixed-150G-40ch and others, lower/upper-frequency defaulting to 191300000 and 196150000 MHz, band-allowed/actual/target, attenuation-control-mode-rx/tx auto (default) or manual, target-output-power 5.00..20.00 dBm. ops is the Optical Physical Section, the single physical port layer: role tributary, multi-carrier, general-purpose (default), ase-input or active-multi-carrier, input-psd-profile -30..-6 (default -6), port-expansion no or y-cable. osc is the Optical Supervisory Channel and is the one that carries the supervisory traffic: osc-mode OC3 (155 Mbit/s) or 1GE for HSC OLS, osc-wavelength, osc-control auto (default) or manual, target-output-power -2.5..4.5 dBm, tx-power-adjustment -6..6 dB, voa-attenuation-target-rx 0..30 dB (default 10), l0-comm-interface-type ipv4 or ipv6, lof-soak-timer short (default, about 3 ms) or long (adds about 2300 ms).

The behaviour is configured on the trib-ptp facility, attribute tributary-disable-action, which states what the network element does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed. The default is laser-shut-off; other values are none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais, and send-nos for 1830 GX G30 only. Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off. The action can be delayed by tributary-disable-holdoff-timer, range 0..10000 milliseconds, default 0, where 0 disables the hold-off; it applies only when the TDA action is laser turn-off, holding the optical signal as it is until the configured hold-off timer expires and only then turning off the laser. Related switches on the same object are near-end-tda (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tda-degrade-mode (default disabled) and forward-defect-trigger (true/false, default true), which decides whether a client forward defect such as LF or ODU-AIS flows through to the line side or instead triggers an egress TDA action.

You create by hand the objects that have an add form: super-channel (add super-channel-<name> carriers <value> carrier-mode <value>), flexo-group (add flexo-group-<name> carriers rate modulation-format group-id), otu (add otu-1-5-L1-1-OTU4-1 parent flexo-group-1-5-L1-1 time-slots 1), the low-order odu (add odu-<name> odu-type ODU4i/ODUflexi parent-odu ... time-slots ...), trib-ptp and xcon. The system creates optical-carrier, optical-channel and flexo (set/show only, no add), and the high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created. The stated pre-condition on odu is: Super-channel must be added before Low Order ODUs can be added. Check managed-by (system or user) on any facility; only user-created facilities can be user deleted, and odu class shows high-order, low-order or mapped.

The bit error rate test is the bert command (Operational Mode): bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=ingress test-duration=10, then bert get, bert stop test-id=TestX (test-id mandatory for stop) and bert delete. test-signal-type is none, PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV or scrambled-idles; monitoring type adds fec-frames. test-duration min 10 s, max 1000 hrs, 0 means indefinite. You inject a test pattern per facility on odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction>: test-signal-type none (default), PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31, PRBS31_NONINV; test-signal-direction ingress, egress or both (default ingress); test-signal-monitoring true/false (default false). Loop it back with the loopback attribute on otu, odu or optical-carrier: none (default), facility or terminal, with loopback-mode loopback or loopback-and-continue.

L1 encryption is carried by secure-entity, and both of its references are mandatory: add secure-entity-<name> supporting-facility <value> remote-secure-entity <value>. supporting-facility is the local facility being encrypted (optical-carrier on 1830 GX G40, odu on 1830 GX G30, OTUflex for CHM7/CHM7x L1 service encryption); remote-secure-entity is the AID of the matching far-end optical carrier, ODU or OTUFlex, so that facility must already exist at the other end. enabled defaults to false, so set enabled true. re-key-frequency is 3600..86400 s, default 28800; re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic or continue-traffic (default continue-traffic); traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s, default 0; alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited. Underneath, IKEv2 must be up: an ikev2-local-instance with scope data-path-encryption on a card whose host-card-encryption-capability is yes, plus an ikev2-peer with destination set to the far end and authentication-scheme x.509-certificate (default, requiring local-certificate and peer-certificate) or pre-shared-key.

The telemetry object configures persistent and dynamic telemetry (show telemetry, set telemetry id <string>, string 0..4096); it is system-managed and cannot be manually deleted. show subscriptions lists the subscriptions currently configured. For one of them, show current-subscription-<subscription-name> gives related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc), session-protocol gnmi, encoding json|bytes|proto|ascii|json-ietf (default json-ietf), transfer-mode stream|once|poll (default stream), updates-only (default false) and user-access. What each one is watching comes from show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>: subscription-path (1..520 chars), subscription-path-origin, subscription-path-mode target-defined|on-change|sample (default target-defined), sample-interval and heartbeat-interval in ms (both default 0), suppress-redundant (default true). For a target-defined stream, an unset sample-interval is adjusted to 10 s and a heartbeat below 10 s is raised to 20 s.

At rest the configuration database is encrypted; show db-protection-scheme reports encryption-algorithm xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 in XTS mode, 64-byte block), integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512 or none, integrity-status passed-on-bootup / failed-on-bootup / disabled, and mode encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity. The mode can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. Before you can take a copy, the db-passphrase must be configured: take-snapshot is only accepted if db-passphrase is set globally (set security-policies db-passphrase) or supplied inline (take-snapshot db-passphrase=***). The passphrase is a minimum of 40 characters (security-policies range 40..200), must contain no dictionary words, and special characters follow the 85-character Z85 set. Automatic DB snapshots are not enabled until it is set. take-snapshot [db-instance=] accepts temp (default), manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek, rollback, plus an optional description (0..128). Existing snapshots are listed with show database.

Start with show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]. It lists system routes from all sources; source-protocol tells you whether the entry came from OSPF, BGP or static, and special-next-hop is none, blackhole or unreachable (blackhole and unreachable routes have no next-hop created under the route, so they will not forward). Then check resolution with show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address], for example show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN. The instance it landed in is the RIB: show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]. Every route in a RIB belongs to a single address family (ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast), the vrf leaf gives the VRF the RIB is bound to, and for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family. show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description] shows the VRF itself, with type mgmt (management) or internal.

The rejection comes from security-policies. strict-password-check (default true) enforces minimum length 8, at least one lower case letter, one upper case letter, one number and one symbol, and the user name may not be part of the password; if disabled the only rule left is a minimum length of 1. minimum-password-length is separately configurable, range 1..200, default 8. enforce-password-history-check (default true) blocks reuse of the previous passwords, with password-history-size range 1..200, default 5. These policies only affect newly defined passwords. The lockout is per user: max-invalid-login is the number of consecutive invalid logins before the account is suspended, range 0..255, default 5, and suspension-time is the suspension duration, range 0..1440 minutes, default 5. show user-<name> gives user-status (lockout) and failed-logins, which resets on a successful login; password-aging-interval defaults to 90 days (0..999). To clear the stuck session, list them with show session and run kill-session <session-id>, where session-id is <ip-address>:<port>; it cannot be your own session (use exit for that).

Untouched syslog defaults: remote-logging-switch true, source-address localhost, log-file-message-coalescence true, log-relay false, assignment-method both, niap-compliant-logging false, privacy-mode false, alarm-report-control allowed. Local files: log-file number-of-files is the maximum retained, range 1..20, default 10, and when rotating because max-file-size is reached the oldest files beyond that count are discarded; max-file-size range 1..30 MB, default 30; source-facilities default all; severity is informational and above by default; sensitive-data none for a regular log file (only for log-file-default-audit-dbg). The default system log file cannot be edited or deleted. Console logging is off by default (log-console enabled false). Remote collectors default to port 514, transport udp, message-format rfc5424, enabled true, origin manual, sensitive-data none. The single switch that kills everything remote is set syslog remote-logging-switch false, which disables all remote logging destinations.

What is raised now: show current-alarms, which also reports number-of-alarms and last-changed (timestamp of the last raise or clear); show alarms and show alarm-<alarm-id> give per-alarm detail such as perceived-severity, service-affecting, reported-time, corrective-action and operator-state. Most alarms have both an automatic raise and an automatic clear criteria. The small subset without a clear criteria is cleared by hand with clear [-f] alarm [alarm-type=]<value> [[resource=]<value>], for example clear alarm DBRESTOREFAIL; find them with show alarm-inventory can-be-cleared-by-user=true. This applies only to system-wide alarms not associated with a particular resource. Operator state is set with set-alarm-state [state=]<value> [[acknowledge-text=]<value>] (all-alarms | alarm-id-list=<value>,...), 1 to 10 alarm ids, states none, ack, close. Whether inhibiting reporting drops alarms already up is decided system-wide by alarm-control arc-behavior: leave-alarms (default) leaves them raised, clear-alarms clears them when ARC is set to inhibit.

Temperature comes from real-time PM: show pm displays a per-resource real-time table with instant, avg, min and max, including temperature (C) for a line card such as card-1-1 and for card-1-FANCTRL-1, temperature/input-current/input-power/input-voltage for each card-1-PEM-n, inlet-temperature (C) and actual-power-draw (W) for chassis-1, and fan-speed (percent) per card-1-FAN-n. Narrow it with the pm-filter fields AID, resource, resource-type, data-type or parameter, for example show pm card-1-7, and use -i=<chassis-name> to scope to one chassis, -t for a standard table, -n= for max records per chassis (default 1000). show pm-resource-<resource> gives real-time-supervision and real-time-data-last-reset for that instance. Physically the state shows on the LEDs: show leds or show led status, with per-FRU entries like led-1-1/fault, led-1-1/power, led-1-FANCTRL-1/fanN-fault and chassis-critical/major/minor, status values off, green, flashing-green, yellow, amber, red, flashing-red, cycling, not-available. show slot and card avail-state also reflect it.

The line is the ots facility. show ots-<name> gives span-loss-derived-rx and span-loss-derived-tx, the measured span loss from OSC powers including losses external to the fiber, 0..99 dB where 99 dB means OLOS; span-loss-transmit and span-loss-receive, the configured fiber loss, 0..80 dB (receive also allows 99 dB, default 0, and changing it is traffic affecting); span-loss-reference measured (default) or configured, which selects which of the two the system uses for automatic target OXCon powers; span-loss-alarm-threshold, autonomously set and persistent, default 99 dB, which can be forced to refresh with the update command in measured mode; span-loss-aging-margin-rx 0.00..10.00 dB, default 1.0; external-attenuation-tx/rx 0..30 dB; fiber-type-rx/tx (default SSMF) and fiber-length-derived-rx/tx. The amplifier shows the compensation: gain-operating and gain-target 0..40 dB, gain-range-actual, gain-adjustment -20.00..20.00, optimum-edfa-gain, input-power-mon and output-power-mon -99.00..99.00 dBm, tilt-actual/tilt-target/tilt-adjustment -5..5 dB, control-mode auto-max-pw (default) or manual, span-loss-control enabled by default, and control-state converged, fine-tuning, adjusting or stopped.

Going down: trib-ptp, the tributary client physical termination between the transceiver (TOM) and the client protocol, carrying service-type such as 100GBE, 400GBE or OTU4; then the client protocol layer (ethernet, or a client otu); then the low order odu (ODU4i, ODUflexi, ODU4, ODUflex) with its trib-port-number and time-slots; the xcon, which is the Layer 1 digital service joining source and destination (direction two-way); the high order ODU (class high-order, ODUCn/ODUCni), which the system creates automatically when the SCH is created; then otu and flexo-group (carriers, rate, modulation-format, group-id) with the per-interface flexo (foic-type foic1.2 through foic4.16, fec-type default ofec); then optical-carrier, grouped by super-channel, and finally line-ptp. The digital domain hands over to the optical one at the optical-carrier: that is the first object holding frequency, actual-frequency, wavelength, tx-power, baud-rate, modulation-format, grid-spacing and spectral-bandwidth, and it is bound upward through the carriers attribute of flexo-group and super-channel. Walk the chain on any facility with supporting-facilities and supported-facilities.

No, they are two different objects. A counter limit is a PM threshold: add or set pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> [low-threshold <value>] [high-threshold <value>], values uint64/int64/decimal64 or na or not-supported, default na, direction ingress|egress|all|na (default all), location all|na|near-end|far-end (default all); delete removes it. Crossing it only gets reported if TCA supervision is on, via tca-supervision true|false on pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>, or default-tca-supervision on pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/... for newly created resources. System defaults and allowed range for a parameter come from show pm-threshold-profile-... [default-low-threshold] [default-high-threshold] [min-value] [max-value]. Changing how loudly an existing fault is reported is instead set alarm-severity-entry-<resource-type>/<alarm-type>/<direction>/<location> severity <value> (critical, event, major, minor, not-reported, warning), or set alarm-severity-profile <profile-entry> severity <value>. Both alarm severity objects are system-managed and cannot be manually deleted.

Stop the reporting with alarm-report-control on the card: set card-<name> alarm-report-control inhibited (values allowed, inhibited). The same attribute exists on the facilities the card hosts (trib-ptp, otu, odu, flexo, optical-carrier, ots, amplifier, line-ptp and so on), where the default is allowed, so inhibit those too if you want silence at facility level. You can also put the card into set card-<name> admin-state maintenance (admin-state values lock, unlock, maintenance). What happens to the alarms it has already raised is not decided on the card: it is the system-wide switch set alarm-control arc-behavior. leave-alarms, the default, leaves current alarms in a raised state when ARC is set to inhibit; clear-alarms clears the currently raised alarms when ARC is set to inhibit. The companion switch alarm-control alarm-soaking-behavior is automatic (soaking time from the FM profile) by default, or no-soak. Verify with show alarm-control and show current-alarms.

A secure application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. show secure-application-<id> [type] [active-certificate-id] [in-use] [status] [verify-client-cert] tells you which one it presents: active-certificate-id is the assigned list (string 0..128, e.g. set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY), and in-use is the leafref to active-certificate-id, that is, the certificate actually in use. type is server or client, status is enabled or disabled, and verify-client-cert is disabled (default) or required, where required is what TLS mutual authentication needs and only takes effect for new TLS connections. Before it will come up, import the end-entity certificate and its CA chain with import-certificate: import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <PEM string> <passphrase> and import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=trusted-cert-1 <PEM string>, adding -i to pull intermediates out of a bundle; root certificates must be installed individually. Then check show local-certificate-<id> status (valid, pending-import, expired, revoked, untrusted, future), trust-chain and used-by.

Pipe the show pm output through the CSV display filter: show pm <command flag> | display csv, which produces CSV importable to a spreadsheet such as Excel; display xml and display json are also available. Restrict it to the 15-minute bins with the pm-filter fields, for example show pm pm-15min, and add AID, parameter, resource, resource-type or data-type filters to narrow further (use show pm <tab> for the complete list of supported filters). Bin 0 is the current data and bins 1 to n are history; select a range with -sbin=<number> and -ebin=<number>, or a time window with -st=<timestamp> and -et=<timestamp> in the form 2021-02-01T10:00:00+01:00. Other flags: -t forces the standard single generic table format, -n=<number-of-records> caps records per chassis (default 1000), -s=<skip-records> pages through the data, and -i=<chassis-name> scopes to one chassis (only once per command).

Look it up in the PM catalog with show pm-catalog <string>, where string is the catalog name. For example show pm-catalog parameter-undersized returns pm-parameter-undersized with units packets and type counter. The equivalent per-parameter view is show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type], for instance show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds, and show pm-parameter on its own lists all PM parameters. units is drawn from na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors and MHz; type is counter or gauge. Both commands are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Turn off data supervision for that resource with set pm-control <entity> data-supervision <true|false>, for example set pm-control pm-resource-card-1-1 data-supervision false. data-supervision is the real-time data supervision flag for the resource; its values are true and false and the default is true. show pm-control lists the currently existing resources in the system that support PM data. The equivalent per-instance control is set pm-resource-<resource> real-time-supervision false (true/false, default true), and show pm-resource-<resource> reports real-time-supervision along with resource-type, AID and real-time-data-last-reset. Both are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Note that global-data-supervision on pm-profile must be left at manual for per-resource control to apply, since auto-enabled globally enables PM data-supervision.

Yes. pm-control-entry is exactly that scope: one resource, one period, one direction, one location. Run set pm-control-entry-<resource>/pm-15min/ingress/near-end tca-supervision true. The key fields are resource (Instance ID), period (PM period, e.g. pm-15min or pm-24h), direction ingress, egress, all or na (default all) and location all, na, near-end or far-end (default all). The same entry carries data-supervision (true/false) if you want to separate data collection from threshold crossing supervision. show pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location> [supported-parameters] [data-supervision] [tca-supervision] reads it back, where supported-parameters is the list of PM parameters that resource type supports for that direction and location, with a maximum of 100 elements. Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show pm-parameter-<parameter> [units] [type]. The type attribute is the answer to counter versus gauge: its only values are counter and gauge. units gives the reported unit, taken from na, dBm, ms, ps, ps/nm, dB, seconds, packets, events, octets, bits, blocks, times, percent, bit-ratio, C, frames, W, V, A, rpm, ps2, mA, words, cw, nm, bytes, errors and MHz. Example: show pm-parameter pm-parameter-undersized returns units packets and type counter. show pm-parameter on its own lists all PM parameters, and show pm-parameter-severely-errored-seconds targets one by name. The same information is in the catalog via show pm-catalog <catalog-name>. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, through the pm-profile object, which holds all resources that support PM data together with their related default configuration. Run set pm-profile global-data-supervision auto-enabled. The attribute takes auto-enabled or manual and defaults to manual. auto-enabled is the global enabling of the PM data-supervision flag, so you do not have to toggle it individually; manual means the flag is controlled via pm-profile-entry, or directly per pm-control-entry. Read it back with show pm-profile. The pm-profile object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Set the per-resource-type defaults on pm-profile-entry: set pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> default-data-supervision true. default-data-supervision controls, for newly created resources of this type, whether they have PM data supervision automatically enabled; the companion default-tca-supervision does the same for threshold crossing supervision. Both take true or false. The key fields are resource-type (Instance ID), direction ingress, egress, all or na (default all), location all, na, near-end or far-end (default all), and period (PM period such as pm-15min or pm-24h). Read it back with show pm-profile-entry-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period> [default-data-supervision] [default-tca-supervision]. This is per resource type; existing instances are still controlled by pm-control-entry, and pm-profile global-data-supervision must stay at manual for these entries to govern.

Read real-time-data-last-reset on the resource: show pm-resource-<resource> [resource-type] [AID] [real-time-supervision] [real-time-data-last-reset], for example show pm-resource-trib-ptp-1-7-T9. real-time-data-last-reset is the date and time of the last real-time data reset for that resource; if the data was never reset, it is the date and time of the resource's creation. The same output gives resource-type, AID (string, length 1..64) and real-time-supervision (true/false, default true), plus the pm-control-entry children such as pm-control-entry-trib-ptp-1-7-T9/pm-15min/ingress/near-end. The counters themselves are cleared with clear pm real-time, optionally narrowed by resource, resource-type, AID, direction, location or period. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Create a pm-threshold on that instance: add pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/errored-seconds high-threshold <value>, then use set to change it, show to read it and delete pm-threshold-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>/<parameter> to remove it. resource is an Instance ID, period is the PM period (for example pm-15min or pm-24h), direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all) and location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all). high-threshold and low-threshold accept a Number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na for not applicable, or not-supported; the default is na. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the crossing to be reported, tca-supervision must be true on the matching pm-control-entry-<resource>/<period>/<direction>/<location>.

The pm-threshold-profile object holds the PM configuration per parameter for a resource type. Run show pm-threshold-profile-<resource-type>/<direction>/<location>/<period>/<parameter> [low-threshold] [high-threshold] [default-low-threshold] [default-high-threshold] [min-value] [max-value]. default-low-threshold and default-high-threshold are the system defined default values for that parameter, and min-value and max-value are the minimum and maximum values allowed for it; all four are show-only. low-threshold and high-threshold are the configured values and can be set. All of them accept a Number (uint64, int64 or decimal64), or na, or not-supported. direction is ingress, egress, all or na (default all) and location is all, na, near-end or far-end (default all). Example: set pm-threshold-profile-OTUC14i/ingress/near-end/pm-24h/errored-seconds high-threshold 1200.

Use 'set clock timezone <value>' (Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode). The timezone default is Universal-Time-Coordinated and the value comes from the named zone list, for example 'set clock timezone Beijing-Chongqing-Hong_Kong-Urumqi[GMT+08:00]'. To see where the node gets its time, read the time-source attribute: 'show clock time-source'. Values are ntp (the NE uses NTP for synchronization) and manual (the NE uses its internal clock); the default is manual. 'show clock' with no attribute also returns current-time, universal-time, timezone, uptime, uptime-seconds, DST-active (true/false, default false) and last-time-jump, which is reported as '<time1> to <time2>' and ignores jumps of less than 10 seconds. If the DNS server is not properly configured, 'show clock' can take up to 2 minutes to return.

Yes. node-type can only be set or changed on 1830 GX G34c chassis, where the default is ILA; since R7.0 the G34c also supports OADM. Use 'set ne node-type OADM'. Permitted values of node-type are ILA, OADM and XPDR (G31/G32 support OADM only, G42 defaults to XPDR). To configure OADM, two conditions must hold first: no OMS monitoring-mode in the system may be 'ila-with-equalization' or 'not-monitored', that is no 'spectrum' (or 'ochm') objects exist in OADM, and no direction-* must exist. To go back to ILA: no OMS monitoring-mode on the dwdm-line ports may be 'intrusive', that is no RD or PAx card can exist, and no degree, no oxcon and no nmc must exist. Check the current value with 'show ne node-type'.

'show ne-function' lists the NE generic functions in one place. It is a show-only command with no parameters, available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. The output enumerates each direction and each amplifier by name, plus the ne-function entry itself. The guide's G30 example returns direction-1 through direction-8, amplifier-raman-1-7, amplifier-1-1-A, amplifier-1-1-B, amplifier-1-3.1-drop, amplifier-1-5-A, amplifier-1-5-B, amplifier-2-1-A, amplifier-2-1-B, amplifier-2-3-A, amplifier-2-3-B, and ne-function.

Use the ntp object: 'set ntp ntp-enabled true ntp-auth-enabled true'. ntp-enabled defaults to true and ntp-auth-enabled defaults to false, so authentication is the attribute you actually have to turn on.
