Use show supported-carrier-mode-<name>/<carrier-mode> [capacity] [client-mode] [baud-rate] [application] [compatibility-id] [status] [supported-subtypes], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. carrier-mode is an acronymized code (handle) indicating the optical carrier line mode 4-tuple, string length 1..15, formatted <Capacity><ClientMode>.<Baud Rate><Application ID>, for example 600E.84P, 100X.73U or 325M.66P. capacity is the net capacity of the optical carrier in gbps, so that column answers the capacity question. client-mode gives the digital client modes mapped into and transported by the carriers within the superchannel and is ethernet or ethernet-otn. baud-rate is the modulated symbol rate. application is the optical transport application ID the mode is optimized for, string 1..15. compatibility-id identifies carrier modes that can be applied simultaneously, and status is the state of the carrier mode. supported-subtypes lists the subtypes each carrier mode supports, string 0..32, maximum 20 elements.

Use show supported-gain-range-<name>/<gain-range-type> [gain-range-min] [gain-range-max], available in Operational and Candidate configuration mode. gain-range-type is the type of gain-range and takes low, high or standard. gain-range-min is the minimum settable gain-target for that type of range ('standard'/'low'/'high') and gain-range-max is the maximum settable gain-target for that range; both are of type gain-value with no stated default. The name key is documented as a flag to enable or disable access control with values true or false and default false. So to see the actual dB limits behind low, standard and high, query the entity for the gain-range-type of interest and read gain-range-min and gain-range-max.

Different power profiles are supported to reflect different scenarios when using a card. The user is able to define, per card instance, which profile is in effect, and that choice has an impact on the power estimation for the system. To see what a card type offers, use show supported-power-profile-<card-type>/<name> [profile-description] [power-draw] [default], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. card-type is the card type (string) and name is the profile name (string). profile-description is a description of the profile, string length 0..255. power-draw is the power draw of the associated equipment when not in low-power, of type decimal64. default is true or false and tells you whether that profile is the default one. No defaults are stated for these read-only attributes.

The router ID comes from router-id-mode, which is a flag indicating whether the router-id is the loopback IP. It takes use-loopback or manual and defaults to use-loopback, so by default the instance takes the loopback IP. If you set router-id-mode manual you supply the value explicitly with router-id, which accepts an IPv4 or IPv6 address; 0.0.0.0/0 is not supported for IPv4 and 0::0.0 is not supported for IPv6. The syntax is add bgp-instance-<instance-id> local-as <value> [description <value>] [router-id-mode <value>] [router-id <value>], and both attributes can be changed later with set bgp-instance-<instance-id>. instance-id is a string of length 1..255, local-as is mandatory on add and is a number in the range 1..4294967295, and description is a string 0..128. Example: add bgp-instance-10 local-as 24 router-id-mode use-loopback. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The bgp-neighbor defaults are connect-retry-interval 120 seconds (range 1..65535, the interval between attempts to establish a session), hold-time 90 seconds (range 3..65535, typically set to 3x the keepalive-interval) and keepalive-interval 30 seconds (range 1..21845, typically 1/3 of the hold-time). negotiated-hold-time is read-only, range 0..65535, default 0. Yes, you can authenticate the session: secure-session sets the authentication method to none or TCP-MD5, defaulting to none, and password carries the TCP-MD5 authentication key in ASCII format, string 0..80. Syntax: add bgp-neighbor-<instance-id>/<remote-address> peer-as <value> [afi-safis <value>] [enabled <value>] [description <value>] [secure-session <value>] [password <value>] [connect-retry-interval <value>] [hold-time <value>] [keepalive-interval <value>]. peer-as is 1..4294967295 and enabled defaults to true. session-state shows Idle, Connect, Active, OpenSent, OpenConfirm, Established or Close, default Idle.

The routes to be advertised to an external AS must already exist in the forwarding table installed by an Interior Gateway Protocol (IGP) such as OSPF, or by static routes, but not by BGP itself. If the prefix is not present in the IGP tables, you must configure a blackhole static route for it: set the special-next-hop parameter of the static route command to blackhole, for example add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> special-next-hop blackhole (special-next-hop takes the value blackhole and is available on ipv4-static-route and ipv6-static-route in add, set and show). The bgp-network object itself is created with add bgp-network-<instance-id>/<remote-address>/<network-prefix>, where instance-id is a string 1..255, remote-address is the BGP peer address in IPv4 or IPv6 format (0.0.0.0/0 and 0::0.0 are not supported) and network-prefix is a decimal number 1..64, or 128. A maximum of 100 bgp-network MOs can be configured.

The comm-channel mtu is the maximum transmission unit size in octets for the physical Ethernet port of the comm channel, an unsigned 16-bit integer. The range is platform dependent: 1280..1500 octets on the 1830 GX G30 only, and 1280..9202 octets on the 1830 GX G40 only. The default is 1500, except that on 1830 GX G40 the default is 1518 for these interface types: DCN, AUX, AUX2, OFEC-CC, Craft, CHM6 and UCM4. Pre-condition: mtu is available only when mode is L3 (mode takes L1 for L1 ETH User Channel Mode, L2 for the L2 iGCC interface, or L3 for L3 IP Mode, default L3). Set it with add -m comm-channel-<name> type <value> parent <value> [... mtu <value> ...] or set comm-channel-<name> mtu <value>. Related L3-only attributes are mru (64..1500 octets, default 1500), restart-timer (1..10 seconds, default 3), max-failure (2..10, default 5) and peer-address (default 0.0.0.0).

LLDP is not on by default. lldp-admin-status defaults to disabled, meaning the LLDP agent neither transmits nor receives LLDP frames on the port; the other values are tx-only (transmits but does not store remote system information), rx-only (receives but does not transmit) and tx-and-rx. It cannot be modified if mode is L1. Enable it with, for example, set comm-eth-1-5-ETH1 lldp-admin-status tx-and-rx. lldp-transmit-interval is the LLDP Tx TLV interval, 1..16383 seconds, default 30. lldp-mgmt-addr-if selects which interface IP is advertised as the management address (1-AUX-1, 1-AUX-2, DCN, DCN-2 (G30 only), 1-AUX-1-B, 1-AUX-2-B, DCN-B, DCN-2-B (G30 only), L0-MGMT); it is empty by default and applies when lldp-admin-status is tx-only or tx-and-rx. For speed, auto-negotiation defaults to enabled. duplex-mode (default full), rate (1, 10, 100, 1000, 10000 Mbits or maximum, default maximum) and flow-control (default disabled) are only valid when auto-negotiation is disabled; read back operational-rate, operational-duplex-mode and operational-flow-control. mtu is 1280..1500 octets, default 1500.

Use the global dhcp-relay command: set dhcp-relay [mode <value>] [server-address <value>] and show dhcp-relay [mode] [server-address], available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. mode is the flag indicating the dhcp-relay mode of operation and takes disabled, ipv4 or ipv6, with default disabled. server-address holds the DHCP server IP addresses as an IPv4 or IPv6 server address; when relay is enabled at least one IP address should be configured. Examples: set dhcp-relay mode ipv4, or both at once with set dhcp-relay mode ipv4 server-address 10.220.20.3. This is the global setting; per-interface enabling is done separately with set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true, which obeys the global dhcp-relay settings.

Yes. The dns command has assignment-method, which indicates whether the system contains manual and/or dhcp configured values. It takes manual, dhcp or both, and the default is both, so out of the box the node accepts name servers from DHCP as well as manually configured ones. Configure it with set dns [assignment-method <value>] [enabled <value>] [search <value>] and read it back with show dns. enabled is the flag indicating if DNS is enabled, true or false, default true. search is the DNS-search-suffix name, a string of length 0..64 that must contain at least a single dot; to clear it, set the string to an empty string. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Individual servers carry their own origin (dhcp or manual) on the dns-server object.

Add a name server with add dns-server-<address> [origin <value>], where address is the IPv4 or IPv6 address of the DNS server. The origin attribute records the DNS address assignment method: dhcp indicates a DNS address that has been assigned to this system by a DHCP server, and manual indicates the DNS address has been manually configured. The default is manual. So show dns-server-<address> [origin], or show dns-server for the list, tells you which entries came from DHCP. You can also convert a DHCP configured DNS entry into a manually configured one by changing this attribute with set dns-server-<address> origin manual. Remove a server with delete dns-server-<address>. Example: add dns-server-10.100.210.243 origin dhcp. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the if-dhcp-relay object: set if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> dhcp-relay-enabled true, and check it with show if-dhcp-relay-<if-name> [dhcp-relay-enabled]. if-name is the interface object identifier, a string of length 0..255. dhcp-relay-enabled enables the dhcp-relay function on that interface, takes true or false, and defaults to false. It obeys the global dhcp-relay settings, so the global dhcp-relay mode must be ipv4 or ipv6 (its default is disabled) and a server-address configured for relaying to work. Example: set if-dhcp-relay-1-8-dwdm-line-1GE-OSCX1-MGMT dhcp-relay-enabled true. The command runs in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. The same per-interface control appears on the interface object as if-dhcp-relay, false or true, default false.

By default a new interface is static and protected. On add interface-<if-name> if-type <value> [...], ipv4-address-assignment-method and ipv6-address-assignment-method each take static or dhcp and default to static. ipv4-enabled and ipv6-enabled both default to true, so the interface is connected to both stacks and can send and receive IPv4 and IPv6 packets. protection-mode is the user given protection mode and takes unknown (transient, output only), protected (protected by redundant ports) or unprotected (no port redundancy); its default is protected. The separate read-only protection-state reports the current protection of the interface and defaults to unknown. Other defaults: proxy-arp-enabled false (only applicable to the DCN interface), if-dhcp-relay false, admin-state unlock, oper-state disabled, alarm-report-control allowed. if-name is a string 0..64 and if-type is ethernet, software-loopback, point-to-point, ppp or hdlc. Example: set interface-DCN protection-mode protected.

Yes, that is what ip-monitoring does. A monitoring instance periodically pings a destination and the result takes action on configured static-routes. Create one with add ip-monitoring-<name> destination <value> next-hop <value> [probe-interval <value>] [drop-rate <value>] [enabled <value>] [action <value>] [static-route <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>]. action is the action to take when monitoring goes into the 'failed' state, takes none or withdraw, and defaults to withdraw, so the route is pulled by default. static-route is the list of connected static routes for this instance, a string with a maximum of 10 elements. destination is the remote host to monitor (ipv4-address or ipv6-address). next-hop defines the exit interface as an IPv4 or IPv6 source address, and the monitoring instance is not active until the exit interface is configured. probe-interval is the time between two consecutive pings, 0..60 seconds, default 5. drop-rate is the accepted ping drop rate in 10% steps, range 1..10, default 1. enabled is true or false, default true. The route side shows monitoring-state as unmonitored, ok or failed.

Use add ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> netmask <value>; netmask is mandatory and is the subnet specified as a netmask for that address, and only valid netmasks are allowed. Example: add ipv4-address-1-AUX-1/200.20.20.186 netmask '255.255.240.0', or on the DCN port add ipv4-address-DCN-B/10.220.192.213 netmask 255.255.252.0. Read it with show ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip> [netmask] [origin] and remove it with delete ipv4-address-<if-name>/<ip>. Pre-condition: a static IPv4 address cannot be configured when DHCP is enabled on the interface. These addresses are disallowed: addresses beginning with 0 (current network), addresses beginning with 127 (loopback addresses), and addresses beginning with 224 up to 255 (broadcast, multicast and experimental). origin is read-only and reports static, dhcp or auto-config, default static. if-name is a string 0..64; use '?' after ipv4-address- to list the available interfaces. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

distance is the distance to the next hop, a number in the range 1..255, and it defaults to 1. Set it on add ipv4-static-route-<ipv4-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>]. A discard route is created with special-next-hop, whose only value is blackhole (default blackhole), usable in add, set and show. Blackhole static routes are needed because routes advertised to an external AS must exist in the forwarding table installed by an IGP such as OSPF or by static routes, but not by BGP itself; for prefixes not present in IGP tables you configure a blackhole static route. Other attributes: advertised true or false, default false (when true the route is advertised in the routing protocol, and for OSPF it is advertised as an AS external route if OSPF is configured as an ASBR); origin manual or dhcp, default manual; interface must be bound to the same vrf given on the static route. Example: add ipv4-static-route-10.220.0.0/16/MGMT next-hop-address 10.220.225.165.

Almost, but the mandatory argument is prefix-length rather than netmask: add ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> prefix-length <value>, show ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip> [prefix-length] [origin], delete ipv6-address-<if-name>/<ip>. prefix-length is the length of the subnet prefix, a number in the range 1..128, and only valid prefixes are allowed to be configured. Note that an IPv6 /127 subnet is currently supported only on unprotected DCN-A (DCN) interfaces and does not apply to broadcast links with larger subnets. origin is read-only and reports static (statically configured, for example via NETCONF or the CLI), dhcp (assigned by a DHCP server) or auto-config (created by autoconfiguration), with default static. if-name is a string 0..64; use '?' after ipv6-address- to see the available interfaces. Examples: add ipv6-address-1-AUX-1/AAAA::186 prefix-length 10 and add ipv6-address-DCN-B/2620:38:4001:192:10:220:192:213 prefix-length 64. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. Static routes can be added with the DCN-B interface when DCN is operating in active-active mode. Use add ipv6-static-route-<ipv6-destination-prefix>/<vrf> [next-hop-address <value>] [advertised <value>] [distance <value>] [interface <value>] [origin <value>] [label <value>] [special-next-hop <value>] and name DCN-B on the interface parameter, for example add ipv6-static-route-2620:38:4::/64/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN-B (the DCN equivalent is add ipv6-static-route-::/0/MGMT next-hop-address 2620:38:4::8:8000:1 interface DCN). The VRF bound to the interface must match the vrf given on the static route. distance is 1..255, default 1; advertised is true or false, default false; origin is manual or dhcp, default manual; special-next-hop takes blackhole for discard routes. monitoring-state reports unmonitored, ok or failed. Access is Operational and Candidate configuration mode.

Use show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address> [if-subtype] [if-id] [address-oid]. This retrieves management address information about a particular chassis component; there may be multiple management addresses configured on the remote system identified by a particular index whose information is received on the local system, and each management address must have a distinct 'management address type' (subtype) and 'management address' (address). lldp-port is the local port connected to this LLDP neighbor (an instance) and direction is ingress or egress. address-subtype is the type of management address identifier encoding used in the associated address attribute (string), and address is the string used to identify the management address component associated with the remote system, length 0..64, whose purpose is to contact the management entity. if-subtype describes the basis of the interface associated with the address and is unknown, if-index or system-port-number; if-id is the integer interface number; address-oid is the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity advertised by the remote system agent, string 0..128. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

They carry the same attribute set but differ in key structure and in which side's LLDP ports they report. management-address is keyed show management-address-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<address-subtype>/<address>, including a direction key of ingress or egress. management-address-local drops the direction key: show management-address-local-<lldp-port>/<address-subtype>/<address>, and its example, show management-address-local, is described as viewing the management address information from the local LLDP ports. Both take the same read-only attributes: if-subtype (unknown, meaning the interface is not known; if-index, an identifier based on the ifIndex MIB object; or system-port-number, based on the system port numbering convention), if-id (the integer interface number) and address-oid (the OID identifying the hardware component or protocol entity advertised by the remote system agent, string 0..128; for management-address-local that field is currently an empty string). Both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, that is the use-as-source attribute of the networking command. It names the interface to use as the source address and is a string of length 0..64, used in both set and show, with no stated default. Configure it with set networking [use-as-source <value>], for example set networking use-as-source LO-MGMT, and read it back with show networking [use-as-source] or simply show networking. The command is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and use-as-source is the only parameter the networking object takes.

show networking-services. This command shows the list of network services and takes no parameters at all. It is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode, and show is its only verb, so there is no set or delete form and no per-instance key to supply. Example: show networking-services. For related network-wide settings use the separate networking command, which carries use-as-source, the interface to use as the source address.

Next-hop data is keyed by RIB because each next-hop entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family. For each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB per supported address family, so the RIB name is what pins a next hop to an address family. Syntax: show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address]. rib-name is a String of length 1..64 (pattern '([A-Za-z0-9 -.,]*)'), destination-prefix is an IP prefix, interface is the outgoing interface reference (for example DCN), and next-hop-address is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. Available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show next-hop-IPv4/0.0.0.0/0/DCN.

Use clear [-f] ospf [instance=]<value>. It removes and restarts an ospf-instance, and the operation is asynchronous, so the CLI does not wait for the restart to complete. The instance parameter is the id of the ospf-instance, given as a string, and it must be supplied. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation; without it you are prompted to confirm. Access mode is Operational Mode only. Example: clear ospf 1. The ospf-instance command description points at clear for removing an OSPF instance from the configuration asynchronously.

No. ospf-area-type accepts only the value normal, and normal is also the default, so stub and NSSA area types are not offered. Areas are managed with add / set / show / delete ospf-area-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id> [ospf-area-type <value>], where instance-id is uint8 in range 0..255 and ospf-area-id is a dotted-quad. The pre-condition is that the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ospf-area-1/0.0.0.0.

Use the ospf-area-range commands: add / set / show / delete ospf-area-range-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<prefix> [advertise <value>]. This summarizes routes for an OSPF area matching address/mask, and it is applicable to Area Border Routers (ABRs) only, so it has no effect on a non-ABR. advertise takes true or false and defaults to true (true advertises the summary, false hides it). The prefix may be an IPv4 prefix (length up to 32) or an IPv6 prefix (length up to 128), in canonical form with non-prefix bits zero. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created before the area can be added. Example: add ospf-area-range-1/9.9.9.9/10.220.0.0/16 advertise true.

Yes. ospf-instance has a version attribute with values ospfv2 and ospfv3, defaulting to ospfv2; version is settable only on add (it is not in the set syntax). Router id is chosen by router-id-mode, which takes manual or use-loopback and defaults to use-loopback; with use-loopback the pre-condition is that an ipv4 LO-MGMT address must be configured. With manual you supply router-id as a dotted-quad. instance-id is uint8 in range 0..255 and description is a String of length 0..128. show also exposes vrf. Example: add ospf-instance-2 description xyz router-id-mode use-loopback version ospfv3.

On ospf-interface the defaults are hello-interval 10 seconds (uint16, range 1..32767) and router-dead-interval 40 seconds (uint16, range 4..65535). Related defaults: retransmission-interval 5 s (2..3600), transmit-delay 1 s (1..450), ospf-cost 10 (1..65535), priority 1 (0..255, where 0 means not eligible for DR or BDR), enable true, ospf-if-routing auto (active, passive, auto). Yes, you can authenticate: ospf-auth-enable is true/false with default false and is relevant for ospfv2 or ospfv3; ospf-auth-algorithm is none or HMAC_SHA_256 with default HMAC_SHA_256, and ospf-auth-key is an ASCII string of length 0..256, both relevant for ospfv2 only. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance and OSPF area must exist first.

Use show ospf-neighbor-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<router-id> [state] [role] [address] [priority] in Operational Mode. The state values are: down (initial, no Hello packets received), init (Hellos received but bidirectional communication not yet established), 2-way (bidirectional established, DR/BDR election occurs here), exstart (DR and BDR elected, master-slave relation determined), exchange (neighbors exchange DataBaseDescriptor packets with LSA headers), loading (full Link State information exchanged based on DBDs) and full (full adjacency achieved). The role values are drother (Designated Router Other), dr (Designated Router), bdr (Backup Designated Router) and ptp (point-to-point). Note that an OSPF neighbor is deleted when the OSPF interface is down.

Use add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-<instance-id>/<ospf-area-id>/<ospf-if-name>/<spi> integrity-algorithm <value> [ipsec-protocol <value>] [ipsec-mode <value>], with matching set, show and delete forms. spi is a unique uint32 security parameter index in range 256..4294967295. integrity-algorithm is mandatory on add and accepts AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_384_192, AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256, AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_160 and AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96. ipsec-protocol indicates ESP or AH, with ESP as the value and default. ipsec-mode supports transport only, default transport. Pre-condition: the OSPF instance must be created first. Example: add ospfv3-ipsec-security-association-1/0.0.0.0/DCN/256 integrity-algorithm AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128.

Use ping [-c=<count>] [-w=<timeout>] [-s=<pktsize>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <ping-dest>. -i=<interface> specifies the source interface; by default the interface is selected according to the routing table. -v=<vrf> specifies the VRF; by default the MGMT VRF is used. The interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive, so you pick one or the other. -c stops after sending count ECHO_REQUEST packets, -w gives a timeout in seconds before ping exits regardless of packets sent or received, and -s sets the payload octets excluding headers, default 56, plus 8 octets of ICMP header for a total packet size of 64 octets. ping-dest may be an ipv4-address, ipv6-address or domain-name. Example: ping -c=1 -w=10 -s=1024 192.0.2.3.

Use show protocols, which lists them all in one place: ssh, cli, serial-console, netconf, restconf, grpc, snmp, http-file-server and data-model-openconfig. You can drill into any one with show protocols <name>, for example show protocols ssh. Typical attributes shown: ssh has enabled, port 8022, host keys and pre/post-login messages; cli enabled true, port 22, script-dir '/storage/scripts'; serial-console global-switch and global-timeout 60 minutes; netconf enabled true, port 830; restconf enabled true, http-enabled false, https-enabled true, http-port 8080, https-port 8181, cookie-timeout 5 minutes, api-root '/restconf'; grpc enabled true, port 50051; snmp enabled true, port 161, snmp-engine-id; http-file-server http-port 8980, https-port 8981, url-base '/transfer'. Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family]. Each entry represents a RIB identified by the 'name' key, and all routes in a RIB belong to the same address family; for each routing instance the system provides one system-controlled default RIB for each supported address family, so selecting the RIB selects the address family. rib-name is a String of length 1..64, vrf is a leafref to the VRF the RIB is bound to (path '../../vrf/name'), and address-family takes ipv4-unicast or ipv6-unicast. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: show rib-IPv4 displays the RIB identified by the 'IPv4' key.

Use show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol]. The command shows the list of system routes from various sources, such as dynamic protocols and static route, and the source-protocol attribute gives the source protocol for the route entry, for example OSPF, BGP or static. rib-name is a String of length 1..64 and destination-prefix is an IPv4 or IPv6 address. The special-next-hop attribute takes none, blackhole or unreachable with default none: none is normal routes, while for blackhole and unreachable routes no next-hop is created under the route. It applies to IPv4 and IPv6 static routes, rib:routes and IP Monitoring. Example: show route.

Yes. show routing displays the routing information. It takes no parameters at all, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the detail underneath it, use the related commands: show rib-<rib-name> [vrf] [address-family] for RIB entries per address family, show route-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix> [special-next-hop] [source-protocol] for the system routes and their source protocol, show next-hop-<rib-name>/<destination-prefix>/<interface> [next-hop-address] for next hops, and show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description] for the routing instances.

show supporting-interface-<name>/<interface> displays supporting interface information, that is, which underlying IPv4/IPv6 interface supports a given interface. The name parameter is the name of the interface (string), and the interface parameter is a reference to the IPv4/IPv6 interface, expressed as the path ../../../../../networking/interface/if-name. It is a show-only command with no add, set or delete form, and it is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. So it tells you the supporting interface relationship for an interface: the interface name you ask about, and the networking interface if-name that supports it. Running show supporting-interface without a key lists the supporting-interface entries.

Syntax: traceroute [-m=<hopcnt>] [-w=<timeout>] [-i=<interface> | -v=<vrf>] <tr-dest> [pktsize]. The maximum number of hops (-m, the max time-to-live value) defaults to 30, with a range of 1..255 (uint8). The VRF is set with -v=<vrf>; if not provided it defaults to MGMT. -i=<interface> sets the source interface, and by default the interface is selected according to the routing table; the interface and VRF name parameters are mutually exclusive. -w=<timeout> defaults to 2 seconds, range 1..10 (uint16). pktsize is the total probing packet size, default 60 (60 bytes for IPv4). tr-dest may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain-name. Example: traceroute -m=10 -w=3 1.2.3.4.

Use show vrf-<name> [type] [chassis-name] [description], which shows the Virtual Routing and Forwarding (VRF) instance. name is the VRF name, a String of length 0..32. type gives the VRF type with values mgmt (Management VRF) and internal (Internal VRF). chassis-name gives the associated chassis name for that VRF, which is how you see which chassis each instance belongs to. description is a String of length 0..255 describing the VRF and its intended purpose. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: show vrf-MGMT displays the Management VRF attributes.

Use activate [-f] swimage [label <string>] [db-action <empty-db|upgrade-db|rollback|auto>]. A successful swimage activation implies a system restart, so yes, the node restarts. The optional db-action parameter specifies the action applied to the database on activation: auto (the default) processes the database with the system default behavior, empty-db activates with an empty database, upgrade-db activates by upgrading the current database, and rollback rolls back to the previous active software image. If db-action is not provided the system decides automatically. Unless the -f option is given, the user must confirm the activation when prompted. label specifies the sw image/manifest file name; if not specified, the currently installable image is used. Examples: activate swimage db-action=empty-db, activate -f swimage.

No. Only a single location led test can be running at a time, so you cannot flash two cards simultaneously. Use activate location-led [entity=]<value> [[timeout=]<value>] [[led-mode=]<value>], where entity is a chassis or a card. led-mode is flash (default), an amber light blinking at 1 Hz used for LED location, or solid, a steady amber light used for lamp test; in lamp test all chassis LEDs light amber. timeout is a number in the range 0..120 seconds, default 0, which means no timer and the function runs until stopped. To turn it off, use terminate location-led <entity>; invoking it when no test is active has no effect. Note that the timeout parameter does not take effect in 1830 GX G30 R5.1, so terminate must be used, and not all cards support the Location LED test.

Use bootstrap ([local-port=]<value> | [neighbor-address=]<value>) [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-password=]<value>. It bootstraps a neighbor NE by establishing a TLS connection over the OSC link and provisioning the initial administrator account, for use during commissioning when the OSC peer NE has no configured users yet. Select the neighbor either with local-port, the supporting-port of an osc-eth MGMT interface as shown by show interface (for example 1-1-dwdm-line1), or with neighbor-address, the IPv6 link-local address of the OSC peer including zone (string length 7..256, pattern 'fe80:.*'). With local-port the system maps it to the OCE netdev (OCE-<chassis>-<slot>-<vlan-id>) and resolves the peer address via get_osc_neighbors.sh; if resolution fails the RPC is rejected. new-admin-user is mandatory, length 1..32, and follows local user naming rules. new-password may be plain text (standard complexity rules apply) or a SHA512 hash ($6$<salt>$<hash>, salt 2..16 chars). Available in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Type cancel-upgrade. That is the whole command; the only flag is -h, which displays help for the command. It cancels any active upgrade in progress. Access mode is Operational mode, and the pre-condition is that an upgrade must be in progress for the command to execute successfully, so if nothing is running the command will not execute successfully. There are no other parameters, no entity or target to name, and no force flag. To see the state of the upgrade before or after cancelling, use show upgrade-status.

change-ztp-mode enabled starts ZTP, reverts the database to the factory default and triggers a system reboot, so on an in-service node you lose the configuration and the node reboots. The syntax is change-ztp-mode [-f] [ztp-mode=]<value>, where ztp-mode takes enabled or disabled and there is no default; -f forces the command without confirmation, so without it you are prompted. change-ztp-mode disabled disables ZTP and stops ZTP if it is already in progress; the command can be executed while ZTP is running, interrupting it. Access mode is Operational mode. The current ZTP mode configuration is displayed with show ztp.

Use show current-fw, which lists the current firmware available in the cards, or narrow it with forms such as show current-fw-<card-name>-<port-name>/<fw-name>, show current-fw-<card-name>.<slot-name>/<fw-name>, show current-fw-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>/<fw-name> or show current-fw-<name>/<fw-name>, each accepting [fw-version] [expected-fw-version] [fw-status]. Compare fw-version (current version, String 0..32) against expected-fw-version (String 0..32); fw-status states it directly, with values current (firmware is up-to-date), not-current (current firmware is not up-to-date against the expected one) and unavailable (firmware status information is currently unavailable), default unavailable. fw-name is a String of length 0..32. Example: show current-fw-1-3/DCO_1.

download supports these filetype values: crl (a CRL file in PEM format), database (a previously uploaded database), file (any file to the file-system), krp (key replacement package), local-certificate (PKCS#12 with password-protected private key, or PKCS#7 if pending-import), peer-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#12), script (a CLI script), swimage (downloads a manifest file then all files belonging to a SW image) and trusted-certificate (X.509v3 PKCS#7 Root or Intermediate CA). The system automatically stores the downloaded file in an appropriate place, so no local location is needed; use show transfer to see the default storage directory. The exception is filetype file, where the destination parameter may be omitted (default directory, original name), a file-name only, a relative path or an absolute path, and you need write access to it. A downloaded database is stored as a db-instance=temp database, overwriting any existing temp. Source is a file-server plus path, or a URL using ftp, sftp, scp, http, https or file; ftp and http require secure-mode disabled.

Use show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature], which retrieves information about downloaded image files. manifest-file is the downloaded manifest file (String, length 0..256), name is the name of the downloaded software image (String, length 0..256), and signature is the downloaded software image file signature (String, length 0..1024). Running show downloaded-image with no key shows all the downloaded software image files. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

show downloads shows a list of downloads. It takes no parameters, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands: show downloaded-image-<manifest-file>/<name> [signature] retrieves information about downloaded image files including the file signature, and show transfer-status gives the progress of a transfer started asynchronously with download -a.

Yes, with limits. The `file` command (Operational mode) performs basic file and directory operations: `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>`. Supported operations are rename (renames a file or directory), view (listing for a file or directory), delete (deletes a file), sha256sum and md5sum (hash checksums). `new-file-path` is only used with rename and follows pattern '[A-Za-z0-9 \-/\.]*'; `result` reports the file operation result. File system access is restricted to the current user's access, so not all files/directories are editable. Separately, `clear [-f] file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` removes one particular file; filetype may be krp (only 1 krp may exist, so target-file is not needed), script (use `show script` to list available scripts) or swimage (deletes a downloaded swimage which was not yet installed). Examples: `file rename /tmp/a.log /tmp/b.log`, `file delete /tmp/a.log`, `clear file krp`.

Both are described as performing basic file and directory operations and both run in Operational mode, but `file` is the fuller command. `file-operation [[operation=]<value>] [new-file-path=]<value> [file-path=]<value>` supports only three operations: rename, delete, view, with parameters new-file-path (a new path to the file) and file-path (the path to the file), no defaults. `file [operation=]<value> [file-path=]<value> [new-file-path=]<value>` supports five operations: rename, delete, view, sha256sum (SHA256 hash checksum) and md5sum (md5 hash checksum), plus a `result` attribute for the file operation result, and its new-file-path is constrained to pattern '[A-Za-z0-9 \-/\.]*'. The `file` entity also carries the `clear file [filetype=]<value> [target-file=]<value>` form (filetypes krp, script, swimage) and `show file <filename>` to display file contents. So use `file` for checksums and for clearing files; `file-operation` covers only rename/delete/view.

Use `add file-server-<name> server-address <value> protocol <value> [server-port <value>] [user-name <value>] [password <value>] [initial-path <value>] [label <value>]`, with matching set/show/delete and `show file-servers`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration. The protocol values are file, ftp, sftp, scp, http, https; ftp and http are applicable only when secure-mode is set to false, and `file` represents local storage including USB storage and requires initial-path to be provided. server-address may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or domain name. server-port is optional: if not provided the default for the selected protocol is used. Field limits: name String 0...64 characters, user-name 0..64, password 0...128, initial-path 0...256 (the directory used as source/destination), label 0...256. Example: `add file-server-139 server-address '10.220.227.139' protocol 'scp' user-name 'root' password 'Nokia' initial-path '/root'`.

Use `show filetype-<name> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [last-operation]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `name` is the file type for which the transfer happened. `last-completion-status` gives the last transfer status, `last-transfer` is the last transfer start timestamp as a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ (see the set-time command), `last-duration` is the last transfer duration as a time-interval, and `last-operation` reports the last transfer operation with values unknown, upload or download. For a per-operation breakdown with progress and byte counts, use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation>` instead; note that transfer status only exists if at least one operation of that kind was done for the specified filetype.

Plain HTTP is supported but is off by default. Configure it with `set http-file-server [enabled <value>] [http-enabled <value>] [https-enabled <value>] [http-port <value>] [https-port <value>]`, and read it back with `show http-file-server [enabled] [http-enabled] [https-enabled] [http-port] [https-port] [url-base]`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `enabled` is the master switch for file server access, true/false, default true. `http-enabled` is true/false with default false; `https-enabled` is true/false with default true. `http-port` is a Number defaulting to 8980 and `https-port` defaults to 8981. `url-base` is show-only, the base URL used to redirect to the file transfer application, a String of 1..100 characters with default /transfer.

Use the `manifest` show commands (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). `show manifest-<manifest-file> [manifest-signature] [downloaded-on] [information]` gives the file-level view: manifest-signature is a hex-string of length 0..1024, downloaded-on is the download timestamp in format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and information is a String 0..256. `show manifest-component-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<name> [state] [version] [description]` gives per-package detail, where state is installed (software package installed), not-installed, installation-failed (install failed) or unknown, with default unknown; version is a string 0..64 and description 0..512. `show manifest-firmware-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]` lists the firmware included per equipment-type. Example: `show manifest-G30-R5.0.0-F-2021.11.04_20_04-46.manifest`.

No. Versions for the same firmware can be different per equipment-type within one software-load. Use `show packaged-fw-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`, or the shorter `show packaged-fw-<swload-state>/<equipment-type>/<fw-name> [fw-version]`; plain `show packaged-fw` lists all components' firmware versions in the load. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `location-id` is <chassis-id>-<slot-id> of the SW load subcomponent, string 0..64 characters. `swload-state` is active (active software load), inactive or installable. `equipment-type` is the type of equipment (card, etc) that will use the firmware, String 0..32, and `fw-name` and `fw-version` are also String 0..32. Output looks like packaged-fw-active/CHM6/DCO-OEC-FPGA and packaged-fw-active/XMM4/FCP_FPGA.

Yes. `prepare-upgrade` has two options: validate, which validates the software label/manifest, and apply, which applies it. Syntax: `prepare-upgrade [-f] [-i] [-u] [option=]<value> [manifest=]<value> [[db-action=]<value>] [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>`, Operational mode. Flags: -h help, -i ignore validation failures, -u unattended (auto-activate software after prepare-upgrade apply), -f force without confirmation. `db-action` is empty-db, upgrade-db or rollback, default upgrade-db, and is valid for unattended upgrade only. `clear-type` is full (reset to factory defaults, the default), keep-networking (wipe but keep network configuration) or initialize-from-script, and is only valid for an unattended operation with db-action set to empty-db. new-admin-user (0..64 chars) and new-admin-password are mandatory for keep-networking or initialize-from-script. Example: `prepare-upgrade validate -f G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188.manifest`.

`clear [-f] recover-mode` clears the recover-mode flag. It clears the current recover-mode state of the NE, confirming the current configuration as is, re-enabling communication with the line cards and potentially reconfiguring the traffic settings. Because of that reconfiguration it may be traffic impacting. The command runs in Operational Mode and has no parameters; the only flag is -f, which forces the command without confirmation. Normal use is `clear recover-mode` (which prompts for confirmation) or `clear -f recover-mode` to skip the confirmation prompt.

Use `show software-load-<swload-state>` at NE level or `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>` per card, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `swload-state` is active (active software load), inactive, or installable. Selectable attributes are swload-version, swload-manifest, swload-prepared, swload-status, swload-information, swload-activation-type, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label, swload-delta-label and swload-pkg-type. swload-manifest and swload-prepared (true/false) are only of relevance for the installable load, as is swload-activation-type with values direct (no reboot type determined), warmstart (warm reboot required) and coldstart. swload-status covers status-unknown, validate/apply/activate/cancel in-progress, complete, failed and timeout variants. Examples: `show software-load-active`, `show software-load-1-5/active`. For a one-line summary use `swversion`.

Use `show software-location-<location-id>`, where location-id is the location of the equipment, a String of length 0..64 expressed as <chassis-id>-<slot-id>. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `show software-location-1-5` retrieves software location information for the card in chassis 1, slot 5. To narrow to a particular load state on that slot, use `show software-load-<location-id>/<swload-state>`, for example `show software-load-1-5/active`, or go through the umbrella command: `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`, which returns the sw-component list plus swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label for that shelf-slot.

Use `show subtype-constraint-<card-type>/<subtype> [min-capacity] [max-capacity] [supported-applications] [unsupported-applications] [description]`, available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. card-type and subtype each represent a group of related PONs for a card type to which the constraints apply, strings of length 1...20. min-capacity is the minimum capacity supported by this subtype and max-capacity the maximum, both in gbps; a max-capacity of -1 means there is no maximum capacity constraint. supported-applications lists the applications supported by the subtype and unsupported-applications lists those not supported, both of application type; if either list is empty, then that constraint is not applicable. description is a string of length 1...255.

Use `show sw-component-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<name> [state] [version] [description]`, or `show sw-component-<swload-state>/<name>` for the NE-level view; plain `show sw-component` lists all SW load components and attributes. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `state` is the package state and is what tells you about a failure: installed (software package installed), not-installed, installation-failed (software package install failed) or unknown, with default unknown. location-id is <chassis-id>-<slot-id>, string 0..64; swload-state is active, inactive or installable; name is the package name, String 0..256; version is 0..64 and description 0..512. Example: `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`. To drill inside a failing package, use `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>`.

Use `show sw-container-<container-name> [equipment] [state] [description] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime]`, which shows the list of OS-level containers; access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `cpu-usage` is the current CPU usage by the container in percentage, Number range 0 ...100%, and in a multi-core system it indicates the overall usage relative to all cores. `memory-usage` is the current memory usage in percentage, range 0 ...100%. `state` is off (default state, not launched yet), up (container is up and running) or exited. `equipment` is a leafref to the card AID the container runs on, and `uptime` is the time since the container started. Examples: `show sw-container`, `show sw-container-frcu31-1-5_pyapi`. Per-service figures are available with `show sw-service-<sv-name>`, which also has cpu-usage and memory-usage.

Yes. `sw-control-rule` adds service-specific custom rules that override the default action upon service failure: `add sw-control-rule-<service-name> fail-action <value>`, `set sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action <value>]`, `show sw-control-rule-<service-name> [fail-action]`, `delete sw-control-rule-<service-name>`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `service-name` is the name of the service to be monitored, String of length 0..64. `fail-action` takes three values: default-action, which performs the policy of restarting the service, then rebooting the system if the service is not recovered; ignore, which specifies that no automatic action is taken in case of service failure; and system-restart, which performs a warm restart of the system/card software immediately upon service failure. Example: `add sw-control-rule-xmm4-1-1_host_KeyManagement fail-action default-action`.

Yes, `show sw-management` shows information about software locations, activity and downloads. Syntax: `show sw-management [downloads|software-location-<shelf>-<slot> [software-load-active|software-load-inactive|software-load-installable] |software-load-active|software-load-inactive]`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `downloads` shows the download history (a list of downloaded manifest files). `software-load-active` shows active software and `software-load-inactive` shows inactive software, each returning the sw-component and packaged-fw entries plus swload-version, swload-information, swload-vendor, swload-product, swload-label and swload-delta-label. `software-location-<shelf>-<slot>` scopes the same view to one card, and accepts software-load-active, software-load-inactive or software-load-installable. Example: `show sw-management software-location-1-4 software-load-active`.

Use `show sw-service-<sv-name> [equipment] [location] [state] [state-details] [cpu-usage] [memory-usage] [uptime] [last-start-time] [reboot-count]`, or `show sw-services` for all services and containers on the node. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `reboot-count` is the number of times a service has restarted, a uint16, and is the direct indicator of repeated restarts. Pair it with `last-start-time`, the time of the last service start/boot as a date-time in format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, and `uptime`, the time since the service turned up in days:hours:minutes. `state` is off (not being monitored), ok (ready and functional) or fail (failed to launch/turn-up or unresponsive), with `state-details` giving a brief description. `sv-name` is a unique Id per service instance containing card type, shelf and slot. Example: `show sw-service-frcu31-1-5_host_DpEncrMgr`.

`sw-subcomponent` adds one more level of key below the component, so you can see the individual packages inside a software load component. Syntax: `show sw-subcomponent-<location-id>/<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name> [state] [version] [description]`, or `show sw-subcomponent-<swload-state>/<sw-component-name>/<sw-subcomponent-name>` at NE level. `sw-component` is keyed only by <location-id>/<swload-state>/<name>. The reported attributes are the same in both: state with values installed, not-installed, installation-failed or unknown (default unknown), version (String 0..64) and description (String 0..512). sw-component-name and sw-subcomponent-name are strings of length 1..256. Both run in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `show sw-subcomponent-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg/ztp.deb` versus `show sw-component-1-5/active/frcu31_ztp_pkg`.

Run `swversion`. It retrieves the active, inactive and/or installable versions of the software present on the network element. The command takes no parameters and is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Output lists the NE-level loads and then the same per slot, for example: software-load-active R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188; software-load-inactive R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.04.15_14_26-sim-112; software-load-installable R4.0.0 G40-R4.0.0-F-2021.06.03_08_22-sim-188; followed by software-load-1-1/active, software-load-1-1/inactive and software-load-1-1/installable rows. For more detail on any one of them use `show software-load-<swload-state>` or `show sw-management software-load-active`.

Use `show third-party-fw-<fw-name> [file-status] [path] [version] [crc] [vendor] [part-number] [nsa-upgrade-version] [present-in-eqpt] [applicable-eqpt]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `file-status` is the firmware file status with values valid, invalid or missing. `crc` is the cyclic redundancy check of the firmware image, used to validate the file when present, string 0...64. `path` is the path for the firmware image, string 0...255. `applicable-eqpt` is the list of resources that this firmware can be applied to, and `present-in-eqpt` is the list of resources that already contain this version; both lists have max-elements 80. `nsa-upgrade-version` gives the versions from where the upgrade is non service affecting (nsa), string 0...255. vendor and part-number are strings 0...64.

Set it on the `transfer` entity: `set transfer [http-proxy <value>]`, read it back with `show transfer [debug-log-optional-content] [http-proxy]`. Access mode is Operational and Candidate configuration mode. `http-proxy` is the proxy server for internally-generated HTTP requests leaving the NE, which includes certificate revocation-related requests, that is CRL downloads and OCSP requests. Note that this proxy is not used for file transfers. The value is a string of length 0..1024 in the format '[http://]<host>[:<port>]', where 'http://' is optional, <host> may be the IPv4 address, IPv6 address or DNS name of the proxy server, and <port> is optional; if <port> is omitted the default is 1080. Example: `set transfer http-proxy http://1.2.3.4:1080`.

Use `show transfer-status-<filetype>/<operation> [last-completion-status] [last-transfer] [last-duration] [transfer-type] [session-id] [session-user-name] [filename] [transfer-progress] [bytes-transferred] [total-bytes] [details]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. `operation` is upload or download. `transfer-progress` is the transfer completion percentage, 0-100 percent, default 0; `bytes-transferred` and `total-bytes` are uint64 byte counts defaulting to 0, and total-bytes stays zero until known at the transfer start. `details` gives the transfer phase: completed, Failed, idle, preparation or transfer, default idle. `last-completion-status` is a String 0..128 such as success, fail, in-progress or unknown; unknown occurs when the system reboots while a transfer is in-progress. `transfer-type` is sync or async. In synchronous mode a textual progress bar is rendered live in the CLI; for asynchronous transfers (-a) use this command.

Use `show upgrade-status-<resource> [to-swload-version] [status] [start-time] [end-time] [step] [step-start-time] [details]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. Status is reported at NE level, chassis level and card level; `resource` (string 0..255) specifies the object, and for ne and chassis the results provide aggregated summaries of all cards in that scope, so start at the ne resource and then drill into chassis and card to locate the failure. `status` values include idle, upgrade-in-progress, upgrade-complete, upgrade-partially-failed, upgrade-failed, validate-in-progress/-failed/-complete, apply-in-progress/-failed/-complete, activate-in-progress/-failed/-complete, cancel-in-progress/-complete/-failed and no-communication; the default is idle. `step` is the identifier for the current upgrade step (string 0..128) and `step-start-time` when it was initiated; start-time and end-time show 'na' if idle or unfinished since startup, and `details` (0..255) carries the detail.

Use `upload [-a] [-s] filetype=debug-log (destination=<url> | file-server=<name> [path=<path>]) debug-entity=<value> [optional-content=<value>[,<value>]*]`, Operational mode. debug-log uploads logs for diagnostic troubleshooting and includes all other logs; debug-entity is mandatory and targets a chassis or card (if absent, all data is included). -a runs it asynchronously (check with `show transfer-status`); in synchronous mode a live progress bar is rendered. -s skips secure verification (TLS for HTTPS, ssh known host for SCP/SFTP). Certificates differ: filetypes local-certificate, peer-certificate and trusted-certificate require `certificate-name` to name the specific certificate, except for trusted-certificate where omitting the name exports all trusted certificates as a bundle. Only the public part is exported, private keys are not exported, and the output files are in P7 pem format. Example: `upload trusted-certificate destination=sftp://jz@100.113.83.14:/home/jz/demos/all.pem`.

Use `show ztp [ztp-mode] [ztp-state] [ztp-details] [ztp-completion-status]`, in Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode. `ztp-state` is the current state of the ZTP service and walks through ztp-init (the default), dhcp-in-progress, image-download-in-progress, image-install-in-progress, custom-script-execution-in-progress, multi-chassis-setup-in-progress, configuration-apply-in-progress, ztp-completed, ztp-state-unknown, ztp-disabled and wait-before-ztp-restart. `ztp-completion-status` summarizes completion on the node as not-completed (default) or completed. `ztp-details` is additional information on the current state, String 0..256. `ztp-mode` is the user-set mode, disabled or enabled with default enabled; it is set via the change-ztp-mode RPC, which is allowed even when the NBI is locked.

Use the `capabilities` command: `show capabilities-<name>`, where `name` is the name of the card (string, no default). It retrieves the capability information for that card. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For type-level (rather than instance-level) capability data, the companion commands are `show supported-card-<card-type>`, `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name>`, `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name>` and `show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>`.

Provisioning uses `add card-<name> required-type <value> chassis-name <value> slot-name <value>`; those three are mandatory. `required-type` is a String (length 0..32) from the supported list (BAXOFP2, BLANK, BLANK2, CAD10A, CHM1R, CHM2T, CHM6, CHM7, CHM7X, FAN, FAN-CTRL, FRCU, IOPANEL, PEM, RD20TM, SPN2, SPN2C, UCM4, UTM2, XMM4 and others). `chassis-name` is String 1..255, default 1; `slot-name` is a String. Optional on add: required-subtype, card-mode, subslot-name (settable only at creation), power-profile, alias-name, admin-state (default unlock), alarm-report-control (default inhibited), label. Example: `add card-1-4 required-type CHM1R chassis-name 1 slot-name 2`.

On 1830 GX G40 you must set the chassis ambient temperature to 40C before a Native ZR TOM will come up. If `configured-ambient-temperature` is not set, the system raises a port config mismatch alarm and the TOM cannot be provisioned. Set it with `set chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature 40` (the value is a number in Celsius units, no default), or supply it on `add chassis-<name>`. The attribute is the configured ambient temperature for the chassis and is used to compute the FRU's power consumption. It is readable with `show chassis-<name> configured-ambient-temperature`.

Use `set console-<name> baud-rate <value>` / `show console-<name> [baud-rate] [actual-baud-rate] [auto-sensing-state]`. Permitted values are auto-sensing, 9600, 19200, 38400, 57600 and 115200. The default is 9600 in 1830 GX G30 and 115200 in 1830 GX G40. Yes, it can work it out itself: with `auto-sensing` the system auto-detects the baud rate from 'ENTER' presses on the serial console client side, then locks it and reports it in `actual-baud-rate`. `auto-sensing-state` (visible only when auto-sensing is enabled) is sensing or locked, default sensing. Not all cards support auto-sensing; check `console-port-support` in `show supported-card`.

Use `show controller-card-<name> [redundancy-status] [redundancy-standby-status] [number-of-switchover-events] [time-of-last-switchover] [additional-details]`. `redundancy-status` is active, standby or not-in-service (default not-in-service). `redundancy-standby-status` tells you readiness: ready-synchronized (standby is in sync and ready), not-ready-synchronizing (synchronizing data with the active controller), not-ready-synchronize-fail, lock-out (protection in lock-out state), card-not-present; the default is not-ready-synchronizing. `number-of-switchover-events` (uint32) and `time-of-last-switchover` are visible only on the active controller card. `additional-details` is a string 0..128 with synchronization status detail.

Use `show equipment [<option>]`, which displays installed equipment information; access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. With no option it lists everything; supply an equipment option to narrow it to one item, for example `show equipment card-1-1`. Available options vary according to the installation. The output for a card lists its child objects (controller-card, console, ports) plus required-type, required-subtype, category, chassis-name, slot-name, max-power-draw, last-reboot-reason, alias-name, AID, admin-state, oper-state, avail-state, alarm-report-control and label.

Both are controlled by `set equipment-policies` / `show equipment-policies`. `tom-auto-migration` (enabled/disabled) enables automatic update of the TOM subtype based on the present equipment; it affects TOM subtype migration only, not TOM type migration (for example no update between QSFPDD and QSFP28), and the update may directly impact existing configurations. Per-port behavior is reported by `allows-auto-migration` in `show supported-port`. `auto-assigned-degrees` (enabled/disabled) enables automatic degree assignment when a card that supports degrees is provisioned; it defaults to disabled, but enabled if l0-mode-op is hsc-ols. Related: `auto-assigned-directions`, default enabled.

You must enable it. `set equipment-templates use-serdes-templates <value>` / `show equipment-templates use-serdes-templates` controls whether serdes-templates are globally enabled; values are enabled and disabled (the CLI value completion shows false / true) and the default is disabled. On enabling, templates are not applied retroactively; they are applied from that moment onward. On disabling there is no impact: existing serdes configuration is kept on all TOMs, whether it was applied via template or manually. Application of serdes-templates depends on this flag being 'true'; you can force re-application with the `apply-template` command.

Use `show fru-info-<manifest-file>/<equipment-type>`. This displays the packaged FRU information associated with a particular equipment-type. `manifest-file` is the manifest file, a string of length 0..256; `equipment-type` is the type of the equipment, a string of length 0..32. Neither has a default. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. This is packaged (shipped) data keyed by equipment type, as distinct from `show inventory-<name>`, which reports the data read from a FRU that is actually present.

Use the `inventory` command, which shows inventory data for a present FRU: `show inventory-<name> [serial-number] [clei] ...`. `serial-number` is the serial number of the equipment (String) and `clei` is the Common Language Equipment Identifier (String). The AID forms accepted are `inventory-<name>`, `inventory-<chassis-name>-<slot-name>`, `inventory-<card-name>-<port-name>` and `inventory-<card-name>.<slot-name>`. Other attributes on the same command include hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date, insertion-date, number-of-lanes, vendor-compliance-code, actual-power-class, actual-max-power-draw and fw-status. Example: `show inventory-1-3-1`.

Use `show led-<location>/<name> [status]` or `show leds`. The object exists even if the FRU is not physically present. `location` is the AID of the equipment location of the LED (chassis, card or port AID), String 1..32; `name` is the LED name within the FRU, String 1..16. `status` values are: not-available, off, yellow, flashing-yellow, green, flashing-green, red, flashing-red, cycling-with-off, cycling (all supported colors excluding off, used for lamp test), amber and flashing-amber. The default is not-available. Flashing states alternate between off and the named color.

In 1830 GX G40 there are three families of ports: comm-eth, USB and trib/line. comm-eth and USB ports exist on XMMs only and are found on Slot 1 XMMs. The trib/line ports appear on a CHM6 or CHM7 (slots 4-7) only after a TOM is present/provisioned in the CHM6/CHM7. Port objects are managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. The `port-type` attribute reported by `show port-<card-name>-<port-name> port-type` takes: line (line-side colored CWDM/DWDM module), tributary (grey client interfaces), tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, pluggable (the L0 module cage for a QSFP/SFP/SFP+ TOM) and ocm.

Use `show resources-<name> [internal-cell-switch-total-bandwidth] [internal-cell-switch-available-bandwidth] [paired-slot-total-bandwidth] [paired-slot-available-bandwidth]`. The internal cell-switch attributes apply only to SPN2/SPN2C cards and default to 600.000 Gbit/s if the card has paired slot interconnection capability. The paired-slot attributes apply only to SPN2/SPN2C cards that support Paired Slots: they default to 0 if the card has no paired slot interconnection capability, and 500.000 Gbit/s if it does. The same command also shows supported-carriers, unassigned-carriers and supported-sub-components. Example: `show resources-254-1`.

Read the `status` attribute of the serdes object: `show serdes-<card-name>-<port-name>/<serdes-name> [value] [status]`. `status` is the state of the advanced parameter as observable on the system once configured, with values: set (parameter set), unknown (parameter unknown), in-progress (parameter in progress), failed (parameter failed) and not-supported (parameter not supported). The default is unknown. `value` is the parameter value (string). A plain `show serdes` lists every serdes with its value and status, for example `serdes-1-7-T1/TxEQ 1 set`. Serdes entries are managed with add/set/show/delete.

Scope is by TOM part number, card type and port list. serdes-templates are created per `tom-part-number` (string, length 1..16) and apply to all line cards that support serdes; when a TOM with that part-number is plugged in, the template is automatically applied. `ports-applicable` narrows the list of ports: values are 'all' (the default, all ports considered) or port names as strings of length 1..16, up to a maximum of 20 elements. Syntax: `add serdes-template-<name> [tom-part-number <value>] [card-types-applicable <value>] [ports-applicable <value>]`. Manual serdes configuration is still allowed and is kept even if it deviates from the template. Swapping in a TOM with a different part-number resets the serdes configuration and re-applies the new template if one exists. Application depends on `use-serdes-templates` being 'true'.

Each entry is a serdes parameter name plus its value, added under the parent template: `add serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name> value <value>`. Edit with `set serdes-template-entry-<...>/<...> [value <value>]`, remove with `delete`, and read with `show serdes-template-entry-<serdes-template-name>/<serdes-template-entry-name>/<name> [value]`. `name` is the name of the serdes parameter, a string of length 0..256; `value` is the value of the serdes parameter, a string of length 0..256; `tom-part-number` is the TOM part-number the template applies to, string 1..16. Example: `add serdes-template-entry-T-DQ4CNT-NIN/RxEQ value 3`.

Yes. `set serial-console [global-switch <value>] [global-timeout <value>]` / `show serial-console [global-switch] [global-timeout]` set the global configuration of all serial console ports in the system. `global-switch` allows access by serial console; values enabled and disabled, default enabled, and each console port can override this global behavior. `global-timeout` is the serial console inactivity timeout, a number in minutes, default 60; it can be set to zero to disable the inactivity timer. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: `set serial-console global-switch enabled global-timeout 80`. Per-card override is `set console-<name> local-switch` (use-global-switch, force-enable, force-disable).

Use `show slot-<chassis-name>-<slot-name> [AID] [supported-type] [installed-type] [oper-state] [avail-state] [current-equipment]` (or `show slot-<card-name>.<slot-name>` for a subslot). `installed-type` is the currently installed type, `supported-type` the list of types the holder accepts, and `current-equipment` the name of the equipment currently required in this slot (for example 1-1). `oper-state` is enabled or disabled, default disabled. A plain `show slot` lists every slot in the node. For what a slot type can hold before anything is installed, use `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> possible-card-types` (list of up to 15 elements).

Use `show sub-component-<card-name>/<sub-component-name> [AID] [description]`; a plain `show sub-component` lists them all. `card-name` is the name of the card supporting the sub-component (string 0..64), `sub-component-name` is the sub-component name (string), `AID` is the Resource Access Identifier (string 1..64) and `description` is a user configurable description (string 0..128). Access is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example output: `sub-component-1-6/dco-oec`, AID 1-6-dco-oec, 'DCO OEC (Optical Engine Controller) sub-component'. The set of sub-components on a card is also reported by `show resources-<name> supported-sub-components`, which can be addressed for operations such as restart.

Use `show supported-card-<card-type> node-type-compatibility`. Node Type Compatibility refers to the supported NE node-type for a sled card, and is only of relevance for line-card(s) and carrier-card(s). The values are: all (compatible with any node-type), ILA (compatible with the In-Line Amplifier, two-directions node type) and OADM (Optical Add/Drop Multiplexer node type). So a card usable on an in-line amplifier node reports all or ILA. The same command also reports sw-support-revision, supported-subtype, description, default-card-mode, supported-card-mode, card-width, card-height, is-field-replaceable, category, grid-mode-support, max-power-draw, leds, location-led-support, console-port-support, default-console-baud-rate, support-serdes-config, supported-bands and supported-features.

Use `show supported-chassis-<chassis-type> [controller-redundancy-supported] [number-of-front-slots] [number-of-rear-slots]`. `controller-redundancy-supported` is true or false and says whether that chassis type supports controller redundancy. `number-of-front-slots` and `number-of-rear-slots` are uint8 counts of equipment holder slots in the front and back plates. chassis-type is an identityref such as G31, G32, G34c or G42. For example G42 reports controller-redundancy-supported true, 7 front slots and 12 rear slots. The same command reports supported-subtype, default-subtype, description, power-control-supported, fan-adjustment-on-altitude (default false), dust-filter-replacement (default optional-dust-filter), depth in mm, height in RUs, leds, supported-subchassis-type (max 10 elements) and supported-features.

Use `show supported-port-<card-type>/<port-name> [port-type] [configuration-mode] [faceplate-label] [allows-auto-migration] ...`, for example `show supported-port-CHM1R/2`. `port-type` says what the port is for: line, tributary, tributary-subport, usb, comm, uplink, optical, otdr, pluggable or ocm. `configuration-mode` says who configures it: system-configured (the system configures the card in the slot or TOM in the port and the user cannot make changes) or user-configured (the user can provision or de-provision). Also available: direction (not-applicable, tx, rx, rxtx), faceplate-label (1..36), leds (max 10), present (always or in-node-controller-only, default always), default-tom (default none), parent-port, subport-list and allows-auto-migration (true/false, default true).

Use `show supported-slot-<chassis-type>/<slot-name> [possible-card-types] [requires-blank-when-empty] ...`. `requires-blank-when-empty` states whether the slot needs a BLANK filler card when empty; values are not-applicable, optional and required. On a G42, the card slots 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and the PEM slots report required, while the IOPANEL, FAN and FANCTRL slots report not-applicable. `possible-card-types` lists the card types allowed in that slot, up to 15 elements (for example CHM6,UCM4 on G42 slots 4-7). The command also reports slot-location (front/rear), slot-vertical-position, slot-horizontal-position, configuration-mode, auto-provision-capable, default-card, reset-power (W at 55 degrees C), virtual-slot (default false) and leds.

Use `show supported-tom-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type>/<tom-subtype-group> [supported-subtype] [supported-phy-modes] [default-phy-mode]`. It displays capability information for a supported TOM in the scope of a particular card. `supported-phy-mode` lists the phy-modes supported for that TOM on that card and `default-phy-mode` the one used by default; the values are 100GE, 200GE, 400GE, 2x100GE, 4x100GE, 100G, 4x10G, 4x10GE, 1GE, 2G5, 10G, 10GE, 2G5E, 40GE, 40G, 4x100G and 200G. `tom-type` is the form factor (for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28, QSFPDD) and `tom-subtype-group` is a string 0..32 such as '4x100GE-breakout'. Examples: `show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFP28` and `show supported-tom-CHM1R/6/QSFPDD/2x100GE-breakout`.

Use `show supported-tom-power-<card-type>/<port-name>/<tom-type> [supported-power-class] [supported-max-power-draw]`. `supported-power-class` is the maximum MSA power class the host port supports for that pluggable type, a uint8 in the range 1..8 (the port may only partially support that class, so check supported-max-power-draw). `supported-max-power-draw` is the maximum power in watts the host port allows for that pluggable type under supported-power-class, a decimal64. `tom-type` is the pluggable form factor identity matching the TOM required-type (for example CFP2-DCO, QSFP28, QSFPDD). What the installed module actually reports is read with `show inventory-<name> actual-power-class actual-max-power-draw`, which is populated only for third-party transceiver subtypes on hosts that enforce power-class rules.

Yes. When you create a TOM with add tom-<card-name>-<port-name> required-type <value>, the Tributary Port termination point is auto-created with it, and it is automatically deleted when the TOM is deleted. The add form takes required-type (CFP2-DCO, OSFP, QSFP28, QSFPDD, QSFPDD-ZR, QSFPPLUS, SFP, SFPPLUS) plus optional required-subtype (string 0..32), phy-mode, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled), alias-name, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed/inhibited, default allowed), label, enable-serdes (true/false, default false) and power-mode (powered/not-powered, default powered; only applicable to TOMs on the CHM7 card). Example: add tom-1-4-T1 required-type QSFPDD. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use show tom-type-<tom-type> and read the support-third-party-toms attribute, which states whether that TOM type accepts third party TOMs in addition to supported Nokia TOMs; its values are true and false. The same command also returns description (string 0..255), tom-type (identityref), data-rate (uint16, Gbps) and generic-subtype, the 3rd party subtype for that TOM. show tom-type with no key lists all supported TOM types. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. Related: on the TOM itself, power-class-override (enabled/disabled, default disabled) is used to override the power class for a 3rd party TOM.

It appears under unprovisioned-inventory, which lists detected inventory that has not yet been accepted by the Node Controller in a Multi-Chassis configuration. Use show unprovisioned-inventory-<chassis-serial-number>/<slot-name>. The slot-name is empty when the equipment is the chassis itself. Available attributes are hardware-version, actual-type, actual-subtype, sw-support-revision, PON, serial-number (string 1..16), clei, vendor, part-number, manufacture-date (YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ, see set-time), and detection-timestamp, the last time the unprovisioned equipment was detected by the Node Controller. chassis-serial-number and slot-name are strings of length 0..16. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use show usb-<card-name>-<port-name> [type] [present] [available-space] [total-space] [usb-path]; show usb with no key lists all USB ports on the node. usb-path is the local filesystem path where the USB file-system is mounted and can be used as the target or source for file transfer operations (string, length 0..32). available-space is the current free storage space and total-space the total storage space in that file-system, both uint16 in MB. These three attributes apply only when type is storage; the other type value is power-supply, a port used to power external equipment such as passive shelves. present (true/false, default false) indicates whether the USB connector is inserted. Example: show usb-1-5-U1. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use activate-snapshot db-instance <string> db-paraphrase <string> [sanity-check-override <true|false>]. The pre-condition is that a snapshot must have been taken before it can be activated (see take-snapshot). db-instance names the database snapshot to activate and defaults to temp. paraphrase is a short description of the database to be activated, a string of length 40...200. sanity-check-override is an action to override the sanity check, with values true and false and a default of false. The command runs in Operational mode. Examples: activate-snapshot sanity-check-override, and activate-snapshot onehour to activate a snapshot named onehour.

Advanced parameter commands can only be executed on the node after enable-advanced-parameters on the optical carrier is set to true.
