Two documented behaviours explain what you are seeing: if no advanced parameter is configured, or the advanced parameter was deleted, show advanced-parameter reports ERROR: object does not exist; and if an advanced parameter is configured with an invalid value, the configuration is not rejected, but show advanced-parameter reports the failed status for it. The commands are add/set/show/delete advanced-parameter-[<card-name>-<port-name>|<optical-carrier-name>]/<advanced-parameter-name> value <value>. status values are failed, in-progress, not-supported, set and unknown, default unknown. advanced-parameter-name is a string of length 0..256. Supported names, values and defaults for CHM6 and CHM7/7X are in the 1830 GX System Description Guide.

Use apply-template [template-type=]<value> ([[applicable-tom=]<value>[,<value>]*]). For SerDes, template-type is serdes-template, which applies all existing serdes-templates to the TOM list given in applicable-tom; serdes-template is also the default template-type. If no specific TOMs are provided, that is the applicable-tom list is empty, all system TOMs are considered for template application. Example: apply-template serdes-template applies to everything, while apply-template serdes-template tom-1-7-T1 targets that one TOM; multiple TOMs are comma separated. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, use a confirmed commit: commit confirmed [confirm-timeout=<timeout>] [-id=<id>]. The candidate configuration is committed as usual, but if a confirmation does not occur before the timeout elapses, the configuration is rolled back to the pre-commit version, so the confirmation acts as a persist trigger. confirm-timeout is given in seconds and defines how long the commit stays pending before rollback; the default rollback time is 10 minutes. Confirm it with commit persist and abandon it with commit cancel. For a Persistent Confirmed Commit, all of these commands require the -id parameter, which defines the ID shared by commit confirmed, commit persist and commit cancel. All of these must be done in Candidate Configuration mode, entered with configure. commit -m=<message> attaches a custom message to a commit.

Use show config, and to get it back as replayable CLI, pipe it: show config | display commands, storing the result for later usage. This is the documented way to create a CLI script that can be used to restore the system configuration; see the display command for details. show config displays the system configuration and skips configurations that have their default values, so only non-default configuration is shown. The output is fully recursive from the current CLI scope, so running it at the top of the CLI hierarchy gives the complete system configuration. To narrow it, supply an entity-id (instance ID of one entity) or an entity-type when all entities of a given type are relevant: show config [(<entity-id>|<entity-type>)].

It depends on the target you pick. configure <target> takes exclusive or shared, and the default is exclusive. In exclusive mode only this session can make changes to the candidate configuration; in shared mode multiple sessions can make changes to the candidate configuration. The command moves you from operational mode into Candidate Configuration mode and is issued from Operational mode. You can also control how the candidate datastore is initialized: by default it starts from a copy of the Running Datastore; from-default starts from a blank config, removing all non-default configuration from the candidate; from-script=<script> imports configuration from a text file of CLI commands, replacing the running configuration content; from-commit=<commit-id> initializes from a past commit-record, which is only available when the Commit Repository feature is available, that is when the commit-tracking system-policy is enabled. Example: configure exclusive.

Use show current-advanced-parameter-<optical-carrier-name>/<current-advanced-parameter-name> [value]. This command shows the current values of the advanced parameters which are running on the system, as opposed to what you configured with add/set advanced-parameter. show current-advanced-parameter with no key lists them all, and a wildcard restricts to one carrier, for example show current-advanced-parameter-1-4-L2-1/*. Attributes are optical-carrier-name, current-advanced-parameter-name and value, all strings. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode. The running value can legitimately differ from the configured one. Note that PMDEquUpdSpeed cannot be added or modified; it is to be supported in a future release.

No. clear database performs a full wipe of the database contents, sets the NE database to default and reboots the system, and it is potentially traffic affecting and may interrupt connectivity to the system. It does not wipe logs, PM data and other non-configuration data; use the clear system command when you need a secure wipe or factory default. Syntax: clear [-f] database [[clear-type=]<value>] [script=]<value> [new-admin-user=]<value> [new-admin-password=]<value>, where -f forces the command without confirmation. clear-type is full (default, reset to factory defaults), keep-networking (wipe but keep network configurations) or initialize-from-script (wipe then initialize from a pre-stored .cli script, default directory /storage/scripts). keep-networking and initialize-from-script both require new-admin-user and new-admin-password and can only be triggered by the SA user. Transient alarms after the controller card reboot should be ignored.

Use db-migrate [-f] [type=]<value>, where type defines the protection mode to be configured and takes encryption-with-integrity or encryption. To add integrity protection on top of encryption, run db-migrate -f encryption-with-integrity; this enables the integrity check for the system database and will automatically reboot the controller. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. The command runs in Operational Mode. Verify the result with show db-protection-scheme, whose mode attribute reports encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity and states that it can be changed via the db-migrate RPC; with integrity enabled, integrity-algorithm becomes hmac-sha2-512 rather than none.

Use show db-protection-scheme [encryption-algorithm] [integrity-algorithm] [integrity-status] [mode] and read integrity-status, which indicates the status of the integrity check with the values passed-on-bootup, failed-on-bootup and disabled. The same output shows encryption-algorithm, whose value is xts-aes-256-plain64 (AES-256 encryption in XTS mode with 64-byte block size), integrity-algorithm with values hmac-sha2-512 or none, and mode, the current protection scheme of the DB, either encryption-only or encryption-with-integrity, which can be changed via the db-migrate RPC. A node with no integrity protection shows integrity-algorithm none, integrity-status disabled and mode encryption-only. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use diff [-t|-c] candidate, run in Exclusive Candidate Configuration mode. It lists the differences between the candidate datastore configuration and the current system configuration, covering created, deleted and changed objects, and shows only configurable attributes; new data means the candidate configuration and old data means the current system configuration. The default output is normal diff style, where + marks added objects or new values and - marks deleted objects or old values. The -t flag presents the data as a side-by-side diff in a table. The -c flag presents it as CLI commands that would perform the same configuration as was done in the candidate datastore, which is the form you want as commands; -d gives the list of commands being executed. There is also diff commit <id> [<id>] to compare a commit-record against the running configuration or another commit-record, available when commit-records exist (commit-tracking enabled in system-policies) or a pending Confirmed Commit exists.

Run discard-changes. It discards all candidate datastore content and returns the CLI to operational mode. The command takes no parameters and no flags, and its access mode is Candidate Configuration mode.

An extended-config is a non-standard configuration that introduces exceptional behavior globally in the system, so treat it with care and only enable one you understand. Using it requires knowledge of the extended-config name on the user side, and the name must match a name known by the system. The commands are add extended-config-<name>, delete extended-config-<name> and show extended-config-<name> [description]. name is a string of length 0..64. The description attribute (string 0..255) displays the description of the extended-config provided by the system and its effect in the system, so read that before adding one. Access mode is Operational Mode or Candidate Configuration Mode.

Check the Golden Advanced Parameter Table with show golden-advanced-parameter-<card-type>/<name> and read the service-impact attribute, which identifies whether applying this parameter change causes service impact; its values are service-affecting and non-service-affecting. If it is service-affecting you must perform an admin lock or maintenance operation, or other relevant operations. The companion attribute configuration-impact identifies the configuration steps needed to apply the change, with values no-change, no-reacquire, reacquire, full-config-pll-change and full-config-no-pll-change. The same command returns description, type, supported-values (list of ranges or discrete numbers), direction (transmit, receive, transmit-and-receive) and multiplicity, the number of values you must enter for the parameter. All attributes are read-only. Examples: show golden-advanced-parameter-CHM7/* or show golden-advanced-parameter-chm7/EEPNNLMitigation.

Run lock. It locks database access to the current session and grants exclusive write access to that CLI session; it is intended for ensuring configuration mastership for a small time. While the database is locked, another session, CLI or other type, that tries to make a configuration will receive an error. A lock will not be possible if another session is currently holding the lock. The lock is released by using the unlock command, or by closing the session that performed the lock, whether explicitly by the user, by an administrator closing the session, or via inactivity time-out. Syntax is lock [-h], where -h displays help; there are no other parameters. Access mode is Operational Mode.

A named-value-set is addressed by a two-part key: named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>, where db-entry-name is the name of the database entry and named-value-set-name is the user assigned name for that named-value-set. It holds a single value attribute, a string of length 1..1024 characters. The supported operations are add named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value <value>], set with the same form to change it, show named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name> [value] to read it, and delete named-value-set-<db-entry-name>/<named-value-set-name>. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

It can, and by default it does. set recovery restore-from-chassis-storage <value> controls this, with values disabled, auto-restore and auto-in-service, and the default is auto-in-service. With disabled, chassis storage is not used for restoration in this NE. With auto-restore, SW and DB are stored on the chassis storage and restored in recovery mode, and a manual clear recovery-mode command is then needed, which lets you validate the restored system before affecting the HW. With auto-in-service, SW and DB are restored in recovery mode and on successful restore the NC automatically leaves recovery mode. Monitor with show recovery, which reports restore-status (init, image-install-in-progress, db-restore-in-progress, check-completed, failed, disabled, wait-for-upgrade, wait-for-db-restore), backup-status (successful, failed, in-progress, unknown), last-backup and next-backup timestamps, both defaulting to never.

Only if the candidate is empty. rollback must be executed with the commit parameter and optionally a specific commit-id: rollback commit [<commit-id>]; if no commit-id is provided, the most recent commit-record is used. It works both in the Running Datastore, the default, and in the Candidate Datastore, but the rollback operation can be performed on the Candidate Datastore only if it is empty, which is a way to initialize the candidate. The command considers all commit records up to the provided commit-id, obtains the reverse-commands for each record, and replays them in order from latest to oldest, reverting the datastore to the state it was in prior to that commit-record. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

show commit retrieves commit record information and lets you visualize the Commit Repository records, but it is available only when the commit-tracking policy is enabled, or when a pending Confirmed Commit exists. If neither is true on your node there are no records to return. Enable it with set system-policies commit-tracking enabled; note that disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. Syntax is show commit [<id>|-s=<since>|-n=<number-of-records>], where <id> selects a specific commit-record, -s picks a timestamp and shows all records created since it, and -n selects an exact number of records to obtain. Access mode is Operational mode or Candidate Configuration mode.

Use set system-policies commit-tracking enabled to turn on the commit-repository feature. With it enabled, all configuration changes done via the running or candidate datastores are stored as commit-records, which can then be visualized, compared and rolled back; disabling the policy clears the commit-repository of all commit-records. The values are enabled and disabled, with a default of disabled, so commit tracking is off out of the box. The running datastore is writable by default: the companion writable-running policy also defaults to disabled, and disabling that policy makes it impossible to issue configure commands via the running datastore, forcing use of the candidate. In that state the CLI no longer allows add/set/delete except in Candidate mode, NETCONF allows edit-config only via the Candidate Datastore, RESTCONF, gNMI and the WebGUI and TL1 become read-only (gNMI telemetry is still allowed and gNOI is still allowed). Read both with show system-policies [commit-tracking] [writable-running].

The db-passphrase. The system will only accept take-snapshot if the db-passphrase, used for DB snapshot encryption, is configured, either in global configuration as part of security-policies (set security-policies db-passphrase) or locally as a parameter of the command, for example take-snapshot db-passphrase=***. The passphrase must be a minimum of 40 characters, must not contain any dictionary words, and may use special characters in accordance with the 85-character set known as Z85. Automatic DB snapshots are also not enabled until this parameter is set. Syntax: take-snapshot [[db-passphrase=]<value>] [[db-instance=]<value>] [[description=]<value>]. db-instance defaults to temp and may be temp, manual, onehour, oneday, oneweek or rollback; description is a string 0..128. Access mode is Operational Mode. Taking a snapshot whose name already exists overwrites the existing file.

Use the `template` commands. A template entry is an object/attribute pair plus the value to be used as the default for that attribute: `add template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> object <value> attribute <value> value <value> [sequence-id <value>] [label <value>] [condition <value>]`, with matching `set`, `show template-<group>/<name> [sequence-id] [object] [attribute] [value] [label] [condition]` and `delete`. object is the object name (e.g. odu), attribute the attribute name (e.g. admin-state), value is mandatory (e.g. lock); label and condition (e.g. service-type=OTU4) are optional. sequence-id is a Number in range 1..65535 and defines the processing order, lower ids first. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add template-1/FansInMaintenance object card attribute admin-state value maintenance condition card-type=FAN. Entries are pushed with apply-template.

No. A template-group is a configuration group holding a list of template entries, created with `add template-group-<name> [enabled <value>] [label <value>]`. The enabled attribute takes true or false, and its default is true only if there is no other template-group enabled. So the first group you add comes up enabled by itself, but with one already enabled a new group does not default to enabled; only one enabled group is in effect. Check with `show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label]` and remove with `delete template-group-<name>`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add template-group-1.

`show templates`. It shows the configuration that defines the data model for system templates, i.e. the overall templates view on the node. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. To drill down, use `show template-group-<name> [enabled] [label]` for a single template group and `show template-<template-group-name>/<template-name> [sequence-id] [object] [attribute] [value] [label] [condition]` for an individual template entry.

No. `unlock` releases a database previously locked with the `lock` command, but only the session that performed the lock can trigger the unlock. If a session tries to unlock a non-locked database, or a database that was locked by another session, the unlock command will fail. A lock is automatically released if the session that performed the lock is closed, so once the colleague's session drops the database frees itself. After the unlock, any session is able to perform configurations and to take a new lock. Syntax: `unlock [-h]`, where -h displays help for this command. Access mode: Operational Mode.

Yes. `validate candidate <candidate> command <string>` validates the contents of the specified configuration, that is, any CLI command(s) used to edit a configuration datastore by creating, deleting, merging or replacing content, without applying them. candidate is the candidate datastore used as target for validation; command is the command text to validate. If the command is validated, the reply is 'OK'; otherwise the command fails. Multiple CLI commands can be provided in one invocation if separated with ';'. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: validate 'set ne altitude 600'.

A maximum of 7 rounds. Use `add additional-key-exchange-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<additional-key-exchange-id> dh-group <value>` (set/show/delete on the same key), where additional-key-exchange-id is 1..7 and number is the IKE SA proposal number. You must choose a unique key-exchange algorithm for each round, and the rounds must be configured in the same order on both IKE peers; if the configuration does not match, an IKE-CONFIG-MISMATCH alarm is raised. Configuring additional-key-exchange is optional and causes the IKE session to go down immediately and renegotiate the new proposal. dh-group values: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512, ml-kem-768, ml-kem-1024. Port level (CHILD-SA) key exchange is derived from IKE. For PQC safety configure PPK or at least one post-quantum algorithm; ml-kem-1024 is recommended as the strongest.

`show data-path-encryption`. This command shows the datapath encryption attributes. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The related global L1 encryption policy is held on the ikev2 object: `show ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match]`, and per-card IKE state is under `show ikev2-local-instance-<name>` with scope data-path-encryption.

Use `add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>` for a Child SA proposal, or `add encryption-algorithm-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>/<algorithm>/<key-length>` for the IKE SA proposal; only add, show and delete exist (all values are part of the key). algorithm: null, aes-gcm-8, aes-gcm-12, aes-gcm-16, aes-ctr, aes-cbc, aes-ccm-8, aes-ccm-12, aes-ccm-16, chacha20-poly1305. key-length: none, key-length-128, key-length-192, key-length-256, default none. number is the proposal number for the IKE SA, range 1..max. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add encryption-algorithm-ipsec/GX2/1/aes-gcm-8/key-length-192.

On `add ike-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<number>` both integrity-algorithm and dh-group are required; prf is optional. integrity-algorithm: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. dh-group: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448, ml-kem-512. prf: hmac-sha2-256, hmac-sha2-384, hmac-sha2-512, hmac-sha1. number is the proposal number for the IKE SA, range 1..max. protocol-id is read-only, always IKE, and appears in show only. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ike-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/1 dh-group dhe-2048 prf hmac-sha2-256 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-384-192.

The top-level ikev2 object carries exactly one attribute, data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match: `set ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match <value>]` and `show ikev2 [data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match]`. It is a global, L1 encryption-specific policy indicating whether the NE must validate the certificate Subject Alternate Name to match the IKE ID (OPT-IN) or not (OPT-OUT). Permitted values are match and ignore; no default is stated. Access: Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set ikev2 data-path-encryption-san-ike-id-match match.

Read host-card-encryption-capability on the instance: `show ikev2-local-instance-<name> [host-card-encryption-capability] [scope] [host-card] [local-address-assignment-method] [local-address] ...`. It indicates whether the card on which this IKEv2 local instance is running supports encryption; values yes, no, unknown, default unknown. host-card is a reference to the service card the instance runs on. The local IKE address is picked by local-address-assignment-method, values auto or manual with default auto (show only). local-address is the local IPv4 address for the IKEv2 channel with prefix-length 32, settable, default 0.0.0.0. scope takes data-path-encryption, management-ipsec, local-address, local-address-assignment-method. Other settables: label, admin-state (lock, maintenance, unlock; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed, inhibited; default Inhibited). Example: set ikev2-local-instance-1-3 local-address 1.1.180.132.

On ikev2-peer, re-key-frequency is the re-key frequency for the IKE SA with the far-end peer, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800; re-auth-frequency is the re-authentication frequency, range 3600..604800 seconds, default 43200. Range and default values may be context-specific. The stated rule is that re-key-frequency and re-auth-frequency must not be multiples of each other, and they must differ by a few minutes to ensure a significant interval between re-authentication and re-keying. Related failure handling: re-key-fail-policy (kill traffic, continue traffic; default continue-traffic) with re-key-traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s, default 0, and re-auth-fail-policy with re-auth-traffic-kill-offset 0..86400 s, default 0. Set them with `set ikev2-peer-<local-instance>/<peer> re-key-frequency <value> re-auth-frequency <value>`.

Use `add ipsec-sa-proposal-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<number> dh-group <value> [integrity-algorithm <value>]`. dh-group is required, integrity-algorithm is optional. dh-group: dhe-2048, dhe-3072, dhe-4096, dhe-6144, dhe-8192, ecp-256, ecp-384, ecp-521, curve-25519, curve-448. integrity-algorithm: none, hmac-sha2-256-128, hmac-sha2-384-192, hmac-sha2-512-256, hmac-sha1-160, hmac-sha1-96. number is the proposal number, 1..max. protocol-id is read-only and always ESP, and esn (Extended Sequence Number support) is read-only with value esn; both appear only in show. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ipsec-sa-proposal-ipsec/GX2/dns/1 dh-group dhe-3072 integrity-algorithm hmac-sha2-512-256.

Yes. `add ipsec-sa-re-key-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> [frequency <value>] [bytes <value>] [packets <value>]` (also set/show/delete) sets the re-key trigger for the IPsec child SA with the far-end peer. frequency is time based, range 3600..86400 seconds, default 14400. bytes re-keys on the amount of bytes transmitted, range 1048576..max, default 1073741824. packets re-keys on the amount of packets transmitted, either disabled or a number in range 1..9223372036854775808, default disabled. So volume based re-keying on bytes is on by default at 1 GB, while packet based re-keying is off until you set it. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The action attribute of ipsec-spd-entry indicates the IPsec treatment given to matching IP datagrams: protect, bypass or discard, default protect. And yes, it tunnels by default: mode is tunnel or transport with default tunnel. Syntax: `add ipsec-spd-entry-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name> priority <value> [description <value>] [action <value>] [ipsec-protocol <value>] [mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [esn <value>] [anti-replay-window <value>] [dynamic-ts <value>]`. priority is mandatory (uint8) and gives precedence between SPD entries. ipsec-protocol is ESP. esn true/false, default true. anti-replay-window applies when action=protect, range 32..1024, default 64. dynamic-ts disabled/enabled, default disabled. alarm-report-control allowed/inhibited, default allowed. Example: add ipsec-spd-entry-ipsec/GX2/dns priority 1 action protect.

Create a traffic selector under the SPD entry and hang the address and port ranges off it. `add ipsec-traffic-selector-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name> [next-layer-protocol <value>]`; next-layer-protocol is the inner (upper layer) protocol taken from the IPv4 protocol or IPv6 next header field, with values any (value 0), opaque (value 255) or a number in range 0-255, default any. The selector name is a string of length 1..64, pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*). The addresses and ports themselves are added as children of the selector: local-subnet and remote-subnet for the prefixes, local-ports and remote-ports for the port ranges. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add ipsec-traffic-selector-ipsec/GX2/Radius/ts1 next-layer-protocol 17.

Because start and stop are part of the instance identifier, not editable attributes. The AID is local-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>, and only add, show and delete are defined; there is no set. To change a range, delete the existing entry and add the new one. start takes all, opaque or a port number; stop is a port-number and defaults to 0 if not set, but 0 is only accepted when start is all or opaque. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: add local-ports-ipsec/GX2/tacacs/ts1/all and, for a single port, add local-ports-ipsec/GX1/dns/ts1/53/53.

Add it under the traffic selector: `add local-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>`, with matching show and delete forms. prefix is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, and broadcast for IPv4 only) and is part of the key, so there is no set command; to change it, delete and re-add. The parent names are the local instance name and peer name (string 1..64, pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*)), the SPD entry name (string 1..32) and the traffic selector name (string 1..64). Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add local-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/101.10.10.1/32.

That depends on link-security-control on the macsec-entity, which controls the link security policy for handling data packets when the MACsec connection is not available. Values are must-secure and should-secure, and the default is must-secure, so by default unsecured traffic is not passed. Set it with `set macsec-entity-<name> [link-security-control <value>]` or on `add macsec-entity-<name> [supporting-facility <value>] [enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [link-security-control <value>] [replay-protection <value>] [replay-protection-window <value>]`. enabled is true/false, default true; replay-protection is enable/disable; replay-protection-window is the number of packets in range 0..4294967295, default 0. show also exposes oper-state and negotiated-cipher-suite. Example: add macsec-entity-6-3-3 supporting-facility ethernet-6-3-3.

Set it on the macsec-mka object: `set macsec-mka-<name> [connectivity-association-key <value>] [connectivity-association-key-name <value>] [mka-policy <value>] [psk-lifetime <value>] [psk-expiration-warning <value>] [psk-lifetime-enable <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]`. connectivity-association-key is the pre-shared Connectivity Association Key and connectivity-association-key-name its name, both strings of length 0..64. Which end is key server is read from is-key-server, values true/false with default false, via `show macsec-mka-<name> [is-key-server] ...`. psk lifetime/expiration warning is range 1..173 with default 14 days, and psk-lifetime-enable is enabled/disabled. Example: set macsec-mka-6-3-3 connectivity-association-key 1122334411223344556677889900112233445566778899001122334455667788 connectivity-association-key-name aa.

On the mka-policy object, which is the MACsec Key Agreement policy referenced by the macsec entity related to the ethernet facility: `add mka-policy-<name> [key-server-priority <value>] [macsec-cipher-suite <value>] [confidentiality-offset <value>] [sak-rekey-interval <value>]`, with matching set, show and delete. macsec-cipher-suite selects the cipher suite used for Secure Association Key (SAK) derivation. sak-rekey-interval is the SAK re-key interval in seconds, range '0|30..65535', default 30s, so 0 or 30 to 65535. key-server-priority is the priority used by the MKA protocol to select the key server. confidentiality-offset specifies the number of octets in an Ethernet frame that are sent in unencrypted plain-text. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use the `re-auth` command, which performs a re-authentication operation of IKEv2 security associations. Syntax: `re-auth [ikev2-peer=]<value>`, where ikev2-peer is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), given as a string. Access mode: Operational mode. Both the keyword form and the plain AID form work, for example re-auth ikev2-peer=ikev2-NE202 or re-auth ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX2. The scheduled interval is governed separately by re-auth-frequency on the ikev2-peer (3600..604800 seconds, default 43200).

`re-key` performs an on-demand re-key on one of three targets: a data path encryption secure entity, an IKEv2 peer, or an IPsec child security association (Security Policy Database entry). Syntax: `re-key [ipsec-security-association=]<value> | [ikev2-peer=]<value> | [secure-entity=]<value>`. ipsec-security-association points to the IPsec SPD entry object (Child SA), ikev2-peer references the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and secure-entity points to the secure entity object (Child SA); all are strings. Access mode: Operational mode. Examples: re-key secure-entity=NE202-1-4-L1-1 and re-key ikev2-peer-ipsec/GX.

Set the starting port to all and leave the stopping port off: `add remote-ports-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<start>/<stop>`, for example add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/all. start accepts all, opaque or a port number; stop is a port-number and, if not set, the system assumes the value 0, which is only accepted when start is set to all or opaque. Only add, show and delete exist since start and stop are part of the key. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. A single port is given as start=stop, e.g. add remote-ports-ipsec/GX2/protect1/ts1/49/49.

Add a remote-subnet under the traffic selector: `add remote-subnet-<ikev2-local-instance-name>/<ikev2-peer-name>/<ipsec-spd-entry-name>/<ipsec-traffic-selector-name>/<prefix>`, with matching show and delete. prefix is a list of ranges of IPv4/IPv6 addresses (unicast, and broadcast for IPv4 only) and is part of the instance key, so there is no set; change it by deleting and re-adding. The parents are the IKEv2 local instance name and peer name (string 1..64, pattern ([A-Za-z0-9 \-.,]*)), the SPD entry name (string 1..32) and the traffic selector name (string 1..64). Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: add remote-subnet-ipsec/GX2/dns/ts1/102.20.20.2/32.

Use the sc-rx command, which shows the Receiving Secure Channel attributes: 'show sc-rx-<name>/<index> [sci-rx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]'. The 'state' attribute is the one that tells you usage: it is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, with values 'in-use' (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel is in use) and 'not-in-use' (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). The AID is keyed by 'name', a String of length 0..64, plus 'index', the Receiving Secure Channel Index (uint8). 'sci-rx' is the Receiving Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode; sc-rx is show-only.

sc-tx reports the Transmitting Secure Channel attributes and is show-only: there is no add, set or delete for it. Syntax is 'show sc-tx-<name>/<index> [sci-tx] [state] [association-number] [key-identifier] [next-packet-number]'. The key is 'name' (String, length 0..64) plus 'index', the Transmitting Secure Channel Index (uint8). 'sci-tx' is the Transmitting Secure Channel Identifier, a hex-string of length 16. 'state' is the state of the secure channel returned by the MKA stack, with values 'in-use' (Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel is in use) and 'not-in-use' (no Secure Association(s) under this Secure Channel are in use). Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A secure-application is an application that uses an X509v3 certificate as its digital identity. Assign its identity with 'set secure-application-<id> [active-certificate-id <value>] [verify-client-cert <value>]', where 'id' is a string of length 0..20 and 'active-certificate-id' is a string of length 0..128 holding the list of assigned certificates, for example 'set secure-application-WebGUI active-certificate-id client' or, for multiple, 'set secure-application-gRPC active-certificate-id certX,certY'. To require a certificate from clients, set 'verify-client-cert' to 'required' (client certificate is required and validated); the alternative is 'disabled' (client certificate is not requested), which is the default. For TLS Mutual Authentication this must be 'required'. Changes take effect for new TLS connections only and do not affect existing connections. 'show secure-application-<id>' also returns 'type' (server or client), 'in-use' (a leafref to ../active-certificate-id) and 'status' (enabled or disabled); 'show secure-applications' lists them all. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

That is governed by 're-key-fail-policy' on the secure-entity, which indicates the NE's policy and consequent action when re-keying the IKE security association is unsuccessful. Values are 'kill-traffic' and 'continue-traffic', and the default is 'continue-traffic', so by default the node does not drop traffic. If you set 'kill-traffic', 'traffic-kill-offset' indicates the amount of time the system waits before killing all encrypted data security associations tied to that IKE SA; its range is 0..86400 seconds with a default of 0. Both are settable on add and set, for example 'add secure-entity-NE202-1-4-L1-1 supporting-facility optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1 remote-secure-entity '1-4-L1-1' re-key-fail-policy kill-traffic traffic-kill-offset 300'. The related 're-key-frequency' for the IKE SA with the far-end IKE peer ranges 3600..86400 seconds, default 28800.

No. secure-entity-sa-proposal is show-only: 'show secure-entity-sa-proposal-<name>/<number> [encryption-algorithm] [encryption-key-length] [integrity-algorithm] [dh-group]'. Every algorithm attribute has exactly one permitted value, which is also its default: 'encryption-algorithm' is aes-gcm-16, 'encryption-key-length' is key-length-256, 'integrity-algorithm' is none, and 'dh-group' (the Diffie-Hellman group advertised to the far-end secure entity peer) is ecp-521. The proposal 'number' likewise has the single value 1, default 1, and 'name' is the proposal name for the secure entity SA (string). Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. So the secure entity SA algorithm set is fixed and only readable.

Through the security-policy-database object, whose key is the IKE peer itself: 'add security-policy-database-<ikev2-local-instance>/<ikev2-peer-name> [associated-secure-entity <value>]', with matching set, show and delete forms. 'ikev2-local-instance' is the name (ID) of the local IKE protocol daemon instance, 'ikev2-peer' is a reference to the IKE peer object (IKE SA), and 'associated-secure-entity' is the list of all SPD entries associated with this far-end peer for which IKE negotiates security associations (keys). All three are strings. Example on 1830 GX G40: 'add security-policy-database-ikev2-local-instance-1-6/ikev2-NE202-1-4 associated-secure-entity secure-entity-1-6-L1-1'. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, using cdp, which manages manually configured CRL Distribution Points; each CDP supports download and auto-refreshing of a specified CRL. Use 'add cdp-<name> url <value> [enabled <value>] [refresh-interval <value>]', then set/show/delete, plus 'show cdps'. 'url' is the HTTP URL of the CRL in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]/<path to crl file>', where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the path conventionally ends in .crl, for example http://crl.example.org/pki/myCA.crl. 'enabled' (true/false, default false) enables automatic download and periodic refresh; enabling immediately triggers a CRL auto-download, and when disabled no refresh or updates are performed but existing CRLs are unaffected. 'refresh-interval' takes either the special enum 'use-next-update' (next refresh time comes from the current CRL next-update field) or a '[xw] [xd] [xh] [xm] [xs]' string such as '2w', '5d 12h' or '1h 7m 30s'. Show also returns next-update-time, last-update-time and last-update-result (string 0..255). Requires System Administrator privilege; Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use cert-gen, which generates a self-signed certificate, in Operational mode: 'cert-gen [-f] [certificate-name=]<value> [[days=]<value>] [[org-name=]<value>] [[common-name=]<value>] [[subject=]<value>] [SAN=]<value>] [auto-install <true|false>]'. Validity is set by 'days', the number of days a certificate is valid for, which defaults to 365. 'certificate-name' is a string of length 1..128, 'org-name' and 'common-name' are strings of length 1..64, and 'subject' (full certificate subject name) is a string of length 1..1024. You must specify either 'subject' or 'common-name' when generating the self-signed certificate. 'auto-install' (true/false, default true) auto-assigns the certificate to any secure-application without an active certificate. The '-f' flag forces the command without confirmation. Example: 'cert-gen -f certificate-name=self-signed-cert1 days=10 org-name=testorg common-name=testcert auto-install=true'.

Via cert-to-name, which defines a prioritized set of rules used to map an X.509 client certificate to a specific user identity; each rule either extracts a username from a certificate field or maps it directly, optionally restricted to a specific issuer in the trust chain. Use 'add cert-to-name-<id> map-type <value> field <value> mapped-user-name <value> criteria <value> [priority <value>] [issuer <value>] [enabled <value>] [label <value>]', plus set, show and delete. 'map-type' is 'extract' or 'map'. 'field' applies only when map-type is extract and selects the certificate attribute used to determine the identity: common-name, san-any, san-dns-name, san-ip-address, san-rfc822-name, san-upn or san-uri. 'mapped-user-name' is required only when map-type is 'map' and defines the local or remote user identity. 'criteria' defines the attributes and conditions required for the rule to be invoked. 'priority' ranges 1 to 255, 'issuer' filters to certificates from a specific issuer (value 'any'), and 'enabled' is True or False with default True. Example: 'add cert-to-name-rule_name map-type extract field san-dns-name'.

Use the certificate command in Operational mode. Delete with 'clear [-f] certificate [type=]<value> [id=]<value>', where 'type' is trusted, local or peer, and 'id' is the certificate ID (string, length 0..128) which must match a currently installed but unused certificate of that type; press <tab> to obtain the list of certificate-ids that can be cleared. Examples: 'clear certificate local certX', 'clear certificate type=trusted id=certY', 'clear certificate trusted id=root' (which prompts 'Are you sure? [y/n]'); '-f' forces without confirmation. The type field also accepts the bulk purge options purge-all-invalid, purge-all-unused, purge-all-expired, purge-local-unused and purge-peer-unused. To list what is installed, run 'show certificates', which displays all managed local/trusted/peer X509v3 certificates on the system that were imported by download mechanism in PKCS#12 or PKCS#7 secure bundles; 'show certificate-revocation' shows certificate revocations.

Use the crl clear command with a selective clear-target: 'clear [-f] crl [[clear-target=]<value>] [crl-name=]<value>'. The targets are 'single-crl' (remove the CRL specified in <crl-name>; this is the default and <crl-name> is mandatory and must match a currently installed CRL), 'purge-invalid-crls' (purge all invalid CRLs), 'purge-cached-crls' (purge all CRLs that were automatically cached from a configured CDP or certificate CDP extension) and 'purge-all-crls' (purge all CRLs). To drop only stale entries use 'clear crl purge-invalid-crls'; to remove one named list use 'clear crl single-crl myCA-1'. Use <tab> to obtain the list of CRL names that can be cleared. Check first with 'show crls' or 'show crl-<name>', where 'status' reports valid, expired or future and 'type' reports whether the CRL was installed 'manually' or 'cached' from a CDP. Clear runs in Operational mode; Candidate Configuration mode is only for the show command.

csr-gen generates a Certificate Signing Request from user provided information. The consequence of the command is the creation of a local-certificate in the 'pending-import' state, plus the output of a CSR in PKCS#10 PEM format. That CSR is then used with an external Certificate Authority to produce a full certificate, which is downloaded into the system to produce a complete local-certificate. So the node holds a half-formed local-certificate entry with the key pair until the signed certificate is imported. Syntax is 'csr-gen [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] ... [[subject=]<value>] [[SAN=]<value>]'. Access mode is Operational mode. 'key-algorithm' defaults to eccp256; the subject's CN RDN is mandatory, for example 'csr-gen myCertificate subject='/CN=Nokia''.

Use display-cert with the 'display-type' parameter: 'display-cert [certificate=]<value> [display-type=]<value>'. The permitted values are 'all-certificate-hierarchy', 'certificate-details' and 'certificate-hierarchy', and the default is 'all-certificate-hierarchy'. So to see the trust chain rather than just the certificate's own fields, ask for a hierarchy display type; 'certificate-details' is the value that shows only the certificate's own details. 'certificate' is a string naming the certificate to display, and tab completion offers the installed names such as local-certificate-pace_client, local-certificate-server_cert, trusted-certificate-ca_root and trusted-certificate-pace_root. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The command shows the details of a certificate or a CSR.

Use the est command. Enrollment over Secure Transport enables automated certificate management over HTTPS, and the device's EST client replaces the complex, manual steps of the traditional CSR process. Syntax: 'est [target-command=]<value> [[est-ca=]<value>] [certificate-name=]<value> ([[key-algorithm=]<value>] | [[key-from-certificate=]<value>]) [[signature-hash-algorithm=]<value>] [[metadata-template=]<value>] ... [[http-user=]<value>] [[http-password=]<value>]'. 'target-command' selects the operation: 'cacerts', 'enroll' or 're-enroll'. 'est-ca' identifies the CA set for EST and defaults to 1. 'key-algorithm' accepts eccp256, eccp384, eccp251, rsa2048, rsa3072, rsa4096; 'signature-hash-algorithm' is sha512, sha384 or sha256 with default sha256; 'metadata-template' defaults to 'generic' with options from-existing-certificate, from-openssl-cnf, generic, generic-tls-server, generic-tls-client and generic-ikev2-identity. Example when a valid mTLS certificate does not exist: 'est enroll certificate-name=myNewCertificateA subject='/CN=NewCertA' http-user=<username> http-password=<password>'. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Yes, through est-ca: 'set est-ca-<name> [explicit-ca-root <value>] [root-fingerprint <value>] [auto-re-enrollment <value>] [label <value>]'. 'auto-re-enrollment' specifies when re-enrollment is performed for all leaf certificates issued by this EST CA, expressed either as a number of days before expiration (1 to 365) or as a percentage of the 'not after date' minus 'not before date' interval, rounded up, accepted from 10% to 90% in increments of 10%; the value 'disabled' turns it off and is the default. If auto re-enrollment fails for any reason, the RE-ENROLL-FAIL alarm is raised for the affected certificate and re-enrollment is retried once per day until either it succeeds or the certificate becomes invalid, for example by expiring. The CA is pinned by 'explicit-ca-root', the trusted root certificate for the EST CA, together with 'root-fingerprint', which verifies the identity of the Root CA using a SHA-256 or SHA-512 hash to ensure a secure initial connection. Example: 'set est-ca-1 auto-re-enrollment 40'.

The EST server port is set by 'server-port' on the est-server object and defaults to 443. Yes, you can define more than one: est-server entries are keyed as '<name>/<server-name>', so 'add est-server-<name>/<server-name> server-address <value> [server-port <value>] [priority <value>] [enabled <value>] [path-segment <value>]' can be repeated, with matching set, delete and show forms. 'priority' defines the server's precedence and ranges from 1 to 10; if omitted, the priority defaults to the current lowest precedence (highest existing number) plus one, and if a priority of 10 already exists the value must be configured manually. 'enabled' is True or False with default True, and 'path-segment' is an optional label added to the EST base url (string, length 0..64). Example: 'add est-server-1/my-est-server server-address 10.23.55.123 server-port 8443'. Access mode is Operational and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use import-certificate, which imports one or more certificates in PEM format into the NE: 'import-certificate {-i, <certificate type>} [<certificate-name>] <string in PEM format> [<passphrase>]'; 'import-certificate -h' displays help. The certificate type is local-certificate, trusted-certificate or peer-certificate. 'certificate-name' is the name by which the certificate will be known in the system, and 'passphrase' decodes encrypted input certificates (applies to trusted-certificate, local-certificate and bundles). The '-i' flag imports any intermediate certificates present in a PEM string bundle; for files with a single certificate it imports any intermediate certificates specified through the AIA extension. Root certificates need to be installed individually. If no certificate-name is given, the name is derived from the topmost certificate issuer /CN plus a numeric suffix, for example trusted-certificate-Nokia-1 and trusted-certificate-Nokia-2 for issuer /CN=Nokia. Examples: 'import-certificate local-certificate certificate-name=local-cert-1 <string in PEM format> <passphrase>' and 'import-certificate trusted-certificate certificate-name=bundle-1 -i <string in PEM format>'. Access mode is Operational mode.

Check the ISK object before clearing it: 'show ISK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [is-key-in-use] [is-key-verified] [being-deleted] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time]', or 'show ISKs' for the list. 'is-key-in-use' indicates if the key is in use in this FRU (true/false, default false), 'is-key-verified' indicates if the key is verified in this FRU (true/false, default false), and 'being-deleted' is set to true once the system gets an ISK delete command, indicating the system is in the process of deletion and will soon delete this ISK. 'KRK-name' names the Image Root Key that signed this ISK. To remove one, use 'clear [-f] isk [key-name=]<value>', supplying the name of the key to be deleted (String, length 0..64), for example 'clear isk key-name=name'; '-f' forces the command without confirmation. Clear runs in Operational Mode; Candidate Configuration Mode is only for the show command.

Use the KRK commands, which show the list of Image Root Keys and KRK information: 'show KRKs' returns the list, and 'show KRK-<name> [CPU] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload]' returns one key's details, for example 'show KRK-1-5-0-KRK_E1'. 'name' is the unique representation of the object, 'CPU' is the identifier for member CPUs on cards and starts at 0 (uint8), 'key-name' is a String of length 0..64, 'key-serial-number' is a String, 'issuer-name' is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a String of length 0..20, 'key-length' is the key length in bits (uint16), and 'key-payload' is the key payload in hex format, a String of length 0..1100. KRK is show-only; access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

The key-replacement-package command: 'show key-replacement-package [KRP-name] [KRP-version] [key-name] [key-serial-number] [issuer-name] [key-length] [key-payload] [KRK-name] [signature-hash-scheme] [signature-algorithm] [signature-payload] [signature-gen-time] [install-status]'. It is show-only. 'KRP-version' is the package version, 'issuer-name' is the name of the CSA (Code Signing Appliance), a string of length 0..20, and 'KRK-name' is the name of the KRK (Image root key) that signed this ISK. 'signature-hash-scheme' is SHA2 256, SHA2 384 or SHA2 512; 'signature-algorithm' is ECDSA, RSA or none; 'signature-payload' is a hex string 0..1024; 'signature-gen-time' is a date-time in the format YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ. 'install-status' indicates if this KRP has been installed in the system, with values not-installed, installing, installed and failed. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, using the 'revocation-mode' attribute of local-certificate, which controls how the revocation status of the certificate is determined: 'set local-certificate-<id> [revocation-mode <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]'. Values are 'auto', 'force-revoked' and 'force-unrevoked', with 'auto' as the default. Setting 'force-revoked' forces the node to treat the certificate as revoked; 'force-unrevoked' forces the opposite. 'id' is a String of length 1..128 matching the pattern for certificate names. 'show local-certificate-<id>' also returns 'status' (valid, revoked, expired, untrusted, future, pending-import for a CSR awaiting import, plus the legacy in-use, unused and available values) and 'used-by', the list of foreign keys representing secure-applications, ikev2-peers and so on presently using the certificate. 'alarm-report-control' is allowed or inhibited, default allowed. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

Use 'add ocsp-server-<name> url <value> priority <value> [enabled <value>]', with 'set ocsp-server-<name> [priority <value>] [enabled <value>]', 'delete ocsp-server-<name>' and 'show ocsp-server-<name> [url] [enabled] [priority] [last-query]'. Order is set by 'priority', a uint8 in the range 1..10, used to sort the OCSP responders in order of precedence: lower numbered OCSP responders are consulted before higher numbered ones, so give the responder you want tried first the lowest number. 'url' is the HTTP URL of the OCSP responder in the form 'http://<host>[:<port>]', where host may be an IPv4/v6 address or DNS name and the port is optional (otherwise the default HTTP port 80 is used); it is a string of length 0..1024 matching pattern 'http://([^\s/$.?#][^\s/]*)'. 'enabled' (true/false, default false) controls whether this server is consulted for revocation status, and 'last-query' is the timestamp of the last successful query ('never' or a date-and-time). Example: 'add ocsp-server-1 url http://1.2.3.4:8101 priority 3 enabled true'.

A peer-certificate is the X509v3 end-entity certificate that represents a trusted 'remote peer' certificate for the L1 encryption secure application. Manage it with 'set peer-certificate[-id] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>] [revocation-mode <value>]' and 'show peer-certificate[-id] ... [white-listed] ...'. The 'white-listed' flag (true/false, default false) means that if true, the peer-certificate does not have an associated trust-chain and was explicitly white-listed at import time; otherwise it has an associated trust-chain. 'trust-chain' is a leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id. 'status' values are revoked, expired, pending-import, untrusted, future, valid and unsupported (with in-use, unused, available and invalid deprecated in favour of valid/untrusted plus the used-by attribute). 'revocation-mode' is auto, force-revoked or force-unrevoked, default auto; 'alarm-report-control' is inhibited or allowed, default allowed. Access mode is Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

SSH is configured with 'set ssh [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [pre-login-message <value>] [post-login-message <value>]' and read with 'show ssh'. The 'port' attribute is the port listening for ssh login that goes directly to shell; its range is 1..65535 and its default is 8022. It is not on by default: 'enabled', which enables direct access to shell via ssh, takes true or false and defaults to false. 'pre-login-message' is the welcome message displayed before user login (String, length 0..1440) with no default, and 'post-login-message' is displayed after login (String, length 0..1440) and defaults to the standard warning banner stating the system is restricted to authorized users for business purposes and may be monitored. The ssh object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Add an ssh-authorized-key for that user. Each authorized key entry contains a trusted public key for SSHv2 user authentication. Use 'add ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> public-key <value> [label <value>]', with 'set ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [label <value>]', 'show ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id> [public-key-algorithm] [public-key] [label]' and 'delete ssh-authorized-key-<user-name>/<key-id>'. 'user-name' is the user owning the authorized key and can be a local or remote user (String, 0...32); 'key-id' is a unique identifier (name) for this entry (String, 1...64). 'public-key' is the SSHv2 (OpenSSH Portable) host public key component encoded in PEM format as '<key type><SPACE>...base64 encoded OpenSSH public key...<SPACE><comment>', a String of 0..2048 characters. 'public-key-algorithm' is read back as ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072 or ssh-rsa4096. Example: 'add ssh-authorized-key-admin/1 public-key AAAAE2VjZHNh...'. Deleting prompts for confirmation. Access mode is Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `show ssh-host-key-<public-key-algorithm>` (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). These are the global SSHv2 host keys, used by both server-side and client-side SSHv2 based apps. There must be one host key per supported algorithm, so yes, more than one exists. The system auto-generates a host-key in the default DB, and additional host-keys can be added or overwritten via the ssh-keygen RPC. The public-key-algorithm values are ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096 and ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 support starts in R9.0). Each entry shows public-key (OpenSSH/PEM string, 0..2048 chars), label (0..256 chars), fingerprint-algorithm (md5 or sha256) and fingerprint (0..95 chars, pairs of hex digits). `show ssh-host-key` lists all; `show ssh-host-key-ecdsa-sha2-nistp521` shows one.

`ssh-keygen [-b=<key-length>] [-l=<key-label>] [-t=<type>]` (Operational mode) generates a private/public key pair, and the existing keys in the system are replaced with the newly generated pair. `-t` selects rsa, ecdsa or ed25519, default rsa. `-b` sets strength: RSA 2048/3072/4096, ECDSA 256/384/521, ED25519 256. With secure-mode enabled (see security-policies/secure-mode) RSA only supports 4096 and ECDSA supports 384 or 521 (default 384); with secure mode disabled RSA supports 2048, 3072 or 4096 (default 2048) and ECDSA supports 256, 384 or 521 (default 256). ED25519 is 256 regardless of secure mode. `-l` sets the key label; if omitted the label is the value of ne-id. Retrieve the new public key with `show ssh-host-key`.

Create an SSHv2 known-hosts entry: `add ssh-known-host-<id> address <value> public-key-algorithm <value> public-key <value> [label <value>]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `id` is a unique name, String 0..64 characters. `address` is the hostname, IPv4 or IPv6 address of the allowed/known peer host, and may carry a zone index after a % sign for link-local addresses. `public-key-algorithm` is one of ecdsa-sha2-nistp256, ecdsa-sha2-nistp384, ecdsa-sha2-nistp521, ssh-rsa2048, ssh-rsa3072, ssh-rsa4096, ssh-ed25519 (ED25519 support starts in R9.0). `public-key` is the OpenSSH host public key in PEM form, String 0..2048 characters. `label` is a user defined String 0..256. Afterwards only `set ssh-known-host-<id> label <value>` is settable; use `show` to view and `delete ssh-known-host-<id>` to remove.

The `trusted-certificate` object holds the X509v3 CA (Root and Intermediate) certificates trusted by the system. Use `show trusted-certificate[-id]` to view version (v3), serial-number, subject-name, issuer, trust-chain (leafref to /ne/system/security/certificates/trusted-certificate/id), valid-from, valid-to, modification-time, status (in-use, unused, revoked, expired, available, pending-import, invalid, untrusted, future, valid, unsupported), public-key-length (rsa2048/rsa3072/rsa4096/ecdsa256/ecdsa384/ecdsa521), public-key-type (rsa, ecdsa), signature-key-type (rsa, ecdsa, rsassa-pss), signature-hash-algorithm (sha256, sha384, sha512, sha1), certificate-bytes, key-usage and extended-key-usage. Settable: revocation-mode (auto, force-revoked, force-unrevoked; default auto), alarm-report-control (allowed, inhibited; default allowed) and label. Removal is done with `clear certificate`. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Issue `terminate cable-id` (Operational mode) to stop all running CableID verification tests. Because verification is performed on a port-pair basis, the test can only be terminated after the current port-pair verification completes and before the test starts for the next port-pair: the in-progress port-pair runs to completion, then the test exits. The maximum delay to terminate is one port-pair verification time. The test is known to be terminated once cable-id-status `cable-id-state` changes to *idle*, so after issuing the command use `show cable-id cable-id-status` to confirm the cable-id entity is back in the idle state. Related: `show cable-id` lists the cable-id entities; the test itself is started with the `verify` command.

The CableID signal can only be sourced or terminated by CAD10A and RD20TM sleds; the signal is transparently passed in the OPSM. The CableID path starts at the *end A* port and terminates at the *end Z* port, where the signal is sourced/terminated, that is at a CAD10A DWDM port or an RD20TM ADE port. Accordingly `show cable-id-path-<name>` reports card-type-a and card-type-z with values RD20TM or CAD10A, plus port-a and port-z (port AIDs). The card type is derived from the provisioned fiber-connection at the port-A/port-Z attribute: when a fiber-connection is created, the CableID function examines whether it is associated with a port on a CableID capable sled and, if so, captures that card type into the CableID path topology. In R8.0.1 the supported sleds are CAD10A and RD20TM.

Yes. `show cable-id-status [cable-id-state] [test-progress]` is the container holding the process status and progress information of a CableID-based fiber connection verification, and you are allowed to issue `show cable-id cable-id-status` at any time to query the progress. `cable-id-state` is idle (verification not running), running-incl-switching (running for both active and protected paths) or running-no-switching (running only for the active path); default idle. `test-progress` is a string (0..255 chars), default 'None': it reads "Not applicable" if cable-id-state is disabled, or "N out of M completed" while running, where M is the total number of port-pairs to be tested and N the number of port-pairs whose testing has completed. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Each carrier can discover up to one node. It is possible for multiple collocated carriers to discover the same node multiple times, each time connected to a different remote carrier. Use `show carrier-neighbor-<local-carrier> [last-update] [age] [local-carrier-id] [ne-id] [ne-name] [ne-type] [remote-carrier-id] [ipv4-loopback-address] [ipv6-loopback-address]` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `local-carrier` is the local carrier instance that discovered the neighbor node (string 0..16). ne-id and ne-name are strings 0..256, ne-type 0..64, remote-carrier-id 0..64 and is the AID of the remote carrier connected to the local carrier, implying a specific remote port id. last-update is a date-time in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ format. The loopback addresses may be empty if not configured.

Use `show connection-ports-<degree-number>/<index> [port-name]` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `degree-number` is a uint16 in range 1..20 and must be greater than zero and not greater than max-degrees. `index` is a uint32 in range 1..2 but is always 1 in the 1830 GX, since dwdm-line ports are bi-directional. `port-name` is an instance-identifier pointing to the dwdm-line port of an RD or ILAx card; as a consequence the OMS of the corresponding dwdm-port is created. `show connection-ports*` lists every connection port in the node, for example connection-ports-1/1 -> port-1-3-dwdm-line1, connection-ports-5/1 -> port-4-1-dwdm-line1. `show connection-ports-5/1` shows just that one entry.

Use `show custom-tlv-<lldp-port>/<direction>/<oui>/<subtype> [value]`, which shows the list of Organizational Specific TLVs (Type-Length-Value) parameter information. Access is Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. `lldp-port` is the local port associated with the LLDP agent, string length 0..64. `direction` is the direction associated with the LLDP statistics, ingress or egress. `oui` is the Organization Unique Identifier of this TLV, the hexadecimal representation of the 24 bit identifier, string length 1..6. `subtype` is the sub-type identifier of the TLV within the scope of that OUI, string length 1..507. `value` is the retrieved TLV content.

No. The external-fiber-connection is set autonomously by TNMS, and although it is possible to configure it manually, it is not recommended to do so. It is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations. Syntax: `add external-fiber-connection-<name> src-port-name <value> dst-port-name <value> [label] [scope] [src-node-id] [src-card-name] [dst-node-id] [dst-card-name] [fiber-connection-type]`. Before R8.0 the user also had to set port external-connectivity to *yes*. `scope` is general-purpose (default) or cable-id; if scope is not cable-id the CableID verification excludes the connection. After upgrade to R8.0.1 or later scope defaults to general-purpose, so to enable CableID you must delete the existing entries and add new ones with scope cable-id. fiber-connection-type is one-way or two-way, default two-way.

A `fiber-connection` is the physical link representation of a connection between two distinct ports (or two distinct sub-ports) in the same NE, in an OADM/ILA topology. An `external-fiber-connection` is the physical link representation of a connection between two ports of L0 cards in different NEs, or in the same NE in disaggregated configurations, and it is set autonomously by TNMS (manual configuration is possible but not recommended). fiber-connection takes `name` (0..64 chars), `label` (0..256), `src-port` and `dst-port` as instance identifiers, and `fiber-connection-type` one-way or two-way, default two-way; add/set/show/delete are all available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode with no pre- or post-condition. external-fiber-connection instead uses string src-port-name/dst-port-name plus node-id and card-name fields, and adds the `scope` attribute (general-purpose or cable-id).

Yes. `icdp` is the Nokia Carrier Discovery Protocol, and its only attribute `global-switch` is a flag to enable icdp with values true or false and a default of true, so the protocol is on by default. Use `set icdp global-switch <true|false>` to change it and `show icdp [global-switch]` to view it, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The icdp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Example: `set icdp global-switch true`.

INCI is the Inter-NE Communication Interface, an API based communication infrastructure for control plane communication across different network elements, for example between a Transponder (such as CHM6 on 1830 GX G40) and line systems (FLEXILS). It uses gRPC server/client as the core mechanism: when the INCI service is enabled the gRPC server starts and binds to the local IP address, and when an INCI neighbor instance is configured gRPC client sessions are established. It is not running by default: the `inci-enabled` switch takes true or false with a default of false. Enable it with `set inci inci-enabled true` and check with `show inci [inci-enabled]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode.

Compare the `configured-node-name` you provisioned against the `discovered-node-name` reported by the far end. `configured-node-name` is the user provisioned name of the remote NE, string 0..128, and is explicitly used to compare against the discovered-node-name; `discovered-node-name` is the name of the remote NE as sent by the remote NE, string 0..128. `discovered-node-id` (string 0..12) gives the node ID of the remote node as received from it. Use `show inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> [neighbor-address] [neighbor-port] [connection-status] [configured-node-name] [discovered-node-name] [discovered-node-id] [alarm-report-control] [oper-state]`. Both names are supplied at creation: `add inci-neighbor-<neighbor-id> neighbor-address <value> configured-node-name <value> [alarm-report-control <allowed|inhibited>]`, where alarm-report-control defaults to inhibited and oper-state is enabled or disabled.

Two attributes on `interface-neighbor` control this. `discovery-cycle-time` is the periodicity at which sndp discover messages are sent, range 30..300 seconds, default 30. `discovery-timeout` is the time after which discovery is considered failed; when this timeout occurs the neighbor-adjacency-state transitions to blackout. Its range is 300..1800 seconds, default 300. Set them with `set interface-neighbor-<local-interface> [discovery-cycle-time <value>] [discovery-timeout <value>] [discovery-enabled <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [label <value>]` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `discovery-enabled` is true or false, default true. `neighbor-adjacency-state` shows blackout, discovery, holding or unknown, default unknown; oper-state is enabled or disabled, default disabled.

No. `show links` displays the links container within the topology, and these links are dynamically filled in by the system, allowing the NCT topology to be derived and displayed. The command takes no parameters and is available in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The related `show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port>` shows NCT connectivity information, the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE, and those links are likewise dynamically filled in by the system.

The global `lldp` object carries a single attribute, `hold-on-timer`: the time to keep neighbor information in case the neighbor does not have an explicit Time-To-Live (TTL) TLV. It is a number of seconds and defaults to 900. Use `show lldp [hold-on-timer]` to view it and `set lldp [hold-on-timer <value>]` to change it, for example `set lldp hold-on-timer 60`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. The lldp object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Per-neighbor, `show lldp-neighbor` reports a `ttl` giving the number of seconds until the remote system information expires; if the remote system does not provide a ttl value, that parameter is set to the global hold-on-timer.

`show lldp-local-info-<lldp-port> [chassis-id-subtype] [chassis-id] [port-id-subtype] [port-id] [port-description] [system-name] [system-description] [supported-capabilities] [enabled-capabilities]` shows the LLDP local system information sent on an lldp-port. chassis-id-subtype is chassis-component and the 1830 GX NE uses the chassis serial number as chassis-id. port-id-subtype is local and the NE uses the port AID as port-id. port-description uses the port name, system-name uses the NE name, and system-description uses the string 'Nokia Corporation.Converged OS, Version <release id> _ build <software label>'. All these strings are 0..255 characters. supported-capabilities and enabled-capabilities take router and bridge. `show lldp-local-info` covers all LLDP ports; example for an AUX port: `show lldp-local-info-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4`.

No, the egress direction is not supported. `show lldp-neighbor-<lldp-port>/<direction>` shows the LLDP remote system discovered by the lldp-port, and the `direction` key, the direction in which the neighbor was detected, only takes the value ingress. Example: `show -r lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-1-3/ingress`, or `show -r lldp-neighbor-comm-eth-1-11-ETH4/ingress` for an AUX port on a 1830 GX G30. The same restriction applies to `lldp-port-statistics`, whose direction parameter is also ingress only. Neighbor information is kept indefinitely, until the port is decommissioned or the data is manually cleared by the user. Attributes include last-update, age (seconds since discovery), chassis-id-subtype/chassis-id, port-id-subtype/port-id, port-description, system-name, system-description, supported/enabled-capabilities and ttl.

No. All counter values in a particular `lldp-port-statistics` entry are maintained on a continuing basis and are not deleted upon expiration of the TTL timing counters associated with the LLDP neighbor information. All statistical counters associated with a particular port on the local LLDP agent do become frozen whenever `lldp-admin-status` is disabled for that port. Use `show lldp-port-statistics-<lldp-port>/<direction> [last-change-time] [last-clear-time] [total-ageouts] [total-discarded-frames] [error-frames] [total-frames-in] [total-frames-out] [total-discarded-tlvs] [total-unrecognized-tlvs]`; direction is ingress (egress is not supported). total-ageout counts the times a neighbour's information was deleted from the lldp-neighbor list due to TTL timer expiration. All counters default to 0; last-clear-time defaults to 0000-01-01T00:00:00Z.

Use `show nct-connection-<src-port>/<dst-port> [src-chassis] [dst-chassis] [src-chassis-state] [dst-chassis-state]`, which gives NCT connectivity information, the existing links between NCT ports in a multi-chassis NE, dynamically filled in by the system. `src-chassis-state` and `dst-chassis-state` take node controller, provisioned or unprovisioned, so the controller shelf shows as node-controller and shelves not yet accepted show as unprovisioned. src-port and dst-port must be NCT ports: if the port belongs to a commissioned chassis it is the AID of the port, and if it belongs to an unprovisioned chassis it has the format '<chassis-serial-number>-<slot>-NCT-<id>'. Likewise src-chassis and dst-chassis are the chassis AID when commissioned and the chassis serial number when unprovisioned. All are strings 0..64. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

The `sndp` command controls the SNDP feature through a single attribute, `sndp-enabled`, which is a switch with values true or false and a default of true. Use `set sndp [sndp-enabled <value>]` to change it and `show sndp [sndp-enabled]` to view it, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. SNDP is the discovery mechanism behind interface neighbors: `interface-neighbor` `discovery-cycle-time` is described as the periodicity at which sndp discover messages will be sent (30..300 seconds, default 30), and per-interface discovery is separately controlled by `discovery-enabled` (true/false, default true).

`add submarine-link-<name> src-node-id <value> src-port-name <value> dst-node-id <value> dst-port-name <value> degree-target-tx-power <value> [...]`. The mandatory attributes are src-node-id and dst-node-id (the NE names of the source and destination nodes, strings 0..256), src-port-name and dst-port-name (the OTS dwdm-line port of the degree at each endpoint, strings 0..128), and degree-target-tx-power, the target transmit power for the degree, the launch power at the ROADM into the primary fiber link. `fiber-length` defines the fiber length in km of the associated fiber pair ID, a decimal64 in range 0..25000 km with default 0, and it excludes the length of the branch segments. Other attributes: label, src/dst-card-name, fiber-connection-type (two-way default, two-way only for submarine links), link-name, fiber-pair-id, segment-list, bu-segment-index (uint16, default 0), rx/tx-fiber-type, gsnr, degree-expected-rx-power, commissioning-snr-margin, launch-condition (flat-tx or pfib, default pfib) and allocated-spectrum-list (start/end frequency pairs, max 32 elements).

`show supporting-fiber-connection-<name> [fiber-connection-list]` shows the list of fiber connections supporting an entity. `name` is the name of the entity, String 0..64, and `fiber-connection-list` is the supported fiber connection path, an instance-identifier. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. It is the container referenced by cable-id-path: `show -r cable-id-path-<name>` displays the supporting-fiber-connection container and its fiber-connection-list along with all cable-id-path parameters for the port pair, for example output lines 'supporting-fiber-connection-1-6-ade6-1-8-ade6' and 'fiber-connection-list  supporting-fiber-connection-R1'.

Use `clear [-f] topology [target=]<value>` in Operational mode; it manually removes existing topology neighbor information. The target is an instance-identifier (no default) and may be an lldp-neighbor instance discovered via LLDP, a carrier-neighbor instance discovered via ICMP, or an lldp-port-statistics instance holding the details of an LLDP-enabled port. Use 'clear topology <tab>' to list the valid topology objects, and the -f flag to force the command without confirmation. Example: clear topology lldp-neighbor-ethernet-1-4-T1-1. Reading is separate: `show topology` (also allowed in Candidate Configuration mode) takes inci, links, lldp, icdp or sndp.

Run `verify [-f] type-select=fiber-connection [target-select=<port-id>] [allow-switching]` in Operational mode. fiber-connection is currently the only verification type. target-select is the port instance-identifier on the CableID-capable sled; if it is omitted the verification runs on all paths, and if the port is in several CableID paths all of them are checked. allow-switching is boolean, default false: false verifies active paths only with no system-initiated switching (safe while in service); true allows CableID to initiate switching on the OPSM so both active and inactive paths are verified. Pre-condition: the equipment-policies cable-id-control attribute must be enabled. The command prompts for confirmation (-f skips it), is non-blocking, answers 'Verification started. Use show cable-id-status command to obtain latest verification status', and raises the CID-verification-in-progress alarm against the NE until all queued requests complete. Example: verify fiber-connection port-1-6-ade3 allow-switching=true

`bert` runs in Operational mode. Start with e.g. `bert start test-id=TestX resource=ethernet-1-6-T1 test-signal-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-monitoring-type=scrambled-idles test-signal-direction=ingress test-signal-monitoring-direction=ingress test-duration=10`, and stop with `bert stop test-id=TestX`; test-id is mandatory for the stop. test-id is alphanumeric [A-Z][a-z][0-9] and is system generated if you do not supply one. test-signal-type: none (default), PRBS31, PRBS31NONINV, scrambled-idles (100GE/400GE use scrambled-idles, ODU4 uses PRBS31/PRBS31NONINV). test-signal-monitoring-type adds fec-frames for CarrierCTP. Directions are ingress or egress. test-duration is in seconds, min 10 up to 1000 hrs, and 0 (the default) means indefinite. Multiple simultaneous BERTs can run on a facility. Records are read with `bert get` (by test-id, resource or AID) and removed with `bert delete`.

You cannot create one.
