The cid-ptp facility is created by the system when a card supporting the CableID function is created, for example RD20TM or CAD10A, and it represents the CableID SFP and its connection to the card via the CID port. managed-by reports 'system', and only user-created facilities can be user deleted, which is why the command set is just `set cid-ptp-<name> [label <value>] [admin-state <value>]` and `show cid-ptp-<name>` (Operational and Candidate Configuration mode). admin-state is not editable and the only supported value is unlock; CableID operation is not affected by the cid-ptp admin-state. The 'used' attribute is true when CableID functionality is supported, false by default. Example: show cid-ptp-1-4-spcid, or show cid-ptp-1-6-spu for the CAD10A SPU port.

The eth-zr Digital Coherent 400ZR facility is auto-instantiated when the ZR TOM is provisioned; interface-type reads 400ZR (Media-interface 400ZR-CFEC-DP-16QAM) and rate 400.000 Gbit/s. fec-type is settable, default ofec, with permitted values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4 (EFEC-I4), i7 (EFEC-I7), sdfec15 (15% SDFEC-Differential), sdfec15nd (15% SDFEC-Non-Differential), staircase7 (7% HDFEC Staircase) and ufec7 (7% UFEC). Degrade is controlled per alarm: fdd-monitoring and fed-monitoring (enabled/disabled, default disabled) enable FEC Detected Degrade and FEC Excessive Degrade monitoring. fdd-threshold defaults to 0.0195 avg BER and fdd-clear-threshold to 0.01062; fed-threshold defaults to 0.0206 avg BER and fed-clear-threshold to 0.01125. All four are decimal64(9) in the range 0.000000001..0.1 avg BER. link-degrade-indication shows none, local-degraded, remote-degraded or local-and-remote-degraded. Example: set eth-zr-1-6-T8 fed-threshold 0.011870000

The limit is the ethernet facility's max-packet-length attribute, the maximum transfer unit in octets, set with `set ethernet-<name> max-packet-length <value>`. The default is 1518 octets. The range is 1280..18000 octets on the 1830 GX G30 and 1518..18000 octets on the 1830 GX G40, so 18000 octets is the largest frame accepted. Two restrictions apply: max-packet-length is configurable at card level only and applies to all interfaces on that card, and it is used only for determining the undersized/oversized packet count in 100GbE PMs. The attribute is available with both set and show, in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

`show facilities` lists the facilities configured on the node. It takes no parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. The output is a flat list of facility instance names, for example on a 1830 GX G40: super-channel-group-1-4-L1, super-channel-1-4-L1-1, optical-carrier-1-4-L1-1, optical-channel-1-4-L1-1, trib-ptp-1-4-T11, comm-channel-1-4-L1-1, otu-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni, otu-1-4-T11, ethernet-1-4-T2, odu-1-4-L1-1-ODUCni, odu-1-4-L2-1-ODUflexi-1 and so on. Use the per-facility commands (show ethernet-<name>, show odu-<name>, etc.) for the attributes of any individual entry.

The Fibre Channel facility is managed with `set fc-<name>` / `show fc-<name>` in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. The FC-specific read-only attribute is fc-type, with values FC1G, FC2G, FC4G, FC8G, FC16G and FC32G. Two settable attributes are FC-specific to the 32GFC client: tts enables or disables Transmitter Training Signal support (enabled/disabled, default disabled), and laser-toggling-for-tts enables or disables laser toggling when tts is enabled/disabled for the 32GFC client (enabled/disabled, default enabled). The rest of the facility is the common client set: label, admin-state (lock/unlock/maintenance, default unlock), alarm-report-control, tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode (GMP default, plus BMP, openZR+, FlexE-4x100G, GFP-F, GFP-F-extOPU2, AMP, iGMP, none), loopback (none/facility/terminal), loopback-mode, and test-signal-type/direction (default ingress)/monitoring.

The flexo facility reports foic-type, the FOICx.k identification where k parallel lanes carry a FlexO-x interface and order x is the interface rate in units of 100G (G.709.3 FlexO-LR and G.709.1 FlexO-SR). The available types are foic1.2, foic1.4, foic2.4, foic2.8, foic3.6, foic4.8 and foic4.16, with foic4.8 as the default; foic-type is show only, as is fec-type (not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC; default ofec). resource-mode is settable and selects how the FlexO resource is used: ADM for add-drop, or XC for add-drop with regen. The default is ADM. Example: set flexo-1-5-L1-1 resource-mode 'XC'. Other settable attributes are label, admin-state, alarm-report-control, iid and the fdd/fed raise and clear thresholds.

`add flexo-group-<name> carriers <value> rate <value> modulation-format <value> group-id <value>` - name plus those four are the mandatory arguments; label, admin-state, alarm-report-control and fec-type are optional. carriers is the list of carriers bound to the facility, string length 1..32. rate is the carried signal basic rate class in Gbit/s. modulation-format is one of not-applicable, DP-QPSK, DP-16QAM, DP-8QAM, BPSK. group-id indicates the interface group instance the FlexO-x interface belongs to, an integer in the range 1..1048575, and it must be unique in the NE. fec-type defaults to ofec (values not-applicable, cfec, ofec, noFEC, G709, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7, ufec7); admin-state defaults to unlock. The command runs in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode, and `delete flexo-group-<name>` removes it.

`set high-speed-monitoring [enabled <value>] [port <value>]` and `show high-speed-monitoring [enabled] [port]`, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. It has exactly two attributes: enabled is the user configurable switch that turns high speed monitoring on or off, values true or false with a default of false; port is the user configurable port, a uint16 in the range 1..max with a default of 57500. So the command configures whether high speed monitoring runs and which port it uses, nothing else.

The interlaken facility represents the SPN2 Interlaken interface, managed with `set interlaken-<name>` / `show interlaken-<name>` in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Its capacity attribute is the total capacity of the Interlaken interface and is fixed and show only at 500 Gbit/s. The facility is system created (managed-by system), so you can only edit label (string 0..256), admin-state (lock, unlock, maintenance; default unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed, the default, or inhibited) and loopback (none by default, facility to test towards the facility side, terminal to test towards the terminal side). The remaining attributes - supporting-card, supporting-port, supporting-facilities, supported-facilities, AID, oper-state, avail-state - are show only. Example: set interlaken-66-1-8 label interlaken_66_1

On line-ptp, auto-in-service is driven by two attributes usable on add, set and show. auto-in-service-enabled is the auto-in-service switch for the facility, true or false with a default of false. valid-signal-time is the configurable time that represents detection of a valid signal, used by the auto-in-service mechanism, a number in the range 1..7200 minutes with a default of 480. Once the mechanism is running, the show-only remaining-valid-signal-time reports the actual remaining time for the facility to be automatically enabled, in the same 1..7200 minute range. Example output: auto-in-service-enabled false, valid-signal-time 480 minutes, remaining-valid-signal-time 0 minutes. Both are also available on trib-ptp with the same ranges and defaults.

They are different commands. `show network-xconnect` is show only, has no parameters, and lists the services of multiple user cross connections commissioned in this NE; it runs in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. `nw-xconnect` is the configuration command for an individual networking cross-connection: `add nw-xconnect-<name> endpoint1 <value> endpoint2 <value> [xcon-type <value>] [rate <value>]`, plus `set nw-xconnect-<name> [rate <value>]`, `show nw-xconnect-<name>` and `delete nw-xconnect-<name>`. xcon-type is one of L1-ETH-TO-GCC0, L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 (default), L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC, and rate is 1..20 Mbps. So use network-xconnect to view the list and nw-xconnect to create, modify, view or delete a specific cross-connection.

nw-xconnect supports four user channel cross-connection types and there is no GCC-to-OSC combination among them: L1-ETH-TO-GCC0, L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 (the default), L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC. You can therefore bridge GCC0 to GCC0, OSC to OSC, or bring either onto an L1 Ethernet management port. Both endpoints are mandatory on creation. For L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and L1-ETH-TO-OSC endpoint1 is an instance-identifier to a comm-eth MO of a chassis; for L1-GCC0-TO-GCC0 it is a GCC0 comm-channel MO and for L1-OSC-TO-OSC an OSCX-5 comm-channel MO. endpoint2 is a GCC0 comm-channel for the GCC0 types and an OSC-5 comm-channel for the OSC types. rate is 1..20 Mbps, defaulting to 13 for L1-ETH-TO-GCC0 and 20 for L1-ETH-TO-OSC and L1-OSC-TO-OSC. Example: add nw-xconnect-test1 xcon-type L1-ETH-TO-OSC endpoint1 comm-eth-1-16-ETH4 endpoint2 comm-channel-1-6-dwdm-line-OSCX5

No. The high order ODU is automatically created when an SCH is created; when a CHM6 has an OTU configured on it, use `show odu` to determine whether the ODU exists. What you create yourself are the low order ODUs, ODU4i (100G) or ODUflexi (400G), which the XCONs are mapped into. The pre-condition for that is that the super-channel must be added before low order ODUs can be added. Add them with `add odu-<name> odu-type <value>` plus parent-odu pointing at the parent HO-ODU name, and time-slots or opucn-time-slots (opucn-time-slots is optional and derived automatically if omitted). The show-only class attribute reports high-order, low-order (the default) or mapped, and is set by the system based on the order of creation. Example: add odu-1-1 odu-type ODU4i parent-odu '1-7-L1-1-ODUCni' time-slots 1..80

Yes. odu-diagnostics instances are keyed as `odu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction>` where direction is ingress or egress, and each direction has its own values, so you can set a different trace per direction with add, set, show and delete. Under tti-style ITU-T-G709 (the default) the TTI is split and you configure tx-sapi, tx-dapi and tx-operator with expected-sapi, expected-dapi and expected-operator; SAPI and DAPI are 1..15 printable ASCII characters (or a 0x hex string up to 32), operator bytes 1..32 (hex up to 66), all defaulting to "". Under tti-style proprietary the TTI is a single 64 byte string, configured through tx-tti and expected-tti (1..64 ASCII, or 0x hex up to 130). tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting selects the TIM criteria: disabled (default), full-64-bytes, SAPI, DAPI, OPER, SAPI-DAPI, SAPI-OPER, DAPI-OPER or SAPI-DAPI-OPER. Example: set odu-diagnostics-Lodu4i/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPIDAPI-OPER

Yes, FEC is on by default on an OTU. fec-mode, the configured Forward Error Correction mode on the OTUk/OTUCn client, takes enabled or disabled and defaults to enabled. fec-generation-mode, the FEC generation mode towards the far-end receiver, also takes enabled or disabled and defaults to enabled. fec-type defaults to ofec; the permitted values are not-applicable, cfec, ofec, G709, noFEC, i4, i7, sdfec15, sdfec15nd, staircase7 and ufec7. All three are available on add, set and show, in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode, for example `set otu-<name> fec-type ofec`. The related show-only service-mode-qualifier reports nofec when the transported payload carries no FEC.

Set tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting on the otu-diagnostics instance for the direction concerned: `set otu-diagnostics-<name>/<direction> tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI`, where direction is ingress or egress and each direction has its own values. The attribute says whether the TTI-Mismatch (TIM) alarm is reported or masked and, when reported, the criteria used. Values: disabled (the default), full-64-bytes, SAPI, DAPI, OPER, SAPI-DAPI, SAPI-OPER, DAPI-OPER and SAPI-DAPI-OPER. Choosing SAPI alarms only on a mismatched Source Access Point Identifier rather than the whole 64-byte trace. It requires tti-style ITU-T-G709 (the default), which splits the TTI into SAPI, DAPI and OPER bytes and uses expected-sapi/expected-dapi/expected-operator; these are mutually exclusive with the proprietary tx-tti/expected-tti buffer. Example: set otu-diagnostics-1-4-L1-1-OTUCni/ingress tti-mismatch-alarm-reporting SAPI

The stm facility carries the Synchronous Transport Module N signal (reference ITU-T G.691), and its show-only stm-type attribute lists exactly two SDH signal types: STM-16 and STM-64. The facility is managed with `set stm-<name>` / `show stm-<name>` in Operational and Candidate Configuration mode. Settable attributes include label, admin-state (Lock, Unlock, Maintenance; default Unlock), alarm-report-control (allowed by default, or inhibited), tx-mapping-mode and expected-mapping-mode, tti-style (ITU-T-G709 default, or proprietary), tim-monitor (enabled/disabled, default disabled), tx-tti and expected-tti (tti-64), loopback and loopback-mode (none, facility, terminal; default none), and test-signal-type (none by default; PRBS31Q, PRBS13Q, scrambled-idles, PRBS9, PRBS31) with test-signal-direction Ingress. Example: set stm-1-5-T9.2 tx-mapping-mode BMP

That is the trib-ptp tributary-disable-action attribute: it says what the network element does towards the client equipment connected over the TOM when a line-side failure is observed, either shutting off the laser or inserting a replacement signal. The values are laser-shut-off (the default), none, odu-ais, send-ais-1, send-gais, send-idles, send-lf, send-ms-ais, and send-nos for 1830 GX G30 only. tributary-disable-holdoff-timer delays that action at egress, uint16 0..10000 milliseconds with a default of 0 meaning holdoff disabled; it is applicable only when the TDA action is laser-turnoff, the recommendation being to hold the optical signal until the timer expires and only then turn off the laser. near-end-tda (default disabled) and tda-degrade-mode (BERSD-ODU triggering ALS, default disabled) refine it, and forward-defect-trigger (default true) decides whether a received client forward defect flows through to the line side or triggers an egress TDA action. Example: set trib-ptp-1-5-T2 tributary-disable-action laser-shut-off

Create it with `add xcon-<name> source <value> destination <value> [payload-type <value>] [direction <value>] [label <value>] [circuit-id-suffix <value>]` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode; source and destination are the instance IDs of the two end-points. direction supports only two-way, which is also the default. payload-type covers 100GBE, 400GBE, OTU4, 100G, ODU2, ODU2e and empty. Use `set xcon-<name>` for label and circuit-id-suffix, `show xcon-<name>` and `delete xcon-<name>`. protection-type is a show-only attribute reporting the protection this XCON has, with values y-cable, snc-n, snc-i and unprotected, the default being unprotected. Related show-only fields are type (add, drop, add-drop, express), payload-treatment (transport, switching, transport-without-fec, regen, regen-switching) and network-mapping. Example: add xcon-1 source ethernet-1-4-T1 destination odu-1-4-T1-1-ODUni-1

An L2-bridge is identified by bridge-name, a string of length 0..64 that forms the instance name in the command: `set L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name <value>] [description <value>]` and `show L2-bridge-<bridge-name> [chassis-name] [description]`, both available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. There are only two configurable attributes besides the name: chassis-name, a leafref giving the chassis associated with this L2 bridge, and description, a string of length 0..255 describing the bridge and its intended purpose. Neither has a default value.

Use `clear [-f] app [app-name=]<value>`. The clear app command clears third party apps, and app-name identifies the third party app to remove. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation. The command is available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. app-name is the only parameter; the guide states no other values, ranges or defaults for it. To control rather than remove an application, use appctl with commands restart, netls or exec.

Use `appctl [app-name=]<value> [command=]<value> [[target=]<value>] [[parameters=]<value>[,<value>]*]` in Operational or Candidate Configuration mode. app-name is a leafref to the configured third party app (path /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:sw-management/ioa-ne:third-party-app/ioa-ne:app-name). command is one of restart (restarts the third party application), netls (shows the list of subnet networks used by the containers) and exec (executes a third party application operation given in parameters); there is no default. target says whether the command is executed for the entire system or for a chassis/card AID, taking a string or 'system', and defaults to system. parameters holds optional values passed with the command, applicable when command is restart or exec, with a maximum of 50 elements.

Yes. Use the operational-mode `call-home [dial-out-server-name=]<string>` command, which executes a manual connection trigger to a configured dial-out-server. It forces a connection attempt; if the dial-out-server is currently 'connecting', the command forces an immediate attempt and will not wait for some time before retrying. The dial-out-server-name is the pre-configured name of the dial-out server (string, no default). Pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for this command to execute properly. Examples: `call-home collector-x`, `call-home dialoutservername`; `call-home -h` displays help. A dial-out-server with auto-connect false can still be connected manually via the call-home RPC.

Use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` to list configured telemetry subscriptions with their encoding and transfer mode. The `encoding` attribute specifies the data encoding scheme used for data sent to and from the target device (specifiable for all data, or optionally per-RPC if the target supports it); permitted values are json, bytes, proto, ascii and json-ietf, with a default of json-ietf. The `transfer-mode` attribute specifies the data transfer mode to the target device: stream (values streamed by the target), once (values sent once-off by the target), or poll (values sent in response to a poll request); the default is stream. Related attributes include session-protocol (gnmi, default gnmi), session-type (gnmi-dial-in, gnmi-dial-out-tunnel, gnmi-dial-out-reverse-rpc) and updates-only (true/false, default false).

No. The `data-model` commands manage the available YANG data models for loading/unloading, and the `enabled` attribute defaults to false, so models are not all loaded by default. Turn one on with `set data-model-<name> enabled true`; enabled takes true or false, and a loaded data model means it can be used via the management interfaces. Inspect models with `show data-model-<name> [description] [enabled]`, or `show data-model` to view all available YANG data models for loading/unloading. The `name` (model name) and `description` are strings of length 0..256; description is show-only. Both commands are available in Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

A dial-out-server's `retry-policy` is the retry policy after a timeout, with values progressive-back-off, retry-then-stop and retry-forever; the default is progressive-back-off. The `retry` attribute is the number of retries and is only applicable when retry-policy is retry-then-stop: integer range 0..5, default 3. The `timeout` is the time before the next retry, integer range 1..255 seconds, default 10; it is not applicable for progressive-back-off, which has a dynamic timeout. The `port` is the dial-out-server session port, integer range 1..65535, default 4334 (the default for netconf protocol over ssh). Protocol is netconf or restconf, default netconf; transport is ssh. Example: `set dial-out-server-callhome1 retry-policy retry-then-stop port 4889 timeout 200 retry 5`.

Yes, gNMI/gRPC is enabled by default. The `grpc` object's `enabled` attribute takes true or false and defaults to true, and `port` (the port which listens for gNMI access via gRPC where gRPC is enabled) defaults to 50051. Use `show grpc [enabled] [port] [gnmi-get-encoding-granularity]` to view, and `set grpc enabled false` / `set grpc enabled true` to disable or enable it. `gnmi-get-encoding-granularity` configures the granularity of data in gNMI Get responses when encoded with JSON: per-path puts all path data on one Update message, per-object divides the path data into multiple Update messages, one per YANG container/list entry; the default is per-object. The grpc object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted. Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

NETCONF listens on `port` 830 by default; it is the port which listens for NETCONF access via ssh, of type port-number (uint16, range 1..65535). The `hello-timeout` specifies the number of seconds a session may exist before the hello PDU is received/transmitted; a session is dropped if no hello PDU is received/transmitted before that number of seconds elapses. It is a uint16 in the range 1..3600 seconds with a default of 2. Configure with `set netconf [enabled <value>] [port <value>] [hello-timeout <value>]` and inspect with `show netconf`. NETCONF `enabled` defaults to true, and it is not possible to disable NETCONF from within a NETCONF session. Other attributes: annotate-cli-name (default false) and static-info-in-notifs (max 10 elements).

Plain HTTP is available but off by default. The `http-enabled` switch enables or disables RESTCONF HTTP access; values true/false, default false, and RESTCONF HTTP access is not supported in secure mode. `https-enabled` defaults to true and the overall `enabled` switch defaults to true. Ports: `http-port` default 8080 and `https-port` default 8181, both in the range 1..65535. Session lifetime is governed by `cookie-timeout`, the timeout of a cookie based RESTCONF session, range 1..300 minutes with a default of 5; the cookie expiration date is reset every time there is activity on the session. Example: `set restconf cookie-timeout 10`. `show restconf` also displays api-root, the root of the RESTCONF API (string length 0..64).

Use `show snmp [enabled] [port] [snmp-engine-id] [engine-boot-count]`. `snmp-engine-id` is the SNMP EngineID of the NE, a show-only string of length 0..256; the EngineID follows EngineID format 3 defined in RFC3411, and the MAC address in the Engine ID is the first MAC address of the MAC addresses Pool of the NE. `engine-boot-count` is the SNMP engine boot count, a uint16 that counts how many times the engine has restarted, default 0; it is also show-only. The settable attributes are `enabled` (true/false, default true, global SNMP access) and `port`, the port where the NE is listening for SNMP requests, range 1..65535, default 161, via `set snmp [enabled <value>] [port <value>]`. Note the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object.

No. The `snmp-community` attribute `community-string-access` is the SNMP access right of this community string, and read-only is its only permitted value as well as its default, so read-write communities cannot be created. Add one with `add snmp-community-<name> community-string <value> [enabled <value>] [community-string-access <value>]`, for example `add snmp-community-mycommunity community-string public community-string-access read-only enabled true`. `name` is the name for the community, different from the community string itself (string length 0..64); `community-string` is a string of length 1..32; `enabled` takes false/true and defaults to true. Use set/show/delete on the same object. Note the trap-community-string is located in the snmp-target object.

Trap listeners are SNMP targets: `add snmp-target-<target-name> snmpv3-user <value> target-address <value> [enabled <value>] [snmp-version <value>] [trap-community-string <value>] [target-port <value>] [target-transport <value>]`. `snmp-version` takes v2c or v3 and defaults to v2c. `trap-community-string` is the community string used for SNMP traps, a string of 0..32 characters, defaulting to infinera. `target-port` is the UDP port number, range 0..65535, default 162, and `target-transport` is udp (default udp). `target-name` is the target listener name (string 0..32); `target-address` is the IPv4/IPv6 address or hostname of the target; `enabled` defaults to true. `snmpv3-user` applies when snmp-version is v3.

A new SNMPv3 user gets `user-sec-level` no-auth-no-priv by default; the permitted values are auth-no-priv, auth-priv and no-auth-no-priv. The privacy algorithms available through `priv-protocol` are DES, AES128, AES192 and AES256, with AES128 as the default. `auth-protocol` has SHA as its only value and default. Create with `add snmpv3-user-<snmpv3-user-name> auth-passphrase <value> priv-passphrase <value> [user-sec-level <value>] [auth-protocol <value>] [priv-protocol <value>]`; auth-passphrase and priv-passphrase are mandatory strings of length 8...64 and the user name is a string of length 1...32. Example: `add snmpv3-user-bob user-sec-level auth-priv auth-protocol SHA auth-passphrase public123 priv-protocol AES128 priv-passphrase private123`.

The `subscription-path-mode` attribute of subscription-path controls how subscription updates are sent: target-defined, on-change or sample, with target-defined as the default. View it with `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name> [subscription-path] [subscription-path-origin] [subscription-path-mode] [sample-interval] [heartbeat-interval] [suppress-redundant]`. `sample-interval` is the time in milliseconds between samples of a telemetry data source (default 0, set to 0 when optional); for a target-defined stream subscription with sample-interval unset, the system automatically adjusts it from 0 to 10 seconds. `heartbeat-interval` (ms, default 0) is the maximum interval that may pass between updates; for a target-defined stream subscription with sample-interval unset and heartbeat-interval below 10 seconds, the system adjusts it to 20 seconds. `suppress-redundant` defaults to true.

Use `show subscriptions`, which shows a list of subscriptions. It takes no command parameters and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. For the configured telemetry subscriptions with their detail, use `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>`, which shows a list representation of the telemetry subscriptions configured in the system, with attributes such as related-session-id, related-dial-out-server, session-type, session-protocol, encoding, transfer-mode, updates-only and user-access. For the individual paths within a subscription, use `show subscription-path` or `show subscription-path-<subscription-name>/<subscription-path-name>`.

Telemetry is configured through the `telemetry` object, which is used to configure persistent and dynamic telemetry. The syntax is `show telemetry` and `set telemetry id <string>`; `id` is described as persistent and dynamic telemetry and is a string of length 0..4096, with no default. The object is managed by the system and cannot be manually deleted, and the commands are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Example: `show telemetry` views the telemetry subscription. Related views are `show subscriptions`, `show current-subscription-<subscription-name>` for configured subscriptions, and `show subscription-path` for the paths, sample-interval and heartbeat-interval of each subscription.

Use `show third-party-app-<app-name> [version] [vendor] [product] [label] [state] [information] [enable]`, or `show third-party-app-info-<location-id>/<app-name> [version] [state] [information]`. The `state` attribute is the third party app state with values running, stopped or failed, defaulting to stopped. The `enable` attribute is the third-party-app enabled state and defaults to false, so an app is not enabled by default; if enabled the app is started (and is also enabled upon system restart), and if disabled the app is stopped. Set with `set third-party-app-<app-name> [state <value>] [enable <value>] ...`. Other attributes: version (string 0..64), vendor (string 0..64), product (string 0..256), information (string 0..1024). Access: Operational and Candidate Configuration mode.

Use `add <tab>` to visualize all entity types that are creatable at that time; the add command page also lists the creatable entities (aaa-server, access-rule, ace, acl, adg, card, chassis, dial-out-server, interface, otu, snmp-community, snmp-target, snmpv3-user, tom, user, xcon and many more), each with a page reference to its own command section where its parameters and defaults are documented. Some entities have mandatory attributes that must be provided upon creation; if a mandatory attribute is not given in the command itself, the CLI automatically asks for it. Syntax is `add [-v|-m|-f] <entity id> [(<attribute> <value>) ...]`; -v validates only, -m merges (best effort add), -f forces without confirmation. Entities managed by the system cannot be created using `add`.

Yes, by default. In all cases the `clear` command requires a user confirmation, and a confirmation prompt is displayed if the -f flag is not provided. The -f flag forces the command without confirmation, which is why the syntax is written `clear [-f] <subcommand> ...`. `clear` runs in Operational Mode and each sub command handles a specific type of clear operation: alarm, app, certificate, crl, database, dns, file, isk, log, ospf, pm, recover-mode, statistics, system and topology. `clear -h` displays help. Note that `clear system factory-reset` with the `shutdown` option is not supported on the L0 cards.

Yes. Use `set cli show-alarm-columns <value>`, which selects the columns to display in the output of the 'show alarm' CLI command. Permitted values are a list of columns separated by a comma ',', `default-columns` to show the pre-defined columns, or `default-columns,<additional-details>` to show the <additional-details> column in addition to the pre-defined columns. The default is default-columns. This configuration has a global effect: it takes effect on all CLI sessions. Examples: `set cli show-alarm-columns col1,col2,col3` and `set cli show-alarm-columns default-columns,corrective-action`. View with `show cli [enabled] [port] [script-dir] [default-interactive-mode] [show-alarm-columns]`; the cli port defaults to 22.

Use `set cli-session-config-<session-id> cli-lines <value>`. `cli-lines` is the configurable number of rows to be used for display before pausing the output, range 10..1000, default 40; after pausing, pressing [SPACEBAR] resumes the display. The companion `cli-columns` is the configurable number of columns to be used for display, range 80..4000, default 80. View with `show cli-session-config-<session-id> [cli-lines] [cli-columns] [interactive-mode] [display-timestamp]`. Examples: `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-lines 30` and `set cli-session-config-10.19.204.27:52361 cli-columns 100`. The same object carries interactive-mode (true/false, default true, per session and not persistent) and display-timestamp (default false).

Yes. The `connect` command establishes an ssh session directly from the CLI: `connect [target-address=]<value> [user-name=]<value> [[port=]<value>]`. `target-address` may be an IPv4 address, IPv6 address or hostname (if DNS is configured); it requires connectivity and is a mandatory attribute. `user-name` is a string of 0..64 characters. `port` is optional: by default port 22 is used, but it can be provided if needed, which is useful to access the shell port. Access mode is Operational Mode. Example: `connect 10.41.24.55 admin port=8022`, which then prompts for the target user's password after adding the host to the list of known hosts.

Yes, use `convert [target-representation=]<value> [command=]<value>`. Target representations are netconf-xml (an entire NETCONF xml payload), netconf-python (Python code performing a NETCONF request), restconf-json (HTTP method, URI, headers and body with JSON payloads), restconf-xml (same with XML payloads), restconf-python, plaintext-to-encrypted, snmp-oids (OIDs for the objects in a 'show' command) and netsnmp-cmd (a shell command performing an SNMP request). The command should be enclosed in quotes; multiple CLI commands separated by ';' are merged into a single payload where possible. Generated Python works with Python 2 or 3 and needs ncclient for NETCONF or requests for RESTCONF; host, IP and user-name are auto filled, only the password must be entered. Example: `convert restconf-python 'ping 1.23.151.23'`.

No. The `default` command assigns default value(s) to the targeted entities, useful to reset an entity after changes, but some configuration attributes will not be reset to default, including mandatory parameters and attributes only settable at creation. If attributes are specified only those are set to their default value; otherwise all possible configuration attributes are defaulted. Syntax: `default [-f] [entity-id=][,]* [[attribute=][,]*]`, where -f forces the command without confirmation and -h displays help. Multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*), for example `default alarm-severity-entry-FAN/*` or `default alarm-severity-entry-*`. Example with attributes: `default tom-1-4-T16 label,phy-mode`. The default command is not supported in 1830 GX G30 Releases 5.0 and 5.1.

Use the -b flag: `delete -b <object>`. Starting from R9.0, `delete` with -b introduces the best effort delete feature that only bypasses the check for object existence without returning a failure, so it displays no error even if the object does not exist; standard `delete <object>` fails if the object does not exist. `delete -b` has the same functionality as a NETCONF 'remove' operation. Note that -b does not raise an error if the specified object is missing, but it may still produce other errors, such as precondition failures. Full syntax is `delete [-f|-v|-b] <entity-id> [<filter> ...]`; -f forces the command without confirmation (a confirmation prompt is otherwise displayed), and -v validates only, replying 'OK' if valid.

`exit` logs you out of the current CLI mode: it terminates the current CLI session if you are in operational mode, or leaves configuration mode if you are in candidate mode. A confirmation prompt is displayed unless the -f flag is provided, which forces the command without confirmation. The syntax is `exit [-h|-f]`, where -h displays help for the command. The keyboard shortcut Ctrl+D has the same effect as `exit -f`, that is, it exits immediately without a confirmation prompt. The command is available in both Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode. Example: `exit -f`.

Use `expect [-r] [<instance>=]<value> [<expected-value>=]<value> [<attribute>=]<value>`, which validates an existing attribute value against an expected value. If the value matches, no output is seen; if it does not, an ERROR message is shown. It is intended for scripts and other automation to guarantee specific assumptions, and can be invoked multiple times to validate multiple attributes; a common application is validating system details at the start of a script. If the script runs in 'stop-on-error' mode, a failed `expect` stops the script immediately. Wildcards to select multiple object instances or attributes are not supported. The -r flag enables regex mode, making expected-value a regular expression instead of a literal string. Examples: `expect ne ne-name GX-NE-123` and `expect -r software-load-active swload-version R5.*`.

Yes, use the export command. Syntax: export [-h] and export [<variable>=[<value>]]. Variables are referenced with ${variable} in any CLI command. The variable name can be any alphanumeric name; the value can be any supported character, including spaces. Variables are locally defined per session, so they are removed after the session is closed and do not survive logout. This is particularly useful in CLI scripts. 'export SLOT_NUMBER=2' declares a variable, 'export SLOT_NUMBER=' deletes it, and 'export' with no argument views all existing variables (output such as export MYSESSIONID='10.100.152.29:56154' and export MYUSERNAME='admin'). Access Mode: Operational Mode and Candidate Configuration Mode.

shell launches a Linux bash shell from within the CLI on the node itself, running as the currently logged in user and allowing only commands accessible to that user; syntax shell [-h] [shell command]. gshell launches a Linux bash shell inside a Guest Container; syntax gshell [-h] [<cmd>]. Both allow execution of a single command instead of an interactive shell, and both return to the CLI prompt when closed the typical way (for example with 'exit'). gshell has a stated pre-condition: the dial-out server must be configured for the command to execute properly. Both are Operational Mode and access is limited to the NA, NE and TT user-groups. Only shell documents elevated execution via a 'sudo' prefix. Examples: gshell ls -l; shell ifconfig.

No. kill-session closes any established session regardless of type (CLI, NETCONF, etc), but the <session-id> cannot match the id of the current session; a normal 'exit' command should be used instead to end your own session. Syntax: kill-session <session-id>, where session-id is an existing id in the form '<ip-address>:<port>'. Use the show session command to display the list of current sessions first. Access Mode: Operational mode, and execution is restricted to the SA user-group. Example: kill-session 10.24.11.25:56212.

Use the message command, which sends a message to other CLI sessions. Syntax: message [message-content=]<value> [[target=]<value>]. message-content is the message text to broadcast, a string of 1-4096 characters. target selects the CLI sessions that receive it: all (all CLI sessions, the default), local (only local sessions, that is serial console or CRAFT), remote (only remote sessions, for example SSH), session-id (only a specific session), or username (all CLI sessions of a specific user). By default the message is broadcast to all CLI sessions. The command can also be executed from NETCONF and RESTCONF, but the message is only sent to CLI sessions. Access Mode: Operational mode. Example: message 'System will reboot in 5 minutes'.

The property commands set or show a type specific property that is auto instantiated by the system but configurable by the user. Syntax: show property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value] [description] and set property-<card-name>/<property-name> [value <value>]. Two property-name values are supported: fast-client-recovery, which indicates if fast client signal recovery is enabled or disabled in case of client signal failures, with values disabled or enabled and default disabled; and max-packet-length, which indicates the maximum packet length supported by the CHM6 / CHM6L DCO, with a range of 1518 to 18000 and default 1518. card-name is the name of the card the property applies to. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Example: set property-1-5/fast-client-recovery value enabled.

Use the run command. Syntax: run task [[task-name=]<value>] and run script [-q] [-y] [-e=<value>] [-r] [[script-name=]<value>] [[arguments=]<value>]. Pre-condition: the task or the script to be called must already be defined. task-name is a leafref to /ioa-ne:ne/ioa-ne:system/ioa-ne:scheduled-tasks/ioa-ne:task/ioa-ne:name. script-name is a relative path to the script directory, and arguments are optional arguments to the script. Flags: -q executes the script in quiet mode showing only command output, -r executes the script as a declarative config script, replacing system configuration with the content of the script, and -e sets the error option with continue (default), stop, or rollback. Access Mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode. Examples: run task collect-diag; run script config.cli -e=stop -q.

Both add, set, show and delete user-configurable scheduled commands, and both support single-occurrence and periodic tasks. task uses add task-<name> command <value> [enabled] [label] [alarm-report-control] [command-type] [frequency] [number-of-runs] [start-time] [end-time] [persistent], with show task-<name> also exposing task-status (scheduled, disabled, finished, ongoing), next-run, previous-run, previous-result (success, fail) and previous-output; name is 0..64 characters, command 1..1024, number-of-runs is no-limit or 1..65535, persistent and enabled default true, alarm-report-control defaults to allowed. scheduled-task addresses the same objects through the scheduled-tasks container: add/set scheduled-task-<name>, show scheduled-tasks, delete scheduled-task-<name>, with enabled, command (0...1024), command-type, frequency, start-time, end-time and persistent, but no label, alarm-report-control or number-of-runs, and timestamps in YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ.

Only if you are an SA user. The session command shows the list of currently established management layer sessions, and only SA users can access the list of all sessions; remaining users can only see their own session. Syntax: show session-<session-id> [session-user] [session-type] [session-protocol] [created-time] [local-ip-address] [dial-out-server-name]. session-id is the IP address and transport layer port number of the session, or 'NA' if the session was initiated from the serial port. session-type values are cli, snmp, netconf, restconf, webgui and gnmi; session-protocol values are telnet, telnet-raw, serial, ssh, ssh-raw, https and http. RESTCONF sessions are visible in CLI only when using Cookie Based Authentication; the keep-alive defaults to 5 minutes and is changed with the restconf cookie-timeout attribute. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes. set assigns values to attributes of existing managed entities and it is possible to set an attribute in multiple instances simultaneously by using wildcards (*): as replacement of the whole instance key (card-*), as replacement of a single instance key (port-1-4-*, port-1-*-3), as replacement of all following keys to the right (odu-1-4,5,6,7-*), for auto-completing instance keys (user-admin*, ethernet-*) and for auto-completing attribute names (admin* instead of admin-state). Brackets represent ranges (card-1-[1..4]) or lists (interface-[DCN,CRAFT]). Syntax: set [-f|-v] [<entity id>] <attribute> <value> [<attribute> <value> ...] [<filter> ...]; one or more filters (<attribute>=<value>) affect only matching entities, and all attribute-value pairs must belong to the same managed entity. -v validates, -f forces without confirmation. The command asks for confirmation when the request may have traffic impact or is implicitly affecting multiple instances. Examples: set port-1-4* admin-state lock; set port port-type=line admin-state lock.

User access to the shell command can be limited to users in the NA, NE and TT user-groups; the same applies to gshell. The shell is launched using the currently logged in user and allows only the commands accessible to that user. Syntax: shell [-h] [shell command]; Access Mode: Operational Mode. Certain commands or scripts can be launched with elevated privileges by prefixing the command with 'sudo', and the permitted set is /bin/ping, /sbin/reboot, /sbin/shutdown, /bin/netstat, /bin/df, /usr/bin/du, /sbin/dhclient, and the scripts /opt/infinera/thanos/local/bin/clear_downloads.sh, config_dns.sh, config_ip.sh, download.sh, install_os.sh, show_dns.sh, show_downloads.sh, show_ip.sh, show_route.sh, tunnelctl.sh, install_app.sh, remove_app.sh, CopyLogsToUSB.sh and docker.sh. Example: shell 'sudo netstat -alnp | grep sshd'.

Yes. If a user executes a show command which generates more than 50000 objects, an error message is displayed to indicate that the output is too large. Narrow the request rather than dumping everything: give a specific <entity-id> or <entity-type>, use filters (<attribute>=<value>), limit recursion with -r=<n> (full recursion if n is not provided), or restrict the content with -c (container instances only), -a (attributes only), -x (configuration/read-write attributes only) or -o (state/read-only attributes only). Wildcards such as card-* and ranges such as card-1-[1..4] also scope the request. For long but permitted output, page it with the more piped command, for example show -r | more. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode.

Yes, with the simulate command, which triggers simulated events in the system (alarms, equipment, etc). Syntax: simulate [trigger=]<value> ([holder-AID=]<value> [type=]<value> [[subtype=]<value>] | [alarmed-entity=]<value> [alarm-type=]<value> [[alarm-direction=]<value>] [[alarm-location=]<value>]). trigger values are raise-alarm, clear-alarm, plug-in-fru and plug-out-fru; note that plug-out-fru is not supported. For equipment simulation, holder-AID is the AID of the equipment holder (slot or port), a string of 1..64, and for plugin the card/tom type must be provided while subtype is optional. For alarms, alarmed-entity and alarm-type identify the alarm, and if either is omitted when clearing, all simulated alarms are cleared; alarm-direction and alarm-location default to auto. The command works in a simulator and on a real system, but a simulation cannot be done if it interferes with real hardware, for example plugging out hardware that is physically present. Access Mode: Operational mode. Example: simulate plug-in-fru 1-5.

Yes. The sleep command specifies a delay for a specified amount of time, and the sleep time may be an arbitrary floating point number. Syntax: sleep -h and sleep <time in seconds>, where the parameter is the duration of the delay in seconds. Access Mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode, and -h displays help for the command. The documented examples are 'sleep 1' to set a delay of 1 second and 'sleep 0.1' to set a delay of 100 milliseconds, so sub-second pauses are supported directly. This is the command to use for pacing steps inside a CLI script, for example between a provisioning command and the show command that checks its result.

Use add task-<name> with a command and a start-time, and leave frequency unset, since frequency is what makes a task periodic. Syntax: add task-<name> command <value> [enabled <value>] [label <value>] [alarm-report-control <value>] [command-type <value>] [frequency <value>] [number-of-runs <value>] [start-time <value>] [end-time <value>] [persistent <value>]. name is 0..64 characters, command is 1..1024 characters, command-type is cli by default, enabled and persistent default to true (persistent means the task survives a system restart), alarm-report-control defaults to allowed. The documented example is: add task-db_backup_once command 'upload database file-server=xfr1' start-time 2021-04-23T05:05:00+00:00 alarm-report-control allowed label 'DB Backup once'. The file server xfr1 must be configured before this command is used. After it runs, show task-<name> reports task-status finished, plus previous-run, previous-result (success or fail) and previous-output.

The terminate command stops a running operation. Syntax: terminate location-led <entity>, terminate otdr [entity=]<value>, terminate otdr-fiber-check [entity=]<value>, terminate loopback [entity=]<value> [, <value>]*, and terminate cable-id. location-led stops a location led test previously started by the activate command on a chassis or a card; invoking it when no test is active has no effect. otdr stops an ongoing OTDR measurement on the given port. otdr-fiber-check stops an ongoing manually triggered OTDR based Raman fiber check on an OTS-R entity; the scan is aborted abruptly, logs and available result files are saved, and ots-r-auto-otdr auto-otdr-state reverts to its previous state. loopback terminates WSS loopback for an NMC entity, and all channels under the loopback in a degree must be terminated. cable-id stops the CableID verification test, which finishes the current port-pair first, so the maximum delay is one port-pair verification time. Confirm with show cable-id cable-id-status: the test has stopped once cable-id-state is idle. Access Mode: Operational Mode.

update performs a specific, type-driven update of object attributes rather than assigning a value you supply, which is what set does. Syntax: update [type=]<value> [[entity-id=]<value>[,<value>]*], and multiple instances can be selected with the wildcard (*). The supported type values are span-loss-alarm-threshold, which updates the OTS attribute span-loss-alarm-threshold; filter-insertion-date-now, which updates the chassis dust filter insertion date to the current date; set-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to the under commissioning state, applicable to NE entities in SLTE systems; and clear-under-commissioning, which sets the entity to the Ready for Service state, also for SLTE NE entities. entity-id gives the instance or instances for the required update. Access Mode: Operational mode. Examples: update span-loss-alarm-threshold ots-1-1-dwdm-line; update filter-insertion-date-now chassis.

Use the tic and toc auxiliary commands. tic starts a timer in seconds for the typed command, and toc displays the elapsed time since the timer was started and the command was executed by the system. Put them either side of the command on one line, separating commands with ';'. For a single command: tic;show log;toc. For a list of commands (a script): tic ;show log ;traceroute 10.128.1.1 ;toc. These are auxiliary commands, add-ons to the main commands, provided as an aid for evaluating the system response to a command or script.

Yes, use help -s. Syntax: help -s <keyword> [<keyword> ...]. It searches the provided keywords in all commands help text and displays the matches in order of relevance. Multiple keywords can be provided, and the result includes matches of commands that include either keyword. Partial keywords can be provided using a wildcard, for example help -s data* to search for any word starting with data. Results appear as a list of help commands that can be used to view the entire help text, and each result includes an excerpt of the help text with the target keyword underlined. Note that the search capability only provides matches in the scope of commands and system features; object and attribute matches are excluded. Examples: help -s inventory; help -s statistics; help -s *config*; help -s database 'cold restart'.

Yes to both: aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions. The alias command defines a more user-friendly alphanumeric string for one or more commands, containers, attributes or values. Syntax: alias [-h] and alias [<name>=<value>]. alias with no arguments prints the current list of aliases in the form 'name=value'. Quotes must be used for multi word values, aliases can reference other aliases, and the <name> of an alias can be used without resolving it by using quotes. Aliases are removed with the unalias command. Access Mode: Operational mode. Examples: alias s=show for a single word alias, and alias sa='show alarm' for a multi word alias.

Use unalias -a, which removes all alias definitions. Syntax: unalias -h, unalias -a, and unalias [<name> ...] to remove named aliases. Removing an alias has impact on all sessions and users, since aliases are persistent and shared among all users and CLI sessions, so unalias -a clears them for everyone, not just your session. The command is always successful unless a supplied <name> is not a defined alias. Aliases can be added and visualized using the alias command. Access Mode: Operational Mode. Examples: unalias foo; unalias bar baz qux; unalias -a.

Use the tree command flags. Syntax: tree [-h] and tree [-a|-o|-d=depth] ([<entity id> ...]). -d=depth sets the maximum display depth of the tree, specifying the number of levels to be displayed; if not specified, all levels are displayed by default, up to max depth. -a displays entity ancestors only, that is only the target entity along with all its ancestors, which gives you just the path down to one entity. -o displays a tree based on a YANG top node. The base of the tree is the current working entity or the provided entity id, only managed entities are shown including all existing instances, no attribute names or values are shown, and output uses the UTF-8 character set. You can also page it with | more. Access Mode: Operational mode, Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: tree -d=2; tree -a interface-DCN; tree card-1-1; tree | more.

edit navigates to any entity in the managed entity hierarchy: edit [-h] and edit <entity-id> [<entity-id> ...]. The entity IDs can be absolute, starting from the root of the system, or relative to the current entity shown in the path banner, and an attempt to edit a nonexistent entity instance will fail. up brings the current path up by one level, changing the selected entity to its parent; syntax up [-h], and it supports no other parameters. top brings the current path to the top of the managed entity hierarchy, [ne], in one step; syntax top [-h]. The effect of all three is visible on the CLI banner, and all three are available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Examples: edit card-1-5 gives [ card-1-5 ], up gives [ equipment ], up again gives [ ne ]; edit chassis-1 slot-2 shows relative addressing.

Use the history command, which displays the current session's command history as a numbered list. Syntax: history [-h]. Each command can be repeated using '!<n>', where n is the number in the history list, and '!!' repeats the previous command; press [ENTER] after either. The [UpArrow] and [DownArrow] keys cycle through the command history buffer in ascending and descending order. The history buffer is associated with a given CLI session, and history information is lost once a user logs out of the CLI session. You can filter history with piped commands, for example history | include 'show'. Access Mode: Operational Mode, Candidate Configuration Mode.

Nothing happens: at the hierarchy top level, the up command has no impact. up brings the current path up by one path level in the managed entity hierarchy, changing the currently selected managed entity to its parent level, and its effect is visible on the CLI banner; at the root [ne] there is no parent, so the banner stays at [ ne ]. The command does not support any parameters other than -h for help, and is available in Operational mode and Candidate Configuration mode. Related commands are edit, which navigates to any entity in the hierarchy, and top, which navigates to the top of the hierarchy root.

They do the same filtering job: both only display lines matching <filter>, and the guide states each is the same as the other. The difference is that, unlike include, grep has several additional filtering options: -a=<n> shows n lines of context after the actual match, -b=<n> shows n lines of context before the actual match, and -n displays line numbers in the result. Syntax: <command> | grep [<option>] <filter> versus <command> | include <filter>. For both, the filter may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed by quotes, supports regex, does a case insensitive comparison (show | grep abc equals show | grep ABC), and multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. Related filters are exclude, begin and until. Examples: show | include ne; tree | grep '1-.-T[4-8]'.

Yes. Pipe the output through the `display` piped command using the `commands` mode: `<command> | display <mode>`. The `commands` mode displays the configurations as CLI 'set' and 'add' commands, and it is specifically useful for creating CLI scripts from the current configuration. To capture the whole configuration, use a recursive show: `show -r | display commands`. The other supported `display` modes for the show command are list (the default display mode, one value per line), table (rows are instances, columns are attributes), csv (comma separated values, useful for pasting into a spreadsheet), keys-table (like table but instance representation is split per individual keys), single-table (like table but merges all tables into one, useful when retrieving the same data in multiple entities), only-values (only the value of the requested attributes, useful for script building), xml (similar to NETCONF responses), json (similar to RESTCONF response), xpath, and interactive (JSON in the 'jless' interactive viewer; use 'q' or CTRL-C to leave, ':help' for help). `<command> | display -h` displays help.

Yes. Combine the `begin` and `until` piped commands, which are explicitly designed to be used together to retrieve a sub-set of an output. `begin` displays the output of the previous command starting from a specified word, and the output begins with the line that matches the word: `<command> | begin <words>`. `until` displays the output of the previous command ending at a specified word, and the output ends with the line that matches the word: `<command> | until <words>`. For both, the `<words>` parameter is the line to begin with / end with, and it may contain spaces if enclosed in quotes. Each also accepts `-h` (`<command> | begin -h`, `<command> | until -h`) to display help for that command. Examples: `show | begin ne-location` starts the system information at the line containing ne-location, and `show | until ne-location` ends the output at that line.

Yes, and the position matters. The `more` piped command displays long outputs incrementally, page by page: `<command> | more [-h]`, where `-h` displays help and `<command>` is any display command such as tree or show. Multiple piped commands can be used sequentially, but `more` needs to be the last one in the command line. Example of paging a filtered listing: `tree | include led | more`; paging a recursive show: `show -r | more`. The page size matches exactly the size of the CLI session window, so it is tied to the terminal size, except for the serial port case where the terminal size is fixed. When the page limit is reached the display is paused; press any key to resume, or [CTRL]+[C] to terminate the display and return to the prompt. <enter> shows the next line, while any other key (including <space>, <tab>, etc.) shows the next page.

It does not fail. With the `sort` piped command, if an unrecognized attribute name is used it is simply ignored. Syntax: `<show command> | sort [-h]` and `<show command> | sort [-i] [<attribute>*]`. `<attribute>` is any attribute name that exists in the context of the output, and a list of attributes can be provided as parameters for sorting. `sort` without parameters displays the output sorted by object instance, the same as the default display (`show card | sort` is the same as `show card` alone). To flip the order, use `-i`, which inverts the order in the output and can be used on its own or together with an attribute list. Examples: `show port | sort port-type`; `show user | sort -i user-group last-login-date` sorts users by user-group then last-login-date, inverted; `show odu | sort -i` shows odus in inverted order. `-h` displays help.

Capitalisation does not matter, and yes, you can give a pattern. The `exclude` piped command filters out the output that contains a defined word or string, i.e. it excludes lines with `<filter>` from the output. Syntax: `<command> | exclude <filter>` (and `<command> | exclude -h` for help), where `<command>` is any normal command that generates output. The `<filter>` does a case insensitive comparison, so `show | exclude abc` and `show | exclude ABC` are equivalent. The filter supports regex (regular expressions), and it may be multiple words separated by spaces if enclosed by quotes, for example `show | exclude 'ne oper'`. Multiple piped commands can be used in a single command. Examples: `show | exclude ne`; `show led | exclude status` displays all leds excluding status leds. Related commands: `include` and `grep`, which filter the output that includes the filtering text.

Use the `highlight` piped command, which visually marks up a word or set of words in the output of the previous command. Syntax: `<command> | highlight <word> [<word>]`, plus `<command> | highlight -h` for help. `<command>` is any normal command that generates output, and `<word>` is any word to highlight; it may contain spaces if enclosed by quotes. More than one word can be provided: without quotes the words are searched for separately, while within quotes they are searched for as a sentence. So to mark a whole phrase, quote it. Examples: `show odu | highlight odu4` highlights the word odu4; `show odu | highlight odu4 oduflex` highlights the two words odu4 and oduflex separately; `show odu | highlight 'idle lower-layer-down' odu4` highlights the sequence of words 'idle lower-layer-down' and the word odu4.

Yes. The `linenum` piped command adds line numbers to the output of the previous command. Syntax: `<command> | linenum`, or `<command> | linenum -h` to display help for the command. It takes no other parameters: `-h` displays help, and `<command>` is any display command such as tree or show. Example: `show | linenum` displays the output with enumerated lines. If you only want numbers on matched lines of a filtered output, the `grep` piped command has an `-n` option that displays line numbers in the result, alongside `-a=<n>` (number of lines of context to show after the actual match) and `-b=<n>` (number of lines of context to show before the actual match).
